JURISDICTION OF CALIFORNIA.
SIXTY-FIRST ANNUAL COMMUNICATION.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the Jurisdiction of California commenced
its Sixty-first Annual Communication at Golden Gate Hall,
in the city of San Francisco, on Tuesday, the 11th day of
October, A. L. 5910, at 10 o'clock A. M.

The Grand Master filled the vacant stations and places
by the 'following appointments: M.'. W .'. George M.
Perine, Deputy Grand Master; R . ·. W. ·. William P. Filmer, Senior Grand Warden; w.·. Edward B. Spencer,
Junior Grand Warden; W.'. 'l'heodore J. Milliken, Senior
Grand Deacon ; W ,'. Mark Levy, Junior Grand Steward.
There being a Constitutional repre~entation, the Grand
Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with music by the
Grand Organist, assisted by a quartette, who sang the "Te
Deum," followed by a prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master then read the Annual Address of
the late Grand Master, written shortly before his death
(being his last official act) , as follows :
BRl!THREN oF THI! GRAND LoDGI! :
In accordance with the requirements of our Constitution, the
following written message is presented setting forth the official acts
of the Grand Master during the year, exhibiting th~ general condition
of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and recommending such legislation as seems expedient for the welfare of the Craft.
It is our privilege at this time to contemplate the result of full
three score years of untiring effort by those who have labored faithfully for Masonry and this Grand Lodge. Our predecessors have
been sowing that we might reap. With hearts filled with gratitude to
our Heavenly Father, who in his Infinite Beneficence, has granted
us another year of almost unparalleled prosperity, we welcome you to
the Sixty-first Annual Communicat.i on of the Grand Lodge.
While we rejoice in this ptosperous condition let us pause for a
moment to pay a last sad tribute to those who have fallen in our
midst.
The ranks of our own Grand Officers and Past Grand Officers remain complete with one exception.
R . ·, W. ·. John Quincy Adams, Past Deputy Grand Master, has
been taken from us after a life of usefulness. He served · this
Grand Lodge as Junior Grand Warden in 1879, Senior Grand Warden ·
in 1880, and Deputy Grand Master in 1881. We will indeed feel his
loss and it is recommended that a committee be appointed to prepare
a suitable tribute to his memory.

KtY WtST DISASTER.
Under the resolution passed by the Grand Lodge at its last Annual Communication relative to sufferers' from the hurricane which
devastated Key West, the draft of the Grand Master of Florida for
$500 was honored November 14, 1909, and the Grand Lodge of Florida,
in its Eighty-first Grand Communication assembled, tendered to this
Grand Lodge its heartfelt thanks for the prompt donation, and transmitted a copy of the resolution which is herewith submitted :
"To THt M:. w:. GRAND LoDGt oF FLORIDA :
The Special Committee to whom was referred that part of the
address of the Most Worshipful Grand Master relating to the aid
given to the sufferers in the Key West storm by the Most Worshipful
Grand Master and the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of the State
of California beg to submit the following resolution, and recommend
its adoption :
"WHERtAS, Our Island City of Key West was on the 11th of
last October s~ept by a disastrous hurricane which left in its wake a
trail of devastation, destitution, suffering and sorrow ; and
"WHERtAs, Immediately upon hearing of the distress, the Most
Worshipful Grand Master of California, Oscar Lawler, wired his
sympathy to our Most Worshipful Grand Master, at the same time
authorizing our Most Worshipful Grand Master to draw on the Grand

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Secretary of the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California for the sum of
$500 to relieve the suffering of the Craft at Key West, which generous
offer· of aid was received and ·accepted at a time when it was sorely
needed; therefore be it
"Rl!SOI.VltD; That the M .'. W .'. Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Florida
in its Eighty-first Grand Communication assembled does hereby tender
to Most Worshipful Brother Oscar Lawler, and the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of California, most heartfelt thanks for the kind words
of sympathy and the generous and prompt donation to aid our distressed and suffering Craft at Key West; and the Craft through the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Florida, takes this method of conveying to M.'. W.'. Brother Lawler and the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of California, most grateful appreciation. Although many
miles separate us from the good Brethren of California, yet we are
drawn near to them by the bonds of the golden chain of fraternal
love. By their liberal aid in time of need they have engraved upon
our minds and hearts a memorial of their generosity and fraternalism
which time cannot blot out nor death efface. May they always in the
field of destiny reap as they have sown.
"RISOLVID further, That the Grand Secretary transmit a copy of
the resolution under the seal of the Grand Lodge to the Most Worshipful Grand Master of the State of California.

Increase of nearly twenty-seven hundred members and·

~ 10111 lines which lead to better fraternal feeling among Lodges and
11111mbers. Many elements have co-operated in producing this result,
1•hlef among which must be mentioned the increased interest in the
work exhibited by the members and officers. As a particular in•l ance exemplifying this it is profitable to mentioft the large and int1reating "get together meeting" in Los Angeles in June of this year
•Ill the Anniversary of St. John the Baptist. Invitations were issued
t1i all the Grand Officers, Past Grand Masters, Chairmen of Committee• of Grand Lodge, and to every Mason in the City of Los An1eles. Eight thousand Masons and their families were present and
royally entertained by the local Lodges, officially represented by the
1everal Masters and Wardens. It was indeed an enjoyable occasion,
and all contributing to its success are entitled to this expressed appreciation of their efforts. It would indeed be well for Masons in
other localities to endeavor to "get together" and thus renew the
Interest of the Brethren in the work of the Craft. It is hoped that the
example set in Los Angeles will be followed from time to time in
other parts of the jurisdiction.

l'ARIS

DISASTER.

Very early in the present year, the entire wodd was horrified
by the overwhelming disaster oc;casioned by the flooding of Paris and
involving the destruction of great portions of that ancient city.
After consultation with members of the French Lodge (La Parfaite Union, No. 17), the French societies, and other charitable persons
of this city, $500.00, from the funds of the Grand Lodge was
transmitted by registered mail to Paris for tji.e relief of those of our
Brethren who were suffering in, this terrible calamity.
The return receipt from the registered letter shows that the money
was delivered to the proper Committee, and although we have received no official recognition of the contribution, there is no doubt
that the money was used to help our stricken Brethren and that suitable acknowledgment . will be received in due course.

It is g ratifying to be able to report that Masonry is prospering
throughout the entire jurisdiction. The past year has been one marked
by the largest net gain in the history of the Grand Lodge,

BOARDS OF RELIEF.

Reports will be submitted to you showing the work accomplished
by these valuable vehicles for affording Masonic assistance to the
poor and distressed traveling from afar.
The question of Masonic relief, involving as it does the securing
of employment for unemployed Brethren, has always been deeply interesting to the Masonic heart, and, during many years of Masonic
work, it has been the subject of much thought to your Grand Master.
Indeed, the briefest consideration of the subject, must establish
the fact that our Fraternity, differing as it does so essentially from
the more modern organizations which establish in advance the
amount of benefits to be paid, and the methods of proving standing
in the Order by certificates and annual' and semi-annual pass-words, is
always faced with a very involved proposition when demand for relief is made upon it.
The universality of Masonry has been held by many of the deepest
students of Masonic History to be one of the ancient landmarks and
from time immemorial we have taught and thought that "once a
Mason always a Mason," and from the earliest times . it has been
held in our Grand Lodge that to refuse MasQollic Charity to those
entitled thereto is a great Masonic offense.
Haying these propositions in mind the proper Brotherly and Fraternal method of dealing with a request for Masonic Charity and
assistance coming from one unknown to us personally, hailing from a
jurisdiction where the method of establishing standing differs from
ours is one of the most difficult things to treat intelligently and faith-

12

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

fully; yet the reputation of the Craft at home and abroad is deeply
concerned in a proper solution of the pr.Oblem, for, on the one hand,
no just request must be denied and, on the other hand, it would be
unfair to the Fraternity to assist any who by their inattention to the
simple rules whereby Masonic standing is to be maintained, have forfeited all right to consideration.
This work is eapecially difficult in a state like ours where thousands of visitors from the East come daily and monthly seeking
especially that health denied them by the more rigorous climate of
their own homes. When we consider further . that re-imbursement by
the Lodge to which the needy Brother belongs is not to be in any
manner a test to be applied, it is clear that a deep knowledge of all
the laws, rules, and regulations of all the Grand Jurisdictions of the
Masonic world is necessary to enable one to pass intelligently upon
the various matters involved in such applications for relief, and it is
now suggested that this Grand Lodge take up seriously with the Boards
of Relief of the State the matter of establishing in the Cities Relief
Committees to be composed of the most experienced Masons in the
vicinity and when appointed to hold during such time as the members shall be willing to serve and that these Committees also have
committed to their charge the important question of securing employment for unemployed Brethren, for it is believed that better results will be accomplished by Committees so formed and constituted.
Within the time prescribed by law renewal certificates renewing
the bonds of the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary were filed
and approved, and, as required by law, bids were received for printing
the proceedings of the Grand Lodge and the contract was let to the
Shannon-Conmy Co., they being the lowest bidders.

SPECIAL

COMMUNICATIONS.

On the 20th of November, 1909, the R.'. W.'. William P. Filmer
convened the Grand Lodge at Fruitvale, and with proper ceremony
dedicated the beautiful Masonic Temple of Fruitvale Lodge, No. 336.
The Grand Lodge was also convened on the 30th of November,
1909, by Brother Filmer, and he at that time laid the corner-stone of
the City Hall at Mountain View by request of the Trustees of that
city.
Brother Filmer also convened the Grand Lodge at Livermore on
the 11th of February, 1910, and . at the request of Livermore Lodge,
No. 218, dedicated to Masonic uses the new hall of that Lodge.
On Friday, the 24th of December, 1909,.R.'. w:. Alonzo J. Monroe,
Senior Grand Warden, convened the Grand Lodge at Eureka and with
impressive ceremonies laid the corner-stone of the magnificent Federal building in that city.
Truckee Lodge, No. 200, having completed a new building to be
used by that Lodge, at the request of the Trustees thereof, on the
15th of February, 1910, R.'. w:. William P. Filmer, Junior Grand
Warden, with due ceremony dedicated the hall in ancient form.
On the 22d of February, 1910, at the request of San Mateo Lodge,
No. 226, I convened the Grand Lodge at San Mateo and laid the
corner-stone of the new Masonic hall in that city.
On the 22d of January, 1910, R.'. w:. Dana R. Weller, Deputy
Grand Master, convened the Grand Lodge at Pomona, and duly dedicated the new hall of Pomona Lodge, No. 246.
The Trustees of the City Library at Richmond having invited the
Grand Lodge to lay the corner-stone of their new structure, I convened the Grand Lodge in the city of Richmond on the 26th of February, 1910, and performed the ceremony according to Masonic rites.
On the 4th of March, 1910, Brother Weller repaired to the city
of Redlands and dedicated to Masonic uses the Lodge-room of 'Redlands Lodge, No. 300.

SP!ICIAI. DISP£NSA'l'IONS.

During the year, upon proper application, a number of Special
Dispensations were issued and reference is hereby made to the Grand
Secretary's Report for a detailed list o{ them. Due caution has always been used in the exercise of. this power of the Grand Master,
who has always required a strict compliance with the Constitutional
provisions in relation to applications therefor; but, indeed, it would
seem that there is a tendency among the Lodges to ask for Dispensations to ballot without reference to a Committee, and to reballot within
the year, without actual need of such action. These Dispensations
should not be asked for without the gravest and most important reasons
requiring such action and never should such a request be made for the
mere convenience of the candidate or of the Lodge.

15

HOM:E.

While on this subject it is eminently proper to mention the
hospital now in course of construction at Decoto. This beautiful, modern, commodious, and necessary structure is the gift of v:. W.'. Bro.
Edward Coleman, Grand Treasurer, at a cost of over $40,000.00. For
years the Trustees have be~n reporting to the Grand Lodge that a
hospital was necessary in order to properly conduct the institution,
and the Fraternity undoubtedly is deeply indebted to . Brother Coleman
for this splendid donation, and in years to come, as our Masons,
their widows and orphans ·receive the care which otherwise they could
not have, Brother Coleman will be remembered with gratitude and
affection. It is fitting that the thanks of this Grand Lodge be tendered
to him for this magnificent exhibition of truly Masonic charity. It is
hoped that the hospital will be ready for dedication during the session
of the· Grand Lodge and if so it is recommended that we call off, visit
the home and take part in the dedication.

FOR

!INDOWM!IN'l'

OF

HOM:ES.

At the last Communication of the Grand Lodge the then Grand
Master was, by resolution, directed to appoint a permanent Committee consisting of nine members of the Grand Lodge and composed of the most able men· suited to this endeavor, to be known as
the Endowment Fund Committee of the Masonic Homes of California .. M.'. w:. Bro. Lawler appointed the present Grand Master
Chairman of the Committee with power to appoint other members to
fill it.
Lack of opportunity and an overwhelming realization of the importance of the work to be performed have alone prevented the appointment of the other members, and with deep regret as to my own
inability to act, the suggestion is now made that the incoming Grand
Master make the necessary appointments in order that the important
work of endowing the Homes may be presently accomplished.
LAYING CORNER-S'l'ON!IS.

MASONIC

HOMJIS.

Being influenced by a sincere desire to carry out the expressed
wishes of the Grand Lodge by ~onsolidating the management of the
Masonic Homes at Decoto and San Gabriel under the trustees appointed in the Grand Lodge, as well as by a firm belief that it was
for the benefit of Masonry in general, and both Homes, that such
consolidation should be immediately effected, such proceedings were
had that all the substantial objects to be gained were accomplished.
Vari~us payments were required to effect this purpose and were authorized to that end. A full account of all these matters will be submitted by the Trustees and it is hoped that their action will meet
with your approval.

Under the heading of Special Communications a list is given of
the meetings held for the purpose of laying Corner-Stones.
It has frequently been held by Grand Masters of this and other
jurisdictions that the Grand Lodge would officiate in laying the cornerstones only of such buildings as were either strictly Masonic in their
character or erected for exclusively public purposes, in fact, this has
been deemed of sufficient importance to make it the subject of a
positive law in many Masonic jurisdictions.
Holding this view of the functions of the Grand Lodge in such
matters, numerou·s invitations to lay the corner-stones of churches
and other buildings not .strictly public in character have been declined.

The Directors of the Masonic Temple Association of Californ~a
have worked zealously toward the actual erection -of a proper Masom.c
Temple on the San Francisco site heretofore selected. Actual deta~l
plans for the erection of j:he building have been prepared by the architects and approved by the first four officers of the ~rand. Lodge. At
this writing these plans are being figured on, and there is no doubt
that the estimated cost of the work, together with .the plans ~nd

The Lodges of San Francisco, as well as. tho~e .througho~~ the
whole State have subscribed liberally toward this buildmg. Ind1v1dual
members in' San Francisco and the vicinity have signed subscription
blanks for such an amount that the temple can be erected with little,
if any, debt against it. The Directors will make the . necessar~ detailed report and it is hoped that the Grand Lodge will be satisfied
with the results of. their labors.

The Committee appointed by the various Grand Lodges to consider matters important to the Craft along the l.ines of a bet~er
understanding between these independent and sovereign .Gran? Bod1~s
in the United States has me~ and the result of its dehberat1ons will
be submitted to you. In order to obviate possible misconstruction of
its proposed action the Committee has issued a communication disclai.ming any intention of establishing a National Grand Lodge or anythmg

that i~ the end much benefit to Masonry will be accomplished and it
is recommended that this Grand Lodge and its representatives to the
Conference assist to the best of their ability in accomplishing the desired result.
The Grand Lodge of Kentucky, through its Grand Master, transmitted to this Grand Lodge a copy of section 175 of its Constitution
relative to charges against Masons in another Grand Lodge Jurisdiction and the Grand Lodge of Oregon, through its Grand Secretary,
has also submitted a memorial requesting the adoption of a uniform
system of dimits; both of these documents are herewith submitted for
your consideration.
GRAND S!lou:TAllY'S OFFIC!l.

During the year it was found advisable to move the Gran'd ~o~ge
offices from the Claus Spreckels Building to the Hewes Bu1ldmg,
6th and Market Streets, San Francisco. The removal was au.tho~­
ized and the Grand Secretary now has commodious quarters which it
is hoped will prove adequate for all purposes until the new temple is
ready for occupancy. Authority was also given to fit up these office.s
in a manner commensurate with the requirements of the work and 1t
is hoped the Grand Lodge will be satisfied with the change.

Many queries have been received during the year which could be
1 ompletely answered by a mere reference to the appropriate section
of the Constitution or "Anderson's Manual." The following decisions,
however, involve questions not clearly decided before and . are su\:Jmltted for your consideration:
1. · When the By-laws of a Lodge are amended, changing the
feea, the change does not become effective until approved by the Grand
Master and until the approval shall have been transmitted to the Grand
Secretary.
2. Wilmington Lodge was chartered to meet in the town of Wilmington and fixed its fee for the three degrees at thirty dollars. The
town of Wilmington was consolidated with the city of Los Angeles
and became a part thereof. The other Lodges in Los Angeles charge
not less than fifty dollars for the three degrees. It was decided that
under the Constitution, as it now stands, Wilmi~gton Lodge being,
after the municipal consolidation, within the city of Los Angeles is
prohibited from conferring the three degrees for less than fifty dollars, except with the consent of all the other Lodges located in Los
Angeles.
3. A challenge may be interposed to any Commissioner at any
time prior to the actual commencement of the trial. If the challenge
be sustained such Commissioner cannot act and the trial must proceed
without filling vacancies so caused as long as a majority of the original
Commissioners remain and act. The verdict must be concurred in by
a number equal to a majority of the Commissioners elected. If the
number of Commissioners is reduced below a majority of the original
number, by vacancies caused by challenges or otherwise, all the election
proceedings are vacated, and a new election must be had for all the
Commissioners.
4. It was asked whether a Lodge, after it was opened, could be
called off for one week. It was ruled that a Masonic Lodge cannot
adjourn, it must be closed and that the Communication of a Lodge
must be closed on the day it is opened.
CONCLUSION.

And now, my Brethren, you have a detailed account of the labors
of the year. It will always be a source of regret that matters beyond
control have prevented many more visitations than those made; but
I cannot close this address without thanking the Brethren one and all
for the kindness and courtesy exhibited by them and particularly for
the uniform courtesy with which suggestions have been received and
the deep attention given to them. Particular~y thanks are due to the
Grand Officers for their loyal support and co-operation. The Grand
Secretary, Brother Whicher, has rendered most important service and
2

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNII.

indeed it would have been impossible to perform the labors of the
year without his assistance; Brother Angellotti, too, has answered
every call upon him and has assisted in deciding questions of' Masonic
law. It. would be impossible to mention all whose services deserve
recognition for so many have cheerfully rendered every assistance in
their power to make the past year a real Masonic success that it might
truly be said that the credit belongs to them one and all.
For your generous confidence and support and your cordial manifestations of Fraternal regard I am truly grateful, and may He who
presides over the Supreme Grand Lodge bless and prosper you all,
and when you are called upon to lay down the Cross and take up the .
Crown "May His Angels Crown your souls with sweet flowers freshly
gathered from the lawns of Paradise."
Fraternally submitted,
W. FRANK PIERCE.
Grand Master.
Dated September 28, 1910.
BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGt:

As we listen to these last words of our Most Worshipful Grand
Master, our hearts must be stirred by feelings of deep emotion and
sincere sorrow at his untimely taking away.
His temple of Masonic work in our Grand Lodge was near its
completion when he was felled 'by the heavy hand of Death, and confusion reigns in our midst. Yet his word is not lost. It remains with
us, to guide us along the paths of truth and virtue and to cheer us
on our journey.
Though we shall miss his kindly face and genial smile, his wise
counsel and thoughtful care, we shall always be truly grateful that
we were permitted for so long to have the benefit of his valuable services to our Fraternity.
As his successor, I most heartily indorse each and every recommendation contained in his address which has just been presented,
and earnestly desire that his wishes as therein expressed may be
gratified in every detail. So far as lies in my power, his policies shall
be pursued during this Communication. Having this in mind, I shall
not presume to supplement the address in any particular, but commend
it entirely to you·r. consideration and judgment.
Fraternally submitted,
DAN A REID WELLER,

w:.

To the M.".
Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand
Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In conformity with the recommendations of the Special Committee
adopted at the last annual communication, the Most Worshipful Grand
Master, W. Frank Pierce, appointed as the five Trus~ees of the Masonic
Home of California, the following:

· GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

38

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

P. G. M. Wm. S. Wells, P . G. M. Thomas Flint, W. Elmer E .
Stone, P. G. M. Motley H. Flint, W. Edward B. Spencer.
The first three from Lodges in the vicinity of Decoto and the
last two from Lodges in . the vicinity of San Gabriel.
Immediately after the closing of the Grand Lodge, your Board of
Trustees met; their tenure of office was determined by lot and the
term of office of each Trustee so fixed as follows :
Wm. S. Wells, one year; Elmer E. Stone, two years; Motley H.
Flint, three years; Thomas Flint, four years; Edward B. Spencer, five
years.
The Board then organized by the election of Wm. S. Wells, President; Motley H. Flint, Vice President and Elmer E. Stone, Secretary.
The board has held regular monthly meetings during the year either
at Decoto or San Gabriel.
In selecting on~ to fill the position of General Superintendent, our
choice happily fell upon Bro. Frank B. Hartman who was employed
and entered upon his duties upon December 1, 1909. He has fulfilled
all our expectations; has been of great assistance to the Board and
succeeded in bringing about better conditions and developing a spirit
of harmony and contentment which has resulted in great happiness to
the residents and proved of great benefit to the Home and its managemeiU, and to him we extend our thanks for his efforts and labors.
The detailed statement of the Secretary and Treasurer will be
found herewith. The Secretary's report shows that the amount of
money on hand is $44,777.40. Of this amount $2,990.80 is due to the
residents of the Home, and after deducting the permanent improvement
fund, we have the sum of $10,246.28 remaining as a balance in the
general fund. W& have received, during the year, $12,688.97, a bequest
from our late beloved Bro. Jacob Hart Neff, and $5,000.00 from the
Schilling Estate, which amounts have been placed to the credit of the
permanent improvement fund, the balance of which is now $29,835.97.
DECOTO HOME.
The usual and necessary yearly repairs have been made, and in
addition the marble steps, where damaged by the earthquake, have
been replaced and all reset; the walls of the main building repaired
and tinted or papered and the woodwork painted; the basements thoroughly cleaned, whitewashed and painted; the fire hydrants, chemical
engines, hose and reels overhauled, fire extinguishers recharged and
fire ladders built; the chicken ranch and cow barns thoroughly renovated and whitewashed.

39

The s~m of $13,500 was appropriated by the last Grand Lodge for
necessary improvements and this amount was placed in the hands of
the Trustees and has been expended for the following purposes:
.

A new and complete modern central steam heating plant, to use
for fuel, has been installed. The children's dormitories on the
third floor of the main building have been partitioned and made into
sixteen nice large, light and sunny rooms and partly furnished. One
of the large rooms on the first floor has been made into two and
complet7l~ _furnished for use of the T'rustees and Grand Lodge Officers
when VISltmg the Home. A bridge connecting the annex with the
mai~ building. h.as been built, which provides a pass~ge way and sun
c~r:1dor or sitting room and a stairway from both buildings to the
dmmg room, and in case of fire an additional and easy exit. This is
all enclosed, well lighted and affords protection from wind and
weather.
01~

N either the orchard or vineyard was rented this year, as no one
cou_ld be found to take them and they were handled by ourselves. The
f~mt crop was fair and supplied an abundance for table use and canning, and the remainder sold, the returns for which and for our
grapes have not, as yet, all been received and will be shown in next
year's accounts. A part of the orchard on the flat was taken out
and ~as P_lanted with stock corn and next year we purpose experimentmg with alfalfa .. Our. gardens have furnished a variety of vegetables and the area will be increased the coming year. The hill land is
rented and th~ home receives a part of the crop. The water supply
has been sufficient for all purposes, except irrigating and our flowers
and grass suffered accordingly during the summer ~onths. We shall
endeavor, during the year, to develop a better supply.
An additional storage reservoir is a necessity. Trees and shrubbery should be planted on the slope. The rooms and halls of the
temple and cottages should be cleaned, tinted and painted. The stables
need a coat of paint. The kitchen floor should be tiled; the septic
tank plant completed .and a change made in the disposition of the
water. A. one-story building, with wide porches, for use of the men
as a readmg room and for recreation is wanted. The cemetery lot
should have a concrete curbing and be placed in creditable. condition.
The total cost all of which would be $3,000 or thereabouts.
SAN GABRIEL.
. The Grand Lodge of California, while pleased with the generous
action of the Bre:hren of Southern California in making a gift of a
home for the children, could not have fully appreciated the ·extent

40

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

or the actual value of it. We now possess :a magnificent piece of property containing ten acres of land in the heart of the beautiful San
Gab~iel Valley, but a short distance from the city limits..o~ Los Angeles. Electric cars right to the gate, best of school fa~1ht1e~ and all
necessary conveniences. Originally a natural park with giant .oak
trees a century or more old, it has been beautified by a harmomous
intermingling of palms, evergreens and the bright foliage ?f the
semi-tropical trees and plants that thrive in their natural beauty m that
climate. This immense building of about one hundred large rooms,
three stories in height was formerly a hotel and with its wide hallways, large parlors a~d reception rooms, cheerfu.1 dining roo~ and
commodious kitchen, all furnished and equipped, its br?ad stairways,
fire escapes and great veranda, over four hundred feet m length, an.d
twelve feet wide completely embowered with climbing rose vines, is
particularly ada;ted to our purposes and was a gift for which this
Grand Lodge owes a debt of gratitude to the generous donors.
The improvements of the year have all been small an~ m.ight be
considered, but the general repair of an institution of this size. In
fact all the work has been done in making changes to make the property more adaptable to our uses. N ~w fencing, changing old fencing,
building poultry houses, new cesspool and outfall, piping, changing
water lines, etc., constitute the general character of the work. The
place possesses no equipment for ~ows, c?ickens, etc., but. we h~pe
during the coming year, to have this provided. The p~umbmg, bemg
old is not good and is a source of expense for repairs, except the
he;ting plant. The registers are .all good and sufficient in number.
The boiler is old, but stands the test of the City Boiler Inspectors of
Los Angeles. The oil reservoir should be rebuilt.
We have about two acres of orchard which yields a nice variety
of fruit for table use, but not sufficient to supply all our .demands.
The rest of the land is used for raising vegetables and berries. Two
good cows furnish all the milk needed and all feed for them must
be purchased as we have no room to raise it. Abou:. four h~ndred
chickens are in our poultry yai;ds, all in fine cond1t1on, owmg to
Brother Bettes' careful attention. Our water supply comes from the
Van Nuys water system and through the kindness of the management
the rate is made $15.00 per month for all purposes.
The physical condition of the children is mos~ sati.sf~ctory. ~ost
of them had the measles last spring during ~n ep1dem1c m the ne1~h­
borhood. One boy was run over by a hay wagon, a!m?st res~ltmg
fatally, and another broke his arm falling from a. tree. This ?ractically
covers the sick list of the year. Care is used 1n the select10n of attendants that they may be of a high character and thoughtful of t?e
many needs of growing children. All employe~s are under strict

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

41

discipline that the good order of the home may be preserved. The
Board is much gratified at the interest manifested by many Masons
in the boys. The State law permits a boy to take up an apprenticeship at the age of fourteen. The boys of the Home may select their
own trade, and positions are waiting for them with sufficient pay from
the start to cover their board and clothing. We have also many inquiries for children for adoption. One child has been adopted this
year into a good family, but most of our children are too old and in
other cases the consent of the parents' cannot be otained.
The buildings should all be painted and the roof of the main
building shingled and painted. A dairy barn and new chicken houses
and yards are required. A new tank for the storage of oil is necessary. A swimming tank could be built at small expense and would
be of great benefit. The plumbing requires overhauling and replacing,
the total cost of which would be $2,500 or thereabouts.
The Board unqualifiedly endorses the tribute paid to Matrons
Noble and Alexander in the report of Superintendent Hartman. They
have worked faithfully· and well for the best interests of their respective Homes and their loyalty and zeal is a source of much gratification
to the Board.
We now approach a subject of much interest and importance to the
Home and the Craft.
In our improvements we had arranged to make a temporary hospital out of one wing of the third floor of the main building, and had
our plans well started when we were called into consultation with the
M.". w:. Grand Master by our well beloved Brother V. W. Edward
Coleman, who informed us that he desired to do some.thing for the
Decato Home which would be of benefit to the aged Masons an:d their
widows and asked our advice and opinion as to the needs and whether
a hospital building would be the best and most acceptable. We agreed
that it would and Brother Coleman then stated that he would build
and present to the Home a fully equipped Hospital. He immediately
employed an architect, had plans and specifications drawn, a contract
let and the building commenced. It was the earnest wish of Brother
Coleman and this Board that it should be completed and ready for
dedication at this Communication, but unavoidable delays have prevented. Brother Coleman has taken a great interest in this work, has
personally attended to much of the detail, visiting the Home to inspect
the work, advising and consulting with the Boa~d during its erection,
and when completed will furnish and transfer it to the custody of your
Board of Trustees.
This handsome building, erected on a site overlooking the Home
and the beautiful valley, with i~s broad verandas and solarium, contains two wards and three private rpoms for fifteen patients, a nurses'

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

room, kitchen, baths, operating and sterilizing room and is complete
in all particulars and a modern hospital.
The love for our fraternity and the interest in the welf11re of
the aged, infirm Mason, which prompted this gift, is characteristic of
the kindly and sympathetic nature of the donor and while we fully
appreciate his natural modesty and his desire to have as little ceremony
over it as may be possible, yet we believe it should receive such
recognition from the Grand Lodge as it deserves, and the Grand
Lodge would desire to give, but we are of the opinion that this· is not
the proper time or place and we recommend that when the building
is completed and ready to be transferred, the Grand Lodge of California be convened in Special Communication at the Masonic Home at
Decato and with appropriate ceremony the Hospital be dedicated and
the magnificent gift be properly acknowledged. We also recommend
that the Board of Trustees be authorized to have made and placed
in the building a bronze tablet suitably inscribed.
As will be seen from the foregoing there was received, during
the year, from the Estate of Brother Neff, the sum of $12,688.97 which
was placed in what the Board has heretofore denominated the Permanent Improvement Fund. This fund has not, in the past, been
drawn upon for any purpose but kept as a reserve and we now recommend that the sum received from Brother N eff's estate be entered
as the first donation and with the balance in the Permanent Improvement Fund, making a total of $29,835.97, be placed in a fund to be
known as the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic Home · of
California, no part of which shall hereafter be used for any purpose,
only the interest thereon to be used and that to go into the General
Fund of the Masonic Home.
Thus a nucleus will be created for a Fund which we trust in a
very short time will grow to such proportions as will take care of our
Homes without the necessity of any per capita tax, and the cherished
name of the honored and loyal Mason which in life was written in
our book of gold "as one that loves his fellow man," and also as one
"whom love of God had blest" will forever in this greatest .of Masonic
charities lead all the rest.
We desire to express the sincere thanks of all to the fraternity
and those who so kindly remembered our families at San Gabriel and
Decoto with their generous gifts at Christmas time and donations
through the year and assure them that the same have been fully appreciated by all. The Board also desires to thank all Lodges, Masters
and Officers of Lodges, and members of the fraternity who have so
interested themselves during the year ·a s to visit and provide entertainment at the Home. Their interest, advice and suggestion has been

of service and their efforts to assist in this work meets our hearty
approval.
We recommend that the usual per capita tax of one dollar be
levied and that there be ;i.ppropriated out of the general fund such
sums as we have herein suggested for permanent improvements at
San Gabriel and Decoto. We would also recommend that from any
surplus that may exist at the end of any year the Board be authorized
to set apart and place in the Permanent Endowment Fund such sum
as they may deem proper.
The Board has had under consideration and submitted to eminent legal authority the question of Incorporation and other matters
relative to perfecting title to its properties, but as yet have reached no
satisfactory conclusion. The matter will be taken up during the year
and an endeavor made to settle these troublesome questions.
The system of accounts heretofore in .use have be~n very crude
and unsatisfactory and your Board has employed a firm of accountants
and has installed a modern system of accounts which went into operation on October 1st.
The recommendations made by the Special Committee and adopted
at the last Annual Communication have been followed during the year
and in the main proven satisfactory and we recommend that no change
be made in the general scheme of maintaining and managing the two
Homes, but that the present system be continued as being highly satisfactory and successful.
Fraternally submitted,·
WM.

ANNUAL REPOR.T OF SUPERINTENDENT.

Di;:coTo, ALAMEDA Co., CALIFORNIA, September 30th, 1910.
To the Boat'd of Trustees of the Ma.soni"c Home .of California.
Brethren : The undersigned presents the twelfth annual report
as Superintendent of the Masonic Homes of California.
At a regular meeting of the Board of Trustees, November 14th,
1909, I was elected Superintendent and entered on my duties December 1, 1909.
We now have at the Home 60 men and 32 women. During the
year there have been 19 admissions, 16 men '!ind three women, and 13
deaths, 10 men and 3 women.
A family spirit has been encouraged and fostered whieh already
dominates the daily life of our large family, made up of members
drawn from all parts of the State. It has been our aim and hope to
develop among all a high type of personal conduct, to maintain a standard of service and mutual helpfulness in "keeping with the cherished
idc::als of the Masonic fraternity, to help by precept and example to
live up to the spirit which made these Homes possible. To this end
the strong are encouraged to help the weak and thus all receive according to their need and give according to their ability.
To gather a large family together composed of varying individualities, to keep the Masonic fires burning on the altars of brotherly love,
to inspire all with good ideals, to work and strive for all that is pure
and noble in the relations of Home life has constantly been the fervent
prayer of myself and the Matrons who have so ably assisted me.
The general health of the residents of the Home has been good.
There are now several confined to their rooms, their sickness being
the result of extreme old age.
Monthly entertainments and social gatherings have, during the
past year, become a feature of our family life. Few if any of the
residents are able to visit their Lodges or friends. Entertainments
of various kinds must be brought to them. Each month during
the past year a miscellaneous program made up of recitations, songs,
readings, games, vaudeville sketches, etc., has been prepared by Home
talent. A chorus made up of residents of the Home take part in our
monthly socials, also lead the singing at our Sunday services, which
are held each week in the Chapel.
Residents and employees have taken hold of this feature of our
social life with enthusiasm and it has provided a source of much happiness and enjoyment for all. 1

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Visiting Lodges have at various times exemplified the work in the
Siminoff Temple. These visits mean much to the Brethren. It helps
to keep them in touch with their Masonic ideals and brings them in
contact with members of the Masonic fraternity.
Thanksgiving Day, Christmas, Washington's and Lincoln's birthday, and Fourth of July were all duly observed with appropriate
exercises in a manner in keeping with the day. May 19th, Jewell Lodge,
No. 374, conferred the third degree in the Temple followed by an
entertainment. May 28th, Sequoia Lodge, No. 349, conferred the
third degree at the Temple. June 4th, Live Oak Lodge, No. 61, gave
an excellent musical program and provided refreshments for all. June
28th, San Jose Lodge, No. 10, arrived in autos and conferred the third
degree at the Temple. On August 14th, the Masonic Board of Relief of
San Francisco inspected the buildings and grounds and spent the day
visiting with the residents. August 17th, Jewell Chapter, 0. E. S.,
entertained the residents in the afternoon. August 27th, Oakland
Lodge, No. 188, gave a pleasing entertainment at the Temple followed
by refreshments. Sequoia Lodge, No. 349, visited the Home on the
afternoon of ' September 16th and in the evening entertained the
family with moving pictures, etc., at the Temple. August 18.th, a garden party was given the ladies of the Home by Mrs. W. Werner, Past
Matron of Orient Chapter at her home in Irvington. Luncheon was
served and a pleasant time enjoyed.
I desire to refer to the highly efficient services of Mrs. Noble,
Matron of the Home. She has faithfully assisted me in furthering the
best interests of the Home. Having a natural talent for her work,
executive ability of a high order, and trained experience of many years
along the lines of Home life, I am deeply indebted to her for the loyal
support she has at all times given me.
There are at the San Gabriel Home forty-five children-twenty-five
boys and twenty girls. Twenty-five children have been admitted during
·
the year and six have left the Home.
The children enjoy ideal conditions in their Southern Home. They
evince a desire to care for their beautiful home, and are daily growing
more useful in their various duties. · They do all the work in their
dormitories, making beds, ·sweeping and scrubbing floors in dormitories and halls and do much emergency work that their young hands
can master. The girls have done nicely in their sewing and cooking.
Some of the oldet girls are now making their own dresses. The boys
while full of play, have spent much of their energy very usefully.
They built a pigeon house with their own tools and have exhibited
many satisfactory specimens of their skill in wood work. They dug
and filled the ditches for pipe and excavated for the foundation for · the
barn and in garden work, surprised all in their care and success with
their vegetables. Small cash prizes were given for this work, which

may account for some of this unusual interest. A most gratifying
feature of the work of the girls is their deep interest in their musical
instruction. This is due to a great extent to the ability and personality of their instructor, Mrs. Nina Holloway Ward, who has become
interested in our girls and practically donates her services.
They attei;id the public schools a short distance away and are
given every advantage possible in order to give them a goo'd start in
life and lay a foundation for the building of a successful manhood and
womanhood. Their home life is ideal. Mrs. Alexander, Matron of the
Home, is well equipped for the duties required of her. She brings to
her work a ripe experience, an understanding of the needs and wants
of a child. The children idolize her and with her love for them, the
daily life at the Home moves along free from unpleasant experiences
which often occurs in a large family when harmony does not prevail'.
I wish to assure her of my appreciation of the good wholesome conditions which she has created in the Home; the results of her kindly
influence are seen in the happy faces of the children of her large
family. ,
·
The cordial interest displayed by Lodges of Masons and Chapters
of the Eastern Star in their frequent visits to the Home is very gratifying to the management as well as to the children. We note on our
register that not only have individual Masons from all parts of Southern California called at the Home, but many Northern friends on their
visits to the South have remembered our children and paid them a
cordial visit.
The hours never drag for lack of entertainment. Many of the
children are gifted in one form or another to make up an impromptu
program for most any occasion. The Mandolin Quartette is popular
with Masonic bodies and they are frequently a feature of the program
in their social evenings. Suitable observance is made of the various
holidays and occasional gatherings are held with their school-mates
either at the Home or residences of the neighbors, all of whom show
·
a kindly interest in their welfare.
Sunday Scbool and Church Services are held regularly in the
Chapel, a separate and well ai;fapted building for that purpose. The
Y. M. C. A. of Los Angeles furnishes pastors for this work without
expense to the Home, who favor no particular denomination in their
work.
Some of the entertainments deserving special mention during the
fiscal year are : Thanksgiving Day, special turkey dinner and evening
program. Christmas, Christmas Tree, a real Santa Claus, songs, etc.
At this time the many presents secured through the donations from
various Masonic bodies were distributed.
Representatives of severa·l Lodges and Chapters called. See
"Donations" for particulars. Watch Party on New Year's; eve. Pop

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

corn and taffy pulling occupied the evening. March 24, Matron's birthday. The children arranged through the attendants and cooks a complete and most successful surprise party. Mr. Bettis' birthday being
the same day, they remembered him also.
April 12. Hollywood Chapter, 0 . E. S., No. 209. Jolly visit,
leaving a new "nighty" each for the children. May 21. Acacia Chapter, No. 21, 0. E. S., gave a children's party, paying the children's
fare to Los Angeles and return.
June 24. St. John's Day. Mandolin Quartette played before 7000
Masons and their families at Shrine Auditorium. June 25. Visit of
all the Grand Lodge Officers attending the Reunion at Los Angeles.
July 1st. Esperanza Chapter, 0 . E. S., visited the Home in a body
and were entertained by the children. July 4. Acacia Chapter, 0. E.
S., with a delegation. of 20 members brought a liberal supply of fireworks, to the delight of the children. July 10. The Board of Relief
of Los Angeles held their monthly meeting in the parlors of the Home,
inspected the buildings and grounds and were entertained by the songs
of the children and the Mandolin Club. Fort~-six members of the
Board were present.
August 29 to September 10 marked two weeks' vacation on Catalina. By the kindness of the Pacific Electric R. R. Co. the Wilmington
Transportation Co. and the Meteor Boat Co., the children were taken
free of charge to Camp Banning and return. The Banning Co. gave
the use of the ground and carried the freight from Avalon. The Trustees of the State School, through Bro. J. P. Greely, gave us the use of
the State's tents and kitchen outfits. The children reveled in this most
enjoyable treat. Boating, fishing on the ocean, picnics in the wooded
canyons, surf bathing and games gave them continuous delightful
amusement.
Grand Master W. Frank Pierce and the members of the Grand
Lodge have on several occasions visited and inspected both Homes.
Many members of the fraternity and their friends interested in the
work of the Homes, have spent many pleasant hours with u~.
I cannot speak too strongly of the benefits the Homes would
derive if the members of the fraternity would make frequent visits. •
The conditions at the close of the year are bright and give promise
of a new era of progress for the Homes. Profiting by past experience,
new lines are opening up and in the administration of affairs, a policy
will be pursued on a practical, economical basis.
And now brethren, it is with a deep sense of feeling on our part
that we measure the responsibility you have intrusted to us. It has
been at all times our sincere desire to carry out the directions of the
Board, though at times, trying conditions necessarily arose, owing to
a transition period which naturally ensues, when new conditions· are
taking place of the old, and if our work during the past year has met

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

with yo~r kind approval, it is due in no small degree to your counsel
and advice, always freely given, in solving many of the difficult and
complex problems that arise in Home life.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK

B. HARTMAN,
Superintendent.

Which report was received, and that portion 'referring
to the gift of a hospital by Brother Coleman was referred

to the Finance Committee. General consideration of the
whole report, particularly that portion relating to an Endowment Fund, was made special order for Thursday morning at 10 o'.clock.
The Grand Master announced that the Grand Orator's
address would be made special order for Wednesday at two
o'clock, and a Me~orial Service in honor of our late Grand
Master would be held Thursday at two o'clock.
M.'. W.'. Edmund C. Atkinson introduced a proposed
amendment to Part II of the Constitution to be known as
Article V, defining the duties of the Grand Lecturer. He
also introduced a resolution proposing to correct the grammatical construction of certain portions of the Constitution,
without changing the sense thereof. Both which were
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The reports of the Boards of Relief of San Francisco,
Los Angeles, Oakland, San Diego, Sacramento and San
Jose were then presented as follows:

A. Troxal.
The calls for aid during the year just past have not been quite so
heavy as the two years next preceding. However, by glancing over
this report it will be observed that distress has not passed us by altogether, and we are glad to report that no worthy application has gone
unaided. We plead guilty, however, to an occasional "touch" by an
unworthy, a fraud or an impostor. These have generally been discovered by the judicious use of the telegraph, and a warning has been sent
out to the Craft. We might say, also, that we have had the pleasure
bf providing employment for several of these bums at the city's rock
pile, through the medium of our police courts.
M1'1'TINGS OF THE BOARD.

Our Board of Relief is composed of the Master and two members of
each Lodge, (generally the Wardens) and one lady, in our city, who
meet on the first Sunda.y morning in each month, and transact whatever business there m<l;Y be; and afterwards there is an exchange of
ideas appertaining to the Craft. The meetings are, therefore, a
"Monthly Get Together Party." The Brethren look forward to these
meetings with much pleasure--and they are the means of promoting
the greatest peace and harmony which prevails among the Brethren in
our city.
·
INVALIDS COMING.

Brethren, throughout the ·united States, who may read this report:
In the name of Humanity, don't send ·your consumptives and otherwise
hopeless invalids to the Pacific Coast, unless they have sufficient means
to take care of themselves. It is not doing them a kindness, and it is
positively unjust to the Craft in the West. It is hard enough for a
well man to get a position, but for an invalid it is im~ossible.
The large corporations and business houses require their employes
to pass a physical examination before .accepting them-and rest assured'
the physicians who make those examinations are honest and give their
em;oyers ~he benefit of the. doubt. Forty years of age is also the limit.

•

THE MASONIC 1'MPLOYMENT BUR1':AU,

operating in conjunction with this Baa.rd of Relief, continues to do
good work. Since its establishment, it has been the means of securing
an average of at least one position (great or small) daily to members
of the Craft.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of Caii'fornia:

The Masonic .Board of Relief o'f Oakland herewith respectfully
presents its annual report, from September 2, 1909 to August 31,
1910, inclusive.
Until January, 1910, the Board's membership is shown in our
report for 1909. From January, 1910, the following brethren have
composed the Board :

Franklin Shulte, S. W. ; Guy Duncan Reynolds, ]. W.

Earle Kelly, S. W.; Charles Henry Davies, J. W.

Henry Sommer, S. W.; John Gust~v Sjoberg, ]. W.
Sequoia "Lodge, No. 349, by Frank Flint Porter, Master; Francis
Delmar Dolbier, S. W.; Charles Chubb, J. W.
Fruitvale Lodge, No. 336, by Frederick Stuart Ellard, Mastef;
Arthut Alfred Barber, S. W.; Frank Oscar Schullerts, ]. W.
Bay View Lodge, No. 401, by LeRoy W. Potter, Master; Gwyn
, J. W.
Harvey Baker, S. W.;
Y erba Buena Lodge, No. 403, by Henry Fletcher Starbuck, Master;

Wednesday in January, 1911, and they are:

Secretary.

were buried with Masonic Honors, under the auspices of this Board:
Benjamin Franklin Thornton, Wadsworth Lodge, No. 25, Sparks,
Nev.; George B. Avery, Ottawa Lodge, No. 51, Marysville, Montana;
George H . Piper, Sebasticook Lodge, No. 146, Clinton, M;aine; John
Alex. McMartin, Petaluma Lodge, No. 180, Petaluma, Cal. ; William
John Stewart, Meridian No. 182, Arbuckle, Cal.; Thomas Henry Hart,
Clinton Lodge, No. 119, Igo, Cal.
The Board is composed of the Masters and Wardens of the Lodges
holding concurrent jurisdiction in Sacramento, which contribute but
dr.aw nothing from the Board; sojourning Master Masons, their widows and orphans alone being recipients. Money refunded is again
given to the needy of the Order.

A communication was presented from the Grand Lodge
of the District of Columbia, stating that that Grand Body
had taken action looking to a general observance of St.
John Baptist's day, June 24, 1917, the bi-centenary of the
formation of the first Grand Lodge of Freemasons, and in- ,
quiring: First, whether the plan of a general form of service for all Masons upon St. John Baptist's day, June 24,
1917, commends itself. Second, whether ottr Grand Lodge
would join in such service and recommend the same to all
particular Lodges under our jurisdiction. And, third,
whether our Grand Lodge has any suggestions to make as
to th e nature or detail of such service. Which was ordered
to be referred to a Special Committee to be later appointed,
and report at the next Annual Communication.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:

notice thereof; that the dues in nearly every instance have accompanied the reports, and that all dues have now been paid.
The reports of the following Lodges were received after the time
required by law, the dates of reception being noted:
St. John's, No. 37, September 7;

Quitman, No. 88, September 28;

Orosi, No. 383, September 14;
Imperial, No. 390, September 15;
West Lake, No. 392, Sept. 21 ;
Turlock, No. 395, September 13.

Your Committee call attention to Section 17, Part III, Article IV,
of the Constitution, which provides that "No Lodge which shall have
failed to make its annual returns, with payment of its dues, as provided
in Section 4, Article II, Part III, and in Section 1, Article V, Part IV,
shall be entitled to representation at the next Annual Communication."
The law requires that annual returns shall be reported not later than
August 15, yet some Lodges are late every year, and some reports are
prepared carelessly, entailing much labor and vexation in the office of
the Grand Secretary, and unnecessary correspondence. We, your Committee recommend that the law be enforced.
The amounts for dues for which the several Lodges of this
jurisdiction were indebted, and which have all been paid, are as follows:

V.". W.". Thomas J. Baker, Grand Lecturer, presented
his annual report, as follows:
To the M .". w:. Grand Lo&ge of California:
I herewith submit to you my report as Grand Lecturer. Another
year has passed and this grand fraternity which we all love is march~
ing onward and upward in its mission for the upbuilding of man, and
diffusing light to all who seek admission therein. I have visited every
district in the State and held schools of instruction, day and night sessions. Generally these schools have been well attended by the officers
and brethren, all anxious to get the work as nearly perfect as possible.
The Lodges are, with but few exceptions, in good financial condition,
and most of them doing much degree work. The Inspectors in the
several districts are all enthusiastic workers and rendering valuable
assistance to the Lodges under their charge. I have received reports
from each and every Inspector, and all report their Lodges, with but
few exceptions, to be doing good work, and the exceptions are in most
cases those who have had no ·candidates. It is difficult for the officers to
retain the work where they have no opportunity to confer degrees.
There have been thirteen new Lodges formed this year, with a net
gain in membership of 2,668, the greatest in the history of the Grand
Lodge.
I desire to express to the Inspectors and brethren my thanks for .
the many courtesies extended to me during the year. The exemplification of the degree work at this Communication of the Grand Lodge
will be as follows: Friendship Lodge, No. 210, San Jose, will confer
the First degree on this evening, Tuesday, October 11th; the Third degree will be conferred by the Inspectors on W ednesd~y evening, October
12th ; and the Second degree will be conferred by Doric Lodge, No. 216,
of this city, on Thursday evening, October 13th. These Lodges and
the Inspectors will endeavor to exemplify the several degrees as nearly
letter perfect as possible.
I wish to· thank the v:. w:. Grand Secretary and his Assistant
for the many courtesies extended to me in their office. I have been
provided with an office where I can instruct the brethren privately, and
a great many of them have availed themselves of this opportunity. I
desire at this time to inform the Inspectors, officers and brethren that
I shall be pleased to have them come to my office at any time they
wish for instruction.
At the last Communication of the Grand Lodge the Ritual Committee was instructed to formulate a candidates' lecture for the Third
degree. The chairman of this committee, on account of · pressure of
business and absence from the city, turned the matter over to me. I
have accordingly prepared a lecture on the lines of the two other coach-

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ing lectures, and have commenced teaching it at the schools of instruction held just prior to the convening of the Grand Lodge.
Within the past year quite a number of the brethren have requested
that the Funeral Service now used should be revised, and also that it
should appear in the Manual. It does not appear in the last edition of
that valued publication. In order that this may be brought before the
Grand Lodge, I suggest that the funeral service be referred to the
incoming Grand Master for revision.

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of Ca•lifornia:
WHEREAS, Janesville Lodge, No. 232, was, up to a few days ago,

Which was referred to the Committee on Finance.
Brother E. M. Billings introduced the following re~olu­
tion:
WHEREAS, We as Masons are at all times taught that the Holy
Bible is the rule and guide of our lives, and upon it all Masons are
obligated, thereby most emphatically requiring full and unquestioned
belief in the Bible; and
WHEREAS, An error has crept into Decision No. 366, which plainly
Rtates : "Of religion we only desire to know that each one asking admission is a sincere believer in God and a future existence"; therefore,
be it
Resolved, That such decision be corrected by adding after the word
"God" the word "Holy Bible," making the sentence read : "Of religion we only desire to know that each one asking admission is a sincere believer in God, the Holy Bible and a future existence."

The same was referred to the Committee on J urisprudence.
Brother Billings also introduced the following:
WHEREAS, The present pay of Representatives, where the rebates
allowed by transportation companies are considered, is not equal; and
WHEREAS, The provisions of Section 10, Article II, Part III, of the
Constitution, which prescribes that each Lodge shall pay its officers
and Representatives, is often disregarded, with the result that some
brother is selected who has other business in the city and is willing to
defray his own expenses, and not infrequently the weaker Lodge is not
represented at all; therefore, it is
Resolved, That Section 10 of Article II, Part III, of the Constitution
be, and the same is hereby, repealed. (Page 57, Manual.)
R esolved, That General Regulation, No. 69, be, and the same is
hereby, repealed. (Page 120, Manual.)
Resolved, That the following be enacted and constitute a General
Regulation of the Grand Lodge :
The pay of Representatives to the Grand Lodge shall be first class
railroad or steamer fare, together with stage fare and cost of berth in
sleeper when required-that is, to defray the actual traveling expenses

At this time also we desire to note our approval of the sentiments
expressed and the attitude assumed by M.". v::. Dana R. Weller in
his address with reference to the untimely death of Grand Master
Pierce, and his most commendable intention to carry out, in so far as
p~ssible, during this Annual Communication, the policies of his illustrious predecessor.
With respect to the use of the funds of this Grand Lodge by the
M.". w:. Grand Master in the alleviation of distress in Key West
Flori?a, ca~sed by the devastating hurricane which visited that city:
and m Pans, France, caused by the overwhelming floods of the past
winter, we most heartily approve of the same. Masonic charity
whether it finds expression in the relief of an individual or of a commu~
nity, is to be commended and, when properly exercised cannot but
result in giving both to the donor and to the beneficiary a' truer appreciation of the obligation which rests upon us to give and those in
distress to receive.
'
We reciprocate the very kind expressions of fraternalism contained
it; the message of thanks sent from the Grand Lodge of Florida, and
sincerely trust that their Masonic pleasure in receiving in some slight
degree approximates ours in the giving.
With respect particularly to the relief granted to those of our faith
injured in the floods of Paris, it appearing from the report of the Grand
Master that no official acknowledgment of the receipt or disposition
of the contribution has as yet been made, we suggest to the incoming
Grand Master the propriety of ascertaining through proper Masonic
channels the disposition of the funds transmitted from this Grand
Lodge. T'his we do, not that we entertain any suspicion that the funds
or. any portion thereof have been misapplied, but solely in order that
this Grand Body, which is merely the trustee of the great body of
Masons in California, may hereafter be able to render a complete account of its stewardship.
We note with pleasure the gratifying statement of the Grand Master that Masonry is prospering throughout the entire jurisdiction: evidenced by :he substantial growth both in membership and in' new
Lod~es. '!'his dem?nstrates that our tenets and principles are still per:
1uas.1ve with ~ankmd, and that if our practices conform thereto the
ilonous prestige of our ancient and honorable institution will continue
to be maintained.
'Ne commend particularly the indorsement by the Grand Master of
the so-called "get together meetings" of the Craft. The social side of
our order must not be overlooked; for if such be the case, the fraternal
nnd therefore most 'important side is apt' to be neglected.

Brother Benjamin F. Bledsoe; Chairman of the Special
Committee to whom had been referred the address of the
Grand Master · and the report of the Grand Secretary, presented the following report :
San Francisco, Cal., Oct. 11th, 1910.
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of Ca1lifornia.:
Your committee, to whom was assigned the consideration and distribution of the .various matters embraced within the reports of the
M.". w:. Grand Master and the v:. w:. Grand Secretary, would
respectfully report that they have had the same under consideration
and beg leave to report thereon as follows:
At the outset, confronted as we are by the recent untimely demise
of our late M.". w:. Grand Master, W. Frank Pierce, whose dread
summons came just as he stood at the very summit of his Masonic
career, we confess at this time an utter inability to give adequate expression to our judgment as to ·his record and services "as man, Mason
and citizen. In his taking away this Grand Body has suffered the irreparable loss of a most forceful leader, the Craft in general have been
deprived of a tireless worker in the Masonic vineyard, and a worldwide humanity has lost the most precious of all of God's gifts to mana friend.
In truth and soberness it may be said that the light from a star
of the first magnitude in the Masonic firmament has been extinguished.
A fit and proper expression of our sorrow and regret demands the
appointment of a Special Committee on Necrology, to whom shall be
confided the duty of voicing our sentiments with respect not only to
our own illustrious dead, but also to those· of other jurisdictions ·who
have been cut down by the Grim Reaper during the past year, mention

The matters embraced under the caption "Boards of Relief," referring to the work of the Boards of the various cities of our State, we
recommend be referred to the Special Committee of Investigation of
Relief, appointed at the last Annual Communication of this Grand
Lodge.
The petitions for new Lodges referred to we recommend be referred to the Committee on Charters.
The importance of that portion of the Grand Master's address advising us of the donation by v:. w:. Edward Coleman, Grand Treasurer, of a sum sufficiently large to erect a suitable hospital at the
Masonic Home· at Decoto justifies, in our judgment, its reference to a
Special Committee in order that suitable and more than mere formal
thanks to Brother Coleman for his most generous and praiseworthy
act may be accorded by this Grand Body. We therefore recommend
that that portion of the M.". w:. Grand Master's address be referred
to the Special Committee heretofore appointed, to prepare and present
suitable resolutions of thanks in the premises.
With reference to the Endowment Fund Committee of the Masonic
Homes of California, mention of the appointment of the chairman of
which was made by the M.". w:. Grand Master, we would recommend
that the committee be continued, with authority to the incoming Grand
Master to appoint the chairman and other members thereof.
We recommend .the reference to the Committee of Jurisprudence of
all decisions of the Grand Master, both in response to queries propounded
and to invitations to lay corner stones, and also the proposed amendments to the Constitution and Uniform Code of By-Laws suggested
by the Grand Secretary.
The requests for fraternal recognition from various Grand Bodies,
and the memorial requesting the adoption of a uniform <limit, we recommend . be referred to the Committees on Correspondence and Jurisprudence, respectively.
We feel constrained to criticise severely the action of some of the
Secretaries in this jurisdiction for their delinquency and dilatoriness in
not forwarding, within the proper time, notices of election, as reported
by the Grand Secretary. Secretaries too often lose sight of the fact
that their delay in such matters works a hardship not upon themselves
or their own Lodges, but upon the Craft as a whole. They should see
to it, therefore, that the greatest degree of diligence, consistent witlt
a proper performance of their official duties, should be employed in this
as in all other respects. ·
We recommend that the matter of the proposed general celebration
of the two hundredth anniversary of the date of the formation of the
first Grand Body · of Freemasons, June 24th, 1717, be referred to the
incoming Grand Master, with power to take such action in this behalf
as witl, in his judgment, conduce to the good of the Craft.

At the_ last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge the following resolution was adopted :
"Resolved, That it is the sense of this Grand Lodge that stock of the
Masonic Temple Association of California be sold to any organized body
composed entirely of Masons."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This resolution was carefully considered by the Directors of the
Masonic Temple Association, and after consulting with many prominent
Masons and officers of Masonic bodies, it was the unanimous opinion of
said Board of Directors that it would be impossible to obtain subscriptions from Masonic bodies alone sufficient to build a Temple adequate to
't he needs of the Craft, but that additional subscriptions from individual
Masons could be obtained, so that with a comparatively small mortgage
sufficient money would be available to erect a Temple such as the
Masons of California should, and would be, proud of.

Since the last Annual Communication 9f the Grand Lodge the
Masonic Temple Association of California has purchased, for the sum
of $22,000, the lot immediately adjoining on the west of the land originally purchased. The lot so purchased has a frontage of 47 feet 9
inches ?~ Oak Street by a depth of 120 feet to Hickory Avenue, with
an add1tional frontage of 21 feet on Hickory Avenue by a depth of
40 feet.
·
The lot of land now owned by the Association has a frontage of
120 feet on Van Ness Avenue, 157 feet 6 inches on Oak Street and 178
feet 6 inches on Hickory Avenue, and is a very desirable and valuable
holding; the total investment for the land being $257,000.
The Directors re-employed Messrs. Bliss & Faville, architects, to
draw plans and make detail drawings for a Temple for both Masonic
and commercial purposes, and great credit is due to Directors S. H.
Kent, Chairman of the Building Committee, and John P. Fraser, both
of whom spent many hours supervising the plans.
After drafting plans acceptable to the Board of Directors, they
were submitted to the M.". w:. Grand Master, the R.". W.". Deputy
Grand Master and the R." · W .". Senior and Junior Grand Wardens ;
and the plans now submitted to this Grand Lodge have been approved
by them.
The plans and spt!cifications were submitted to bidders, and the
Temple will cost, including architects' fees, the sum of $700,000.

To erect the Temple according to the plans and specifications submitted and accepted, it will be necessary to borrow $250,000.00, and the
income will be more than sufficient to pay the interest on that amount.
The Directors feel positive in asserting that if our city continues
to grow in the next two years as it has done in the ~ast fou; yea~s,
that before our Temple can be occupied the commercial portion. will
demand a greater rental than at present estimated by at le~st six to

dividends, · or reduction of mortgage.

"We wish to call your attention to the architectural treatment which
the building has been given and the endeavor to imprint upon its facade
the characteristic qualities of our noble organi'zation. In doing this we
have embodied a great scale in all of its proportions, leaving the wall
surfaces broad and simple, so that the mass of the building becomes
vital and powerful, enriched with ornamentation symbolistic of the fraternity.
"The type of architecture has been inspired by that of the early
Italian period', when its influence was of the most commanding and
dominant character scattering throughout Italy; examples of the masterly treatment of the North, broadened and refined by the influence
of the Southern cities, and which erected during that period some of
the most vital and powerful buildings that the world possesses.
"The opportunity presented by the building offers in its broad wall
surfaces and small window areas a chance seldom offered in modern
days, and we have been keen to take advantage of the opportunity.
"We affirm that the building, if erected as presented by the plans
and specifications and built of the noble material of marble as is contemplated, will not only be the handsomest Masonic Temple in America,
but will be favorably compared with the great temples on the Continent.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Brethren:
Our fraternity has in the many years of its existence, by its clear
light, disarmed enmity and dispelled prejudice; our form of government,
our whole system of laws, as well as their popular exposition, are impressed with the learning, the integrity and the patriotism of the American Mason ; his mind has assisted not only in shaping but in giving
substance to all our institutions.
In every epoch of .our republic, her fame, her prosperity, her glory
have been noted; an institution that upholds such high principles should
and must rear a monument to her name in this glorious State of California-a Temple that must demand admiration for our magnificent
achievements of architecture ; let it be our proudest triumph of art, and
let us remember, in erecting this Temple, that whatever is grand or
intricate or beautiful, every moment of labor expended, every arm . em.ployed, every blow struck, are but the aggregate of the skill and efforts
which have achieved its final success.
In this Temple we shall represent the achievements of architectural
genius, efforts which in grandeur and beauty will be unrivalled in the
world, and which may endure till time shall be no more.
Building such a Temple as our plans portray reflects the added
character of our institution and the intellect of our people. It was expressed by a great mind, "Beautiful architecture is like frozen music."
Our Temple, like our Masonic Body, must stand out bold and grand.
This Temple should present to the world strength, dignity and beauty
of structure so that it will stand an enduring monument to our beloved
fraternity. 'That l>uilding must stand as a symbol of such teachings as ·
we impart. In our strength the shafts of malice that may be, hurled
will fall harmless at our feet, and the fraternity will steadily move onward, extending benign influence over the moral and fraternal realm
of thought, and performing deeds of beneficence and mercy towards
the distressed of its own household.
How fa r, then, may the future of the fraternity be predicable upon
its past and present relations to the progress of mankind.
Consider this struct~re in which we will meet as one of the evidences of the faith which is implanted in the breast of every Mason
within the Grand Jurisdiction of California; that the order has a mission before it which will be grander in its fulfillment than the beautiful
marble Temple which we are about to present to the world. May this
Temple, when completed, stand a beacon light in this glorious State,
shedding its refulgent splendor upon the broad ocean of eternity, and
an earthly memorial of that spiritual building, that "House not made
with hands," eternal in the heavens.
I therefore offer the following resolutions, and recommend their
adoption:
