M.'. W.'. Frank M. Angellotti, Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report:
To the M: . w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
decisions on questions of Masonic law, reported in the Grand Master's
address, and reports thereon as follows :
I. The first decision, which is simply to the effect that an amendment to the By-laws of a Lodge, relative to fees, does not become effective until approved by the Grand Master and the transmission of
that approval to the Grand Secretary, is in strict accord with the provisions -0f Article XIII of the Uniform Code of By-laws. We recommend that the decision be approved.
2. The second decision, which is to the effect that where a city or
town containing but one Lodge is annexed under the laws of the State
to another city or town containing one or more Lodges, and thus becomes a part of said city or town, the Lodge in the city or town thus annexed becomes subject to the provision of Section 8, Article III, Part

'

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

III, of the Constitution prohibiting a Lodge in any place where two
or more Lodges have concurrent jurisdiction from conferring the three
degrees for a less fee than $50.00, except with the consent of all said
Lodges, is also in stri~t accord with the Constitution as it now stands.
We recommend that the decision be approved.
3. The third decision was as follows : "A challenge may be interposed to any Commissioner at any time prior to the actual commencement of the trial. If the challenge be sustained, such Commissioner cannot act and the trial must proceed without filling vacancies so
caused as long as a majority of the original Commissioners remain and
act. The verdict must be concurred in by a number equal to a majority of the Commissioners elected. If the number of Commissioners
is reduced below a majority of the original number, by vacancies caused
by challenge or otherwise, all the election proceedings are vacated, and
a new election must be had for all the Commissioners." It is in strict
accord with the provisions of our law relating to trials, and we recommend its approval.
4. The fourth decision was as follows : "It was asked whether a
Lodge, after it was opened, could be called off for one week. It was
ruled that a Masonic Lodge cannot adjourn ; it must be closed; and
that the meeting of a Lodge must be closed on the day it is opened."
The last sentence of this decision is not absolutely correct. For instance, the business at a stated meeting may be such as to keep the
members engaged until after midnight, and the same may be true of a
meeting convened for the purpose of conferring degrees. A more accurate statement would be that there can be no adjourned meeting, and
that each meeting of a Lodge must be closed when the business which
it is proposed to transact at· that meeting has been concluded. As so
modified, we recommend that the decision be approved.
Respectfully submitted,

At the last Communication various suggestions contained in the
address of Grand Master Lawler were referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence for a report at this Communication:
1. Our law permits a Lodge in this State to confer degrees for
and upon request of a Lodge in another State by which the candidate
has been elected to receive such degrees (Constitution, Section 2, Article
I, Part V). It was suggested by Grand Master Lawler that to insure
against correspondence with clandestine bodies, and to protect against
imposition, all such requests should be made through the Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries of the respective jurisdictions. We agree
that it would be well to make some such requirement for the protection
not only of this jurisdiction, but also the jurisdiction from which the
candidate assumes to hail. It will probably be sufficient to require simply the attestation under seal of his Grand Lodge of the Grand Secretary of the foreign jurisdiction. The matter may be covered by general
regulation. We propose the adoption of the following General Regulation:
"N o Lodge shall confer a degree at the request of and on behalf of
a Lodge belonging to the jurisdiction of any other Grand Lodge, unless
the request of such Lodge be attested by the Grand . Secretary of such
jurisdiction and bear the seal of such Grand Lodge attached."
2. It was suggested that the law should make it the imperative
duty of the appropriate officer to prefer charges against any one convicted in the courts of a crime involving moral turpitude, to the end
that if the conviction in the courts was justified, "the criminal should
find no abiding place in Freemasonry." We cannot doubt that such a
duty exists without special provision therefor, but in order that there
can be no mistake on the part of officers of Lodges in regard thereto,
the suggestion of Grand Master Lawler may well be adopted. We
propose and recommend for adoption the following General Regulation:
"In the event of a final judgment of conviction against a Mason
in the State or Federal ·courts of a crime involving moral turpitude, it
shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of any Lodge"having jurisdiction of such Mason to prefer charges against the Mason so convicted
on account of the matters involved in said COI\Viction; provided, that
such charges have not already been ·preferred, and to press to conclu·sion a trial on account thereof."
3. In the matter of the proposed amendment of Section 1 of Article
XIII of the Uniform Code of By-laws, relating to the method of amendment by the Lodge of its By-laws, we report the following and recommend its adoption :

145

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Section 1 of Article XIII of the Uniform Code of By-laws is hereby
amended to read as follows :
"Section 1. These By-laws, so far as relates to the times of meeting, and the amounts of fees, dues and disbursements by the Charity
Committee, may be amended at any stated meeting by the votes of twothirds of the members present; provided, that written notice of such
amendment shall have been given at the stated meeting next preceding ;
but such amendment shall have no effect until approved by the Grand
Lodge or Grand Master, and until such approval shall have been
transmitted to the Grand Secretary. The Secretary of the Lodge
shall note upon the minutes of the Lodge the notice of proposed
amendment when made, and in transmitting an amendment for approval shall forward a certificate under seal, showing. that the law. h.as
been complied with and that the amendment has recetved the requ1S1te

within the year, should not be .asked for without the greatest and most
Important reason requiring such action. We recommend that his acts in
this matter be approved.

II• were either strictly Masonic in their character or erected for exclu1lvely public purposes, and that, having such views, invitations to lay

.mcl in some, as is stated in the address, is expressly established by law
1111ncted by the Grand Lodge. We recommend that the action of the
Ornnd Master in this behalf be approved.

This being the hour fixed for the annual oration, W. ·.
Charles A. Adams delivered an address on "Masonry in
Business and Politics." It was an address somewhat out
of the beaten path of such efforts, and was so much appreciated that, on motion of R. ·. W. ·. Alonzo J. Monroe, the
hearty thanks of the Grand Lodge were extended to Brother
Adams, and 10,000 copies of his address were ordered
printed, to be distributed by the Grand Secretary to the
Craft throughout the jurisdiction. The full text of the oration is as follows :
MASONRY IN BUSINESS AND POLITICS.
The origin, history and philosophy of Masonry have ever proved
alluring, as well as fruitful and prolific, topics for Grand Orators; and
such is the nature of our Institution with its inexhaustible wealth
of symbolism and sentiment, that ever apparently is there something
yet to be said.
· I have,. however, resisted the allurements of topics such as these,
and have preferred, instead, to improve the opportunity to direct your
attention to a view of Masonry in the concrete.
There will be no pretense at weaving garlands of rhetoric, no
attempt at word painting to picture to your minds the beauties of the
mystical, or mythical, in Masonry; and I want each one of you to
divest your mind of all preconceived ideas of what an oration by a
Grand Orator should be; or, if it will make it more acceptable, to consider what I shall have to say to you not as an oration, but merely as
a plain, honest and sincere talk from one Mason to another upon a
subject which intimately concerns each one of us, "Masonry in Business and Politics."
Now fear not, Brethren, that I purpose introducing into this Grand
Lodge an interdicted topic; this is only another way of saying that I
purpose talking' to you of Masonry in o'ur everyday life; because,
after all, the life of the American Mason, apart from that of his home,
is in business and politics.
First as to business; because, Alas, with us, apparently, business
comes first; and our political action is too frequently dictated by a
regard for our own particular business. I have heard it repeatedly
slated, and the statement justified by the citation of the decisions of
the Committee on Appeals and Grievances, ·n ot only of this, but of other
jurisdictions, that "Masonry is one thing and Business another."

155

GHAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

154

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Brethren, except in the sense in which those decisions must have been
rendered, to the effect that no Mason should be punished because of his
misfortune, or for an honest difference of opinion concerning a business
agreement, I do not believe that "Masonry is one thing and Business
another." As well might it be said that "Honesty is one thing and
Business another;" that " Truth is · one thing and Trade another."
Brethren, did you ever reflect that all Trade, all Commerce is founded
upon Truth? Truth is the backbone of Confidence, and Confidence is
the keynote of Trade.
There is hardly a commercial transaction which can be cited in
which there is not involved this question of confidence in the truth and
honesty of at least one of the contracting parties. Is it unreasonable to
assume that special confidence may be safely reposed in the honesty and
integrity of one in whom has been inculcated the lessons of Masonry?
Should not this be particularly true when we deal with each other?
Our nightly prayer offered up in every Masonic Lodge ta the
Supreme Grand Master is that He will "so influence our hearts and
minds that we may, each one of us, practice out of the lodge, those
great moral duties which are inculcated in it." How that· prayer is
answered, I need not tell you.
To too many of us, I am afraid, our Masonry is what their religion is to some professing Christians ; just as they reserve their
religion for use only on Sundays, so do some of us, I am afraid, reserve our Masonry for our Lodge nights.
No Mason should, of course, bring his business into his Lodge;
but that need not preclude him from taking his Masonry into his
business. N ay, that is his duty; the very name of Mason should be
a guarantee, not alone to the Fraternity, but to the whole world, of
incorruptible honesty, strict integrity, and that personal fidel~ty upon
which every one may, with the utmost confidence, rely.
The merchant who makes no special boast of commercial probity
may attempt to justify the sale of short weight packages as "Trade
Custom;" and may seek to palliate the offense of adulterating his
goods on the score of the "exigencies of unfair competition;" but it is
our proud boast that Masonry sets a higher standard of morals and
virtue than the mere law of the land imposes; and no Mason who
fails to practice as a man, in his business dealings, that which he professes as a Mason, should be permitted to interpose, in extenuation, the
specious plea that "Masonry is one thing and Business another."
The spirit of Masonry should incite us to greater fidelity in the
discharge of every duty; and when a Mason deals with another in
any other manner than .t hat in which he himself would be dealt by, even
though he be not guilty of actual fraud in the eyes of the law, even
though he be not guilty of an offense involving moral turpitude, he
violates the spirit at least, if not the letter of his obligation. He not

only renders himself unworthy to be taken by the hand as a brother,
but he forfeits the right to be known as a Mason.
.
I care not ? ow far, nor with what speed he may have progressed
m the Fraternity. He may be so well provided with the world's
g?ods that he ~ay have been able to pay for degrees enough to make

_Dpon the individual Mason depends the reputation of the Fratermty. Bo.astf~l and proud claims of high morality and virtue, without

If o_ur Institution ever ceases to be, in all things, that which it
was designed to be, it. will be because we talk, and write and think
too much of M asonry m the abstract, and not ertough of Masonry in
~he . c.o ncrete; too much of Masons collectively, and too little of the
md1v1dual Mason.
Th~re seems t~ be a strange disposition, not only within the
Fratermty, but outside of it, in all the movements for the betterment

~ee

e~plo

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of existing conditions, to ignore the importance of the character of the
individual.
Whether the welfare of the general public is to be effected
through a stronger social organization, or through a movement for
greater individual liberty, whether we are to turn to "collectivism" or
"individualism" to avoid the peril to the Republic from the "special
interests," this much seems, to me at least, certain ;-that there will
never be any beneficial, permanent, lasting reform in either our business
or political methods, which does not involve a reform of the individual.
What a government is, and whether truth and justice prevail,
depends upon the individual; because every government is, after all, but
the reflex of the individuals of whom it is composed. No Nation, no
State, no City, ever had a better or worse government than it really
deserved; and much of that of which we complain, in our business and
political methods, is due to the simple fact that it is almost impossible
to convince the ordinary individual that his private interests must
not be served at the expense of the State. Even the best of men,
honest men and otherwise good citizens, will not hesitate to seek from
the Government a special privilege, entirely unmindful of the fact that
it is granted at the expense of the community.
It was only a few weeks ago, that I ran across an article written
by a man who had served many years in Congress, in which it was
stated that 90 per cent of the requests from his constitutents were
for special privileges at the expense of the National Treasury; and
he quoted in its entirety, suppressing only the names, a letter he had
received from the Pastor of his Church in which his good offices,
were sought, and his influence asked, to have placed upon the pensi~n
list, the name of a man who, it was naively admitted, had deserted m
the second year of the war. The Minister's Justification for hi~ .request was that there were thousands of others who wer~ rece1v~ng
pensions to which they were not entitled, and that the man m question
was a burden upon the congregat~on. This, it will be conceded, is an
extraordinary case; but it is more than likely that the Minister who
made that request would be one of the very first to join in the cry
for reform of existing conditions ;-totally unconscious, and in absolute ignorance (at least it is to be hoped so) of the fact that it is
just such requests as that made by him that have brought about the
con"dition which now demands an immediate and radical reform.
But there are those of us who neither seek, nor accept, for ourselves nor for others, special privileges at the expense of the community, who try to live l'ionestly and to deal fairly and justly with all
men, but who as Masons are remiss in the discharge of the civic
duties enjoined upon us.
l confess that I approach this phase of the discussion with some
hesitation ;-not however because I am among the number of those

who believe that this is a matter with which Masonry has no concern;
on the contrary, I believe that there is no higher duty devolving upon
us as Masons than the duty we owe the State as citizens; and one of
the highest duties devolving upon an American citizen is that which
requires him to concern himself with, and take a part in, politics-not
politics in tha.t vile sense of artful or dishonest efforts to secure the
success of party schemes, or even in that less objectionable, but still
restricted, sense of the management of a Political party; but politics in
that higher, broader and larger sense which may be best defined as that
part of ethics which concerns the regulation of a Nation, State or
Community, and the preservation of its safety, peace and prosperity.
In every community there are constantly arising questions which
affect the pub;ic welfare-questions of public morals and good government-concerning which our duty is plain.
But we are today confronted with a condition in which our duty
as Masons is not so clear; a condition which presents a problem to the
solution of which must be brought not only the highest quality of
mind, but which seems to call for a judgment influenced by the peculiar characteristics of the teachings of the Craft.
On the one hand, there are existing evils which must be corrected
if the government is to survive on the lines established by our fathersa government by the People, as well as for the People; on the other
hand, brought about, no doubt, by a recognition of the existence of the
evils of which we complain, and due, perhaps, to an honest and praiseworthy desire to correct them-there is a condition no less intolerable
to the earnest Mason, imbued with the teachings of the Craft, and
who is not swayed by passion or prejudice, nor influenced by the almost
universal popular discontent.
It has come to be the fashion to assail those in high places, and
to impugn their motives and question their honesty. On all sides, from
every source, from the rostrum and from the pulpit, in the columns of
the daily press and in the pages of the monthly magazines, come warnings of a great peril which, it is said, confronts us. We have been
persistently told, and we have begun to believe, that we live in an age
peculiarly subject to the. tyranny of wealth; that all men suffer from
a consuming thirst for gold; that corruption is everywhere ramp.ant,
and that the very foundations of the Republic are tottering beneath the
weight of insatiate greed and inordinate avarice. It would appear that
the world had grown suddenly wicked.
Now, Brethren, Masons should be optimists-not pessimists- •
Things are not as bad as they seem; and the world has not grown
suddenly wicked. There never was a time since the world began when
"man's inhumanity to man" was not the burden of the popular song; and
there never was a time when there did not exist that of which we are

156

157

158

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

now complaining; and this arraignment today of existing conditions is,
of itself, evidence to the thinking man that the world is growing better.
The fact of the matter is that we are passing through what may
be termed the hysteria of an awakened public conscience. Our passions are inflamed by radicals obsessed with the idea of universal corruption. Our judgment is influenced by an appeal to our personal
interests :-For instance, we see the cost of living increasing, and we
are willing to believe that we, the plain people, are the victims of a
gigantic conspiracy designed to crush us. Great good has comegreater good will yet come from this awakening; but the condition is
also pregnant with great evil.
Popular discontent and passion have been stimulated to a pitch
perilously near to class hatred. There has been instilled into the minds
of thousands of our people, a belief that there is no justice in our
Courts for the poor man, and that the deci~ions of our Judges are either
purchased for money, or rendered in accordance with class sympathy.
The highest Court in the land-"The Greatest Court in Christendom"is not, it would appear, secure against unjust criticism. Here Brethren, is a real danger to the Republic.
"The Honest Lawyer" is a jest as old as the profession itself; the
lawyers have survived it, and no harm has been done. But Brethren,
when you make a jest and byword of the honor of our Judges, and
the sanctity of our Courts, you imperil a safeguard of American liberty.
Courts and Judges are not above criticism, and honest Judges do
not resent it; but they have a right to expect, and it is our duty to
insist, that that criticism shall be just. It is not sufficient that the
critic shall be honest, but he must be likewise qualified and competent
to pass judgment upon that which he criticises. Indiscriminate and
unjust and ignorant criticism not only tends to weaken that respect for
our Courts upon which their usefulness depends, but it, of itself, defeats
its very purpose. To criticise a Court for rendering a decision which
proves unpopular; although justified and req11ired by the law, is to invite
and encourage corruption and dishonesty in the judiciary. It serves
notice upon every Judge upon the Bench that the esteem in which he
will be held by the public, and the probability of his re-election, depend
not upon his honesty and integrity-not upon his learning and ability,
but upon his willingness to prostitute his high office to the appeal of
public clamor.
Here, Brethren, I say is a danger to the Republic against which
we must firmly and sternly set our faces; and this is but one of the
evils which result from that unworthy willingness-nay that despicable
eagerness-with which we credit every statement which impugns the
motives, or questions the honesty, of men in public life.
I canMt but believe, unpopular though that belief may be, that inseparably connected with our duty to stand for good government, and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

159

I• > array ourselves with those who are opposing corruption in public

life, is another duty no less incumbent upon us :-incumbent upon us as
iiood citizens as well, and particularly, as good Masons ;-and that is to
uphold the hands of those in authority, and to encourage and support
them with our respect and confidence until, convinced by evidence, and
not influenced by vague suspicion, we have reason to believe that they
have ceased to deserve it.
It seems to me that when we do less than this, we have failed in
•>Ur duty as Masons; because we have not rendered unto every man
his just due; and we have suffered our passions and our prejudices to
become the masters of our judgment.
There is evil enqugh of which we may justly complain. In too
many instances great wealth has been acquired by means, which if
not illegal, are at least, from an ethical standpoint, illegitimate. Too
frequently has organized capital illegitimately and arrogantly interfered with, and attempted to control, the election of candidates for
public office. In too many instances for government by the people
has there been substituted government by what has come to be known
ns "The. Interescs." Bribery and corruption do exist, and are not
excused by the fact that they have always existed.
Today one can hardly pick up one of the popular priced magazines without finding an account either of some illegitimate scheme of
the predatory rich to prey upon the people, or of the exposure, somewhere, of the depths of political degradation to which some men are
willing to descend; and always at the end comes the query, "What are
you going to do about it?"
Truly, Brethren, a difficult question, notwithstanding the fact that
the radical is ready with his answer. Unfortunately, however, there
appear to be as many different answers as there are different kinds of
radical. Just at present there seems to be a trend throughout the
country toward a movement for a third party. This is neither the
time, nor the place, to discuss· that question. This much, however, I
think I may with propriety say concerning it,-reiterating the opinion I
have already expressed. Neither through a third, nor through a thirtieth
party will there come a lasting reform which does not involve a reform
of the individual. The reform of the individual will be brought about
only by a crystallized public sentiment expressed in no uncertain terms
-expressed not in vague generalities as to the desirability for a reform, expressed not by the substitution of office holders of one political
faith for office holders of another political faith,-but expressed by the
manner in which we treat the individual. The means by which the
individual will be reformed are, I believe, at hand, and will effect his
reform when we are big enough and brave enough, and have the moral
I
courage, to make use of them.

160

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

If you and I, and every honest man, here and everywhere, in every
walk of life, will refuse to consider as our social equal the man who
even while keeping within the pale of. the law, transgresses the plain
proprieties of honest business and social inten:ourse, if we refuse. to
take his hand, if we refuse to bow to him in the street, or to recognize
him except as an unclean thing, contact with whom must contaminate ·
every honest man, the goal for which we are contending will soon be
in sight. Men do not strive for great wealth for the mere gratifica.tion of their material wants. All that a man has, Emerson says, will
he give for right relations with his mates. Even the power which
wealth brings will not compensate for the loss of human intercourse
with those who he knows, and the world knows, are honest men, and
whose companionship he desires.
Refuse that intercourse to those whose only claim thereto is the
dishonestly acquired wealth they have accumulated, and the incentive
to amass money is removed. Let it once be known in any community
that no matter what a man may have, or who he may be, if he be not
honest there shall 'be withheld from him the companionship of all
decent men and women, and a greater stride will have been made for
the moral uplift of that community than could ever be effected by all the
power and majesty of the law.
·
When every individual shall have been convinced of the good
which he can individually accomplish, when all of us shall have become
possessed of that great moral courage required for the strict performance of the duty devolving upon us as men, and as Masons, when
we practice out of our Lodges the lessons we are taught in them,
when we 1 in truth, render unto every man his just due, without distinction then there will have been created and crystallized a public
sentime~t against which greed and dishonesty and vice and corruption
will not dare contend.
The objection which has been made to the remedy proposed is
that it is Utopian; so is perfection in government Utopian; and yet we
strive for it. And what, after all, is there Utopian about the ·plan,
except in the single idea that there can be found men willing to blind
their eyes against the dazzling rays of yellow gold? Are the teachings
of our Craft Utopian? Is it Utopian to believe that it is the internal,
and not the external, qualifications which recommend a man, and determine our relationship with him?
There are, no doubt, some of you who know of at least one man
whom you would not permit to enter your homes, and to whom you
refuse social recognition, either because of his occupation, or because of
the fact that by his own misconduct he has forfeited all claim to recognition by decent men. It requires no moral courage upon our part to
socially ostracize such a man, betause a sufficient number of men have
already determined to, and do, withhold their companionship from him;

11nd so it would appear that the remedy suggested is extraordinary and
Utopian not in the direction, but only in the length of the step.
Brethren, because the world is surely and steadily growing better,
the day will come when it will be thought strange and extraordinary
that an honest man was ever willing to consider as his social equal, one
who he had reason to believe, and who was known in the community
H, a malefactor-whether a malefactor of wealth or of poverty.
And until that day comes, and that it may be the sooner here, each
r>f us must do his whole duty as· he sees it; and this, Brethren, as it
1ccms to one who loves Masonry · is our duty as "Masons in Business
nnd Politics ;"-to live honestly and uprightly; to act fairly and justly
with all men ; in business as in all else, to deal as we would be dealt
by; to take an active and intelligent interest, not only in public questions involving the whole nation, the welfare of the whole people, but
na well in the politics of our own communities-to cast our ballots for
no man whom we do not believe upright and honest, and fitted for the
office to which he aspires; and above all, to be faithful and loyal to the
1rovernment under which we live, and to be willing and anxious to
believe that in our public servants, as in other men, goodness and truth
and honor and virtue do exist, and will be discovered when we seek
for their motives with the searchlight of true Masonic charity-that
charity "which envieth not and doth not think evil and rej oiceth not in
iniquity ;"-the simple creed of a good Mason, and an honest American
citizen, the highest and noblest type of manhood.

as prayed for, to: La Mesa, Honolulu, Charter Rock, Calexico, Arlington, Silver Trowel, Lindsay, Elysian and Clovis.
In this connection we cannot refrain from calling special attention
to the exceptional clearness, beauty and exactness of the records of
Silver Trowel Lodge, and the member of your Committee to whom
was assigned the pleasant ditty of examination of these records feels,
together with the Committee as a whole, that a word of commendation is due in this regard. •
In the matter of the petition of Sierra Madre Lodge for a Charter,
your Committee found the records badly arranged and kept, but would
recommend the granting of a Charter to this Lodge with the und.erstanding that their entire record shall •be re-written and properly arranged, and would suggest that the Inspector of that District assume
P,ersonal supervision of ·that task.
In the matter of the petition of Perris Lodge for a Charter, your
Committee finds that while the various legal steps essential to the formation of a new Lodge have been followed, still there are marked errors
and omissions in the records as presented. Afrer consultation with the
Master of this Lodge, and his promise to see these deficiencies supplied,
we deem it our duty to recommend the granting of a Charter to this
Lodge upon this understanding and condition.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In the matter of the application of Waucoba Lodge for a Charter,
your Committee is confronted with a peculiar situation. While the preliminary steps in the formation of this Lodge have been carefully and .
regularly taken, through some misunderstanding, the Secretary has
failed to transmit any records and we have therefore nothing upon
which to act. The Master of this Lodge, however, assures us that the
records have been carefully and correctly kept and are in due form ;
and believing that the Lodge should not suffer unduly for the ignorance
or mistake of the Secretary, when no matter of principle is involved
and the interests of Masonry cannot be made to suffer thereby, we
would recommend in this connection that the Inspector of that District,
together with the Master of the Lodge, make a careful examination of
its records, and if they shall find them in due form and so report to
the Grand Secretary, that a Charter be thereupon issued to Waucoba
Lodge.
In the matter of the consolidation of Hesperian Lodge No. 264
and Santa Maria Lodge No. 340, under the name and number of Hesperian Lodge No. 264, we note that the Secretary of Santa Maria Lodge
states in his minutes that the written consent of more than two-thirds
of the members has been received. This statement ·in the minutes does
not do justice to the occasion or to the facts; the record abundantly·
shows that the legal percentage of consent, namely, more than threefourths, has been obtained, and we would suggest that this manifest
clerical error be corrected for the sake of the perfection of the record.
It appearing then that all legal requirements have· been complied with
we recommend· that the aforesaid consolidation be ratified and confirmed.
In the matter of the consolidation of Nevada Lodge No. 13, Quitman
Lodge No. 88 and Manzanita Lodge No. 102, under the name and
number of Nevada Lodge No 13, it appears that all the legal steps have
been properly taken with the exception that the notice of the proposed
consolidation, directed to the members of Manzanita Lodge No. 102,
is a trifle shorter than the letter of the law prescribes, but inasmuch
as ·the object contemplated by the law, namely, the assent of more
than three-fourths of the members of the Lodge, has been obtained,
we feel that the technical infraction of the strict legal requirement
should be overlooked and recommend that the consolidation of the
Lodges named under the name and number of Nevada Lodge No. 13 be
ratified and confirmed.
It appears that Upland Lodge, located at Upland, California, to
whom a dispensation was granted, not having done any degree work ha~
not applied for a Charter at this Communication of the Grand Lodge.

We would, therefore, recommend that the dispensation issued to that
Lodge be continued in force until the 30th of September, 1911.
All which is fraternally submitted.

Brother Walter F . Haas, from the same Committee,
presented the following report:
To the M.". W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom was referred the papers and correspondence in the matter of charges of unmasonic conduct preferred
against Brother James Jones, a member of Jefferson Lodge, No. 97, .,at
La Porte, by Brother A. Harris, of said Lodge, which charges the
Master refused to entertain, report that the purported charges were insufficient in this: that Brother Harris charges that Brother Jones came
to him and offered to redeem certain mining properties which had
been sold under execution; that, instead of redeeming the property,
Brother Jones let the title pass to the purchaser and subsequently bought
in the property in his own name. But Brother Harris does not charge
that it was his (Harris') intention to redeem the property, or that he
(Harris) had tendered to Brother Jones his (Harris') part of the redemption price. Had these allegations been incorporated in the
charge and specifications, the Master should have entertained the same.
These charges were presented to W. C. Quigley, Master of Jefferson Lodge, No. 97, and ·he refused to entertain them on the ground
that no Masonic offense had been stated in the charges and .specifications. Brother Harris appealed to the Grand Master, and all the papers
connected therewith were turned over to this Committee.

We have had same under consideration and beg leave to report
as follows:
It appears that Brother Harris first made verbal charge in open
Lodge against Brother Jones; that the Master told him to put his
charges in writing as required by our Masonic law, which was subsequently done; but the Master declined to call an election for the reason
that the charges, if proven, as stated, would not constitute a Masonic
offense.

We are ~f the opinion that the Master was justified in refusing to
act upon said charges as preferred, for the reasons hereinabove stated.
We therefore offer the following resolution, and recommend its adoption:

Brother James Jones in said Lodge, be and the same is hereby approved; but this action does not prohibit proper and sufficient charges
being preferred by Brother Harris if he so desires.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom was referred that portion of the report
of the Directors of the Masonic Home relative to the Hospital, the
gift of Very Worshipful Edward Coleman, have had the same under
consideration, and. believe that such a gift should have recognition from
the Grand Lodge at this annual Communication, as well as when
the building is completed and ready to be transferred to the Board
of Directors of the Masonic Home of California. Brother Coleman, in
making such a gift, exemplifies the true teachings of Masonry. Such
a gift as this is but a faint resemblance of Heaven, where unity, harmony and love reign triumphant. This gift of Brother Coleman reflects
the Masonic teachings. It is not simply the gift of this perfectly
equipped building, the relieving of the actual bodily wants, of which
we wish to express our heartfelt appreciation: It requires at our hands
remembrance of Edward Coleman's personal expression of Masonic
love for the Father and Giver of All. What can we do for our
Heavenly Father who has done and is doing so much for us? Just what
Brother Coleman has ·done. In the recognition of His great goodness,
with a greatful heart Brother. Coleman bestows some of the -gifts
which have been bestowed upon him, upon his less fortunate and distressed brethren, who like us all recognize the Fatherhood. The hand
of our beloved Brother, raised in thanksgiving, has opened in charity,
fully exemplifying our beautiful teachings. The virtue of charity is the
duty arising from the Brotherhood of man, which directly flows from
the Fatherhood of God. Such acts of love and charity will act and
guide us as a "Principle," long after our beloved Brother's immortal soul
has passed from among us. May this building stand for many years as
a harmonious principle of pure affection for humanity, and creating love
for the human race, and as an encouragement for all Masons to imitate.
May Masons for generations point with honorable pride at the building,
which will stand as a monument to the memory of Brother Coleman
and his beautifully exemplified Masonic teachings, "Unselfish Charity."

Eulogy by Charles L. Patton.
Toda in a splendid mansion, high on the hills of . our western
tro oli~' overlooking the beautiful bay of San Francisco and the

And today, in this hall, with our columns, jewels, and working
tt>oh draped in mourning, our hearts filled with sorrow, in silence and
11dne&s we lament the untimely death of our Grand Master; and
throughout the world, wherever Masons are found, is a deep and
1lncere grief at the death of this good man; not the cold philosophic
rrlef that comes when we lament the death of a good man unknown
to us, but the deep, the agonizing sorrow that we feel when those
die whom we have known and loved. So true is this, that many say
from the bottom of their hearts, "would that one of us had been taken
In his place, and he spared to continue his work for Masonry and
mankind."'
It now remains for us but to voice this feeling and to record what
manner of man and Mason this was, whose loss is so deeply felt by all.
William Frank Pierce was born January 16, 1855, in the town of
Ripley, Chautauqua County, New York; was educated in the public
1chools and at Alleghany College, Meadville, Pennsylvania. He came .
to California, arriving July 20, 1877, settled in Oakland, and with his
father and brother Charles D. Pierce, engaged in business.
Public life had no charms for him. A man of powerful mind,
masterful in his dealings with men, skilled in financial affairs, with
unerring judgment in matters of business, he met with great success
In all his enterprises. The field of his first endeavors becoming too
nnrrow for his ever growing capacity, he left Oakland in 1888, and in
San Francisco widened and deepened his grasp in things commercial.
Ile was the head of a great banking institution and director and
Mdviser in many successful corporations. The longer he was known
the more intimately all became acquainted with his great worth. It
was found that he neglected nothing. He was faithful to every trust.
The best financiers were glad to confide important matters to his
Judgment. So that, when death came, October 3, 1910, though young
In years, having sufficient of the world's goods, he was preparing to
leave behind him many of his business cares and devote his life to
those matters which always seemed to him more important and of
1reater benefit than the accumulation of money.
It was impossible that the mere gathering together of a large
fortune sh,ould satisfy his intense feeling that he must do something to
make the world greater and better for his having lived, and he found
the true sphere of his usefulness in Masonry.
We give you here his Masonic record, which it is fitting should
be at this time definitely placed upon the pages of our History. It
11 indeed a grand one, but no words of mine could picture the. deep
love of his work and the great grasp of his mind in dealing with those
fundamental truths of the Craft which so many men, though Masons
and though holding ' the ' highest offices in th~ gift of Masonry, fail '

Mystic Shrine and a Past Patron of the Eastern Star.
This record of our Brother's office-holding does not give, nor
can it give, the remotest idea of his activity in the field of Masonry.
In 1906 when the greater part of San Francisco was swept away by
fire and earthquake and the foundations of our Masonic Temple laid
low, the world sprang to our assistance. Masonry everywhere poured
into the treasury the needed money to give relief to the suffering of
the Craft. Then it was that the opportunity came for some great and
noble Mason to show his zeal for his Brethren by organizing the
disbursement of the fund, and, as is always true on important occasions, when the need was greatest, the man was found. Brother Pie~ce
took charge of this tremendous duty, and for more than a year, with
his own fortune in the balance because of the destruction of property
.in this city almost his entire time night and day, was devoted to the ·
great work of relieving distressed Masons, their wives, widows an.d
orphans suffering under the grievous burden cast upon them by ~ht~
awful disaster. It would be impossible for words to convey how important was this work, how tenderly, carefully, and with what
Brotherly love he took charge of it. Nor can we ever tell what an
enormous amount of real thought and brain work he gave to the task.
Ntver was he satisfied to merely give money to a worthy Brother;
he thought of . the future and insisted upon finding employment for
him wherein he could build up his fortune again and achieve greater
success than before, for he always held to the fundamental principle
that true charity consists in helping tho Brethren to help themselves.

Ilundreds, even thousands, of men, women and children are succe·sshll today who owe to our Brother Pierce their new start in life. While
he was so true to the principles of Freemasonry that not a dollar of
the funds of the Craft was disbursed to aid any but those strictly
rntltled to its assistartce, yet, such was his feeling for humanity in
sreneral, that from his private purse he relieved all worthy cases comln1r under his notice even when the recipient was not entitled to
Masonic charity.
I cannot bear to close without at least trying to paint a picture
of Brother Pierce as I saw him and as we all knew him. This it is
almost impossible to do because he was so well balanced physically
and mentally that there were but few salient points which would
present the man to you. Many can be described with a word, for in
them some characteristic stands out and serves to accentuate and
1lve detail to the presentment, but Brother Pierce's character was
10 complete in all its parts, so full of excellencies that there is no
one thing about him upon which we could partic~larly dwell. The
nearest expression I could give of his character would be to convey
to you the tremendous forcefulness of the man, together with his
wondrous gentleness. If he had a fault in the world it was that
he desired to please everybody. He would always do what was right,
but he wanted to do it in a way that would grieve no one. It is 21
pleas~re to think of him in any of the affairs of life, in any of the
functions of Masonry, but I love best to think of him seated in a
chair .with a .d~zen or more of ~is Brethren around him, entertaining
All with reminiscences and stories drawn from his own experience.
Every incident told by him, every thought expressed by him the
most innocent child might hear, yet the deepest mind listen to' with
profit. His indeed was a wonderful nature. So profound was he
that at times one would be startled by the depth of hi& lightest ·
remark, and yet so appreciative of the ligh,ter side of life that all
were entertained by his expressive words.
We can never know the man completely without thinking of him
In his home life. It was a pleasure to see him and his wife working
together in the ways of doing good. I remember the.m both in 1898
laboring for the success of the Masonic Fair which made the buildin~
of the Home at Decoto an actual and accomplished fact. Their home
life was ideal. What a shock when his wife was taken from him but
th:ir daughters were well fitted to take the mother's place. How
faithfully, unselfishly and nobly these three vied one with the other to
lighten the father's burden. Then, too, we all remember how last
year during the session of the Grand Lodge word came to him that
his brother was dying. How quickly he left us and went to his
bedside. Few can ever realize what it meant to him to lose this
brother, his closest associate in childhood, youth and manhood.

Memorial Address of William R . Davis.
William Frank Pierce, Worshipful Grand Master of all Masons
of this jurisdiction, has crossed over. I knew him by a shorter name
1i. Frank, and he knew me by a name as short.
For twenty-five years
we have so hailed each other in unbroken fellowship and with the
Intimacy of boys. Grown to the estate of large manhood in stature,
In mind and in character, he yet maintained throughout these years
the frankness, simplicity and candor of boyhood. Men of the larger
mould employ no affectation in order to be recognized. From their
conscious rectitude emanates a steadier light than shines from the
helmet of a prince and the merit of their lifelong worth outranks
the ostentatious ermine of a king. Frank Pierce was a man of the
larger mould.
IN BusrN.ESS diligent and successful, but square and clean 11s a
cube of marble. Considerate of the rights of others he also knew
his own, and he knew the make of men as if by intuition. He seldom,
If ever, wrongly put up or put down a fellow man. He seemed never to
forget that like begets like, and in extending an accommodation · it
was done with such good will and graciousness withal that if a man
before had paid but scant heed to the moral factor involved in square
dealing, he felt bound to respond to this obligation as a debt of honor.
I le made men better. Himself having honor, he imparted it to others,
11nd no business that his hand ever touched but was bettered by that
touch. In earlier days in Oakland, before there was an organized
Ruilder's Exchange, his place of business was the voluntary meeting
place of the trades and contractors of the city. Every Saturday
night hundreds assembled there, and the store actually became the
unofficial clearing house of the building business of a city. Payments
were made and payrolls receipted there. If a reputable contractor
needed ready money for his men, the Pierces advanced it. At noon
on Saturdays they often drew dry their own account at b? nk to
advance it by evening through contractors' hands to cancel payrolls
and meet the needs of the men and their families. Who would not
hold such an advance a debt of honor? I asked him once if he found
these weekly advances, amounting in the aggregate to no mean sums,
were safe as a business transaction and he answered : "The safest
credits we have in the business." Frank P ierce knew tbat like begets
like.
As CrTIZ!:'.N the same standard of high personality prevailed. Whenever he participated in political or public matters it was in support
only of what he deemed for the public welfare, in aid of the general
concern. We did not always agree upon methods, but we never varied
In mutual respect or departed from the highest reciprocal regard. On
one occasion I remember the delegation from our county of which he

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

was chairman, which had been seated in the State Convention at
Sacramento, was unseated in favor of the contesting delegation of
which I was chairman. When the ruling was announced and the
unseated delegation rose and walked down the aisle while my delegation and myself passed in to the seats which the others had just
vacated Frank and myself met in the aisle. He grasped my hand
as of yore and I his, myself saying "I'm sorry you'.ve got to go, Frank";
and he, "It's all right, Will." In that moment there stood combined in
him both the man and the citizen of the larger mould-fair in contest, loyal in defeat, true as steel in both.
IN THE FAMILY his life was a standard. Able to provide and
protect, he did both as though wife and children were part of himself,
their comfort and welfare his own, in their happiness his, in their
good name and standing his generous pride. A thought of himself
was only to find how self could best serve those bound to him, as
he to them, by the terrestrial ties of a celestial love. To him home
was a castle, he its defender and they the light and joy within it
which by day brightened its daylight and by night shone through its
windows. I know that sorrow has taken the place of that light and
joy, yet there is a sweet and potent memory there which assuages the
bitterness and lights somewhat the face of that sorrow. Though he
be dead, yet he liveth.
CoNsIDl!RING HIM AS A MASON ; I have sometimes likened such characters as his to a steel frame building, and we may well do so in this
presence. To the eye the outer walls of stone, or it may be of marble,
the columns, the pilasters and the rest look like vital parts and supports of the building. Yet we know they are there only to make the
enclosure and incidentalty to ornament the real strength and structure
within. You may strip away the outer walls, the columns, the pilasters
and all the rest, but the structure of the building stands as sound and
strong as ever. On every floor the occupants could remain unharmed
and pursue their vocations as before. The strength of the building is
unimpaired, its frame and character and the life it bears remain
uninjured. So, with such a character as his. The insignia of office,
the regalia of post and station, the habiliments of rank, are no more than
the shell outside the build of character and the life-spirit within.
It may be wealth : Strip that away, yet the tested character in its tried
manhood remains. It may be official position: Transfer that to
another, yet the man of larger mould stands secure in his own rectitude and reliant in his consciousness of the stability of the make and
build of his character. It may even be the hand of death loosening his
every hold upon the things of this world and beckoning him away from
those who have gathered close about him as if with the four walls of
their love, yet the conscious spirit of such a man yielding all hold and
all ties here faces yonder withoiit fear or trepidation, knowing that the

Great Architect and Builder of the universe is not without merciful
consideration of all human kind and that He will not wholly condemn
the framework and build of such a human life.
The memorable record of our brother has been written by the
Masonic pen of the past twenty-five years. Not a blemish nor a blot is
there, nor has one erasure ever had to be made. It is all fair, all just,
all pure. His earthly story is told. He fought the good fight, he
finished the course, he kept the faith. And as his spirit rose from its
habitation of clay, now consigned to its long home, the recording angel
in his book on high had no more to do than to turn to his own transcript of this earthly record, seeing there the sufficient passport for the
soul of William Frank Pierce to pass on through the gates of pearl.
I have said thus much of the high personality of this just man.
Saying no more upon that, and believing indeed that he himself would
wish that I had said less, I pass on to a general thought deemed worthy
of our consideration and appropriate to the place and hour.
There is a constitution not framed by man. We come under its
sway-whence, no science tells. It is the law of things. We join the
terrestrial drift, the cosmic drift, which it pervades, and progresswhither, no learning tells. It is the law of things. What surrounds
and accompanies us is named environment. To this, research, learning,
method. bend themselves until the human eye spells out the microcosm
and penetrates all-holding space. The intellectual flower of every
nation upon the earth, which thus far has come to flower, is questioning, penetrating, conquering, this vast environment. It resists us ; it
molds us; it appalls us. Of this pre-human and supra-human constitution of things it is a part that there is that which will assail, as well
as that to be assailed. Environment is the cosmic anvil; man, the
living hammer. Environment, the banks; man, the river.· Environment, the sky and landscape; man, the eagle who soars in one and
scans the. other. It is the law of things. The lower law is that of the
anvil, resistance; the higher, that of the hammer, mastery. The
lower law is but habitation and air; the higher is flight by wing,vision, the wider horizon and the deeper sky.
It is the immutable law of things. A resisting environment is no
more a part of the great constitution of things than is the law of man's
mastery of it by purpose, discovery, appropriation.
Notwithstanding an environment of abattis, I will assail it. It is
here ; but I, too, am here. It is the law ; but so am I. It resists ; but
I overcome. It challenges; but I prevail. It is the constitution of
things in part against me; but I, too, have the constitution of things
with me.
There is an awareness that is universal. The inanimate tendrils
sway in the air like fingers reaching for support. One tendril touches
the trellis, and the awareness in the vine takes hold of its support as a

186

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

child clasps its father's hand. Who teaches 'the v.ine in the cellar to
creep .to the window? It is aware. Cut the roots of the locust ten
feet deep in the earth, leave the excavation open, and the root becomes
a stem, a foliag~bearing, flowering tree, I have seen it. Awareness
in the root, a mere gatherer of nourishment in the dark, becomes leaf,
trunk, and flower in the light. There is an awareness, whether we
wake or sleep, which renews and remakes our bodies for us. The unconscious eye is exposed to a fierce light, and the guard on duty at
the pupil contracts it, closes the curtains, and shuts out th~ light,-·
awareness on guard. The yet unseeing linnets in the nest hear their
mother's call, and the awareness in the fledgings tells them to open
their mouths for food, which comes neither by road nor rail. There
i$ an awareness in· the unconscious mother-blood of the race, which
~hange~ it by loving alchemy when the time is fulfilled, and pours it as
milk into jhe marble fountain, as well as there is awareness in the
new-born, which .turns its yet unfed lips for sustenance to that holy
fpuntain, a mother's bi:east. Awareness universal,-unconscious and
consc;ious. It is in the constitution of things.
Amidst all this s~nds man, aware of his environment, aware of
the great constitution of things; that it has established around him
resistance and mystery; that. it has ordained, also, the uncovering of
s~crets, th~ progressive acquisition and jurisdiction of man, and has
made him conscious of his power of conquest ·and dominion. Shall he
nqt,. in his conscious awareness, run to the light jf a vine does, climb
up enduring and uplifting supports if the blind tendril does, guard
the higher spirit .that he sees with if the pupil of the eye does, feed
the, helpless if the li.nnet does, and with conscious will turn strength
into achievement if the unconscious mother-blood .of woman turns
it!\elf into milk to strengthen the yet helpless lions of the race?
If anything is true, it is true everywhere and forever that the sum
of the angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles; that greater
means more than less;. that convergence .is different from divergence;
that every point ·is the center of an infinite sphere. But these are no
more a part of the constitution of things, than that sympathy and
antipathy are opposite; · that malevolence and benevolence part ways;
that the giving of a cup of cold water is one thing, and a stab in the
dark is another; that selfishness deserts, unselfishness co-operates and
sacrifices, mercy forgives, and the torches of sentient intelligence give
light to . other kindred understandings. This constitution of things
makes me think that the abstract laws of space and quantity are not
the only perpetuities. There is no reason why greater should be more
than less forever, and yet have benevolence, forever good, perish;
nor why convergence should be different from divergence forever, and
yet have unselfishness perish from constituted things; nor why light
should be different from darkness forever, ana yet there come a time

GHAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

187

when all sentient lights are extinguished from the cosmos, leaving its
1batractions alone, the unconscious perpetuities, to endure. The mathen111tical perpetuities of the cosmos, perceived by the awareness of the
Intellect, are true through no greater lapse of time or wider reaches of
1pace, than are the other laws perceived by the awareness of the under1tanding which takes hold of them, call it what you will. This thought
makes me think we do not perish. A cosmic jest it is, if the laws of
quantity and direction are eternal, and the laws of sentient consciousness run out. The irony of swallowing up in the vortex of annihilation
nil these conscious intelligences, one by one, leaving to remain in perpetuity only insensate abstraction and insensate matter could only
mean that life :md the earth are but a trick in the universe and that
man, the summit of terrestrial creation, is only a cosmic plaything.
Dut the splendor~ of the universe bear upon their face no leer as of
n trick and the glories of the cosmos bear upon their countenance no
grimace as of a jest.
I have gripped this thought as another hold in support of our
belief in immortality and in all reverence leave it with you in addition
to the Masonic faith founded upon holy writ.
Born of woman, man comes into the world its most helpless
creature. He cannot turn in his cradle. He finds his feet and thinks
them playthings. His first journey is upon all fours, his face downward to the earth. He sits unsteady like one drunken. He travels
with trepidation from one chair to the other at hand and glories in the
journey safely ended as though he had made the journey from J erusalem to Joppa. But soon he walks, his face bearing forward, boyhood·
shining in it. And then comes adolescence, when the spirit of high
ambition first whispers in his ear and life takes on a new significance
and his eye a deeper look. Then come maturity and manhood. The
eye challenges the horizon and dares to turn aloft to the stars. The
heart grows, it shelters others, it enfolds them. The intellect partakes
of the truths of the land, the sea and the sky, of the depths of time
and of the depths of space. Helpless yesterday, today he is master of
himself and minister to his fellow men-strong, gentle, just. There is
somewhat of divinity that deigns to dwell beneath the skies in human
habitation. It is ordained by nature and by nature's God that, if he
will, man may be its keeper in the red room of his heart.
Such is man. Such was William Frank Pierce"the elements
So mixed in him, that nature might stand up
And say to all the world, This was a man."

Brother Church, from the same committee, also reported as follows :
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The following communication was referred to your Committee on
Grievances for consideration and such recommendation as it should
deem advisable:
Palo Alto, October 8, 1910.
I was initiated, passed and raised in Bodega Lodge, No. 213, about
1875-76. Remained a member of that Lodge until about 1877, when
several members living at Duncan's Mill withdrew and organized
Brotherhood Lodge of that place, of which I was first Senior Warden,
John Orr, Master; C. E. Tibbits, Junior Warden; S. M. Duncan, Secretary. At the time five or six of us advanced $40.00 each with the understanding it was to be returned to us in dues as soon as possible.
In 1879, I left Duncan's Mill and went to British Columbia. A few
months later I got a note from the Secretary, saying that unless I settled
my dues soon, I would be suspended for non-payment of dues. · Being at
that time down with typhoid fever·, I had my attendant (a brothei:
Mason) write the Secretary of my condition and requested him to apply·
the money I had advanced to my dues, and hearing nothing from him,
supposed he had done so; but on returning a year or so later, found he
had not done so, and that I had been suspended for non-payment.
Becoming indifferent, after the way they had acted in the matter,
and drifting into Arizona and Mexican mining camps where no Masonic
Lodge existed, I neglected taking further action in the matter until a
year or more before the fire, when I called on the Grand Secretary, and
we went over the books of Brotherhood Lodge together: He said he
could see no good reason why I should not be reinstated if I paid one
year's dues into the Grand Lodge, which would reinstate me into
Brotherhood Lodge, and one year's dues, ~hich is customary in such
cases, but asked me to ·call again and in the meantime would look into

192

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

· the matter more thoroughly. I did call several times, but failed to see
him. Three years ago about this time, I saw the Grand Secretary again
and we went and consulted the Grand Master. They concluded they
could do nothing themselves and that it would have to come before the
Grand Lodge, and as I was about to start East to be gone several
months and could not attend to the matter at that time, neglected it
until the present time. These are the facts in the case, with dates as
near as I can remember them.
Respectfully yours,
(Signed) BENTON R. W1LTSE.
P. S.-Know of only one living member of Brotherhood Lodge at

It appears from this statement, which the Committee accepts as a

to recall the facts at this late date, that in the year 1877, when Brotherhood Lodge was organized, he advanced the sum of $40.00 to be applied

whether or not he paid his dues up to the time he left Duncan's Mill in

months thereafter that he would be suspended unless he paid up. It is

was suspended, and he allowed more than twenty years to pass before
making any effort whatever to recover his standing as a Master Mason.
Even during the last eight or ten years his efforts and anxiety have not
been · very considerable or commenda,ble. Our information, however, is
that he is a man of upright conduct and good reputation in the community where he lives, and that he is highly regarded by the brethren of
the Lodge in that vicinity, and that they would without exception be glad
to have him restored to his standing as a Mason, and would thereafter
allow him to affiliate as a member of their Lodge.
Brotherhood Lodge has long been extinct by reason of the voluntary
surrender of its charter. Of course, if Brother Wiltse be restored, it
can only be by the action of this Grand Lodge, and in case of his restoration, he would occupy the position of a non-affiliated Mason or
Mason at large.
With such facts and information as the Committee has been able to
obtain, it thinks it proper and no more than right to recommend that
Brother Wiltse be restored to good standing as a Mason.

"In 1869 a new order appeared in Spain, named the National Grand
Orient of Spain, thereby creating the first schism in Spanish Masonry
and establishing two· jttrisdictions.
"This schismatic Grand Orient appealed for recognition to the
c;rand Orients of the Nations of the world.
"In reply the Grand Orients of England and Switzerland favored
n~ither side but urged uniting while recognition was granted by the
following Grand Orients :-France, Rome, Turin, Naples, Egypt, Haiti,
Columbia, Venezuela, Peru, Mexico, Argentine and minor ones, and by
Albert Pike, S. G. C. of the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States,
who wrote and argued that the men who composed it had no superiors
in Spain, intellectually and socially considered. ·
"In 1880, or eleven years later, the Schismatic National Grand
Orient of Spain ceased to exist.
"The Schism of 1869 left its effect, for in 1889, some of the Schismatic Masons a~ain appeared and in conjunction with Masons ambitious for Masonic power and honors or impelled by personal material
Interests, founded the Spanish Grand Orient. Among them, Miguel
Morayta (a schismatic Mason, who was expelled by the Grand Orient
of Spain for having forsworn his 30th degree-decree of expulsion
pronounced Feb. 23, 1872 and published at the time to the world) is at
present the Sovereign Grand Commander.
"The result of this last schism, now existing for the past twenty
years, operated and maintained by forsworn Masons, many of whom
had been expelled from or were without standing in the Order, has
been most unfortunate for Spanish Masonry.
"The Grand Orient of Spain has striven to avoid it, for it foresaw,
with profound sorrow, the inevitable lowering and lessening of Masonic
influence and actions so necessary in Spain where men are exploited
and considered as things-not as men.
"During these twenty years .Spanish Masonry has suffered retrogression and defeat by revolt in its ranks, yet during that period the
Grand Orient of Spain has labored honestly and constantly to perform
its duty and maintain its authority as being the only regular and legitimate Grand Body of Spain, and though the example of its honest, constant and active labors has sought to draw to itself the recognition and
support of all the Grand Masonic Powers of the Universe, in order to
achieve Masonic Unity in Spain and united Masonic action, to preserve
such public liberties as have been conquered in the past and to continue
our Masonic work for social advancement, etc., etc.

other Grand Orient of Spain-not entitled to recognition.

It will be noticed that a claim has been made that a Lodge called
St. Julie was founded in Madrid at the end of the Eighteenth century.
Where this lodge received its charter is not stated, but the main and
only claim for origin is based on the authority of one Count de GrasseTilly.
A Grand Lodge could not have been formed from this one Lodge,
admitting it was a tegu'larly chartered Lodge from a proper Masonic
power, for the reason that all Masonic Jurists agree that it takes three
regularly chartered Lodges to form a Grand Lodge; hence this Grand
Orient of Spain must rest upon the foundation laid by de Grasse-Tilly.
The next question is,-Where did de Grasse-Tilly get his authority
to constitute Symbolic Lodges of F. & A. ~ · ? We find that he received

bl1 authority, if he ever had any, by virtue of his patent as a Deputy
ln1pector General from the Supreme Council, A. & A. S. R. at
Charleston, South Carolina, in 1802.
WHERE DID THE SUPREME COUNCIL GET THE AUT 110RITY TO CHARTER SYMBOLIC LODGES?
We must bear in mind that the organization of the Grand Lodge
of England, the first in the world, occurred in 1717; hence, in order to
have a clear title to a regularly constituted Grand Lodge it must trace
111 title back to this Grand Lodge. Measured by this standard, all
(~rand Lodges must stand or fall.
Does the Supreme Council for the Southern Jurisdiction of the
United States trace its origin to the Grand Lodge of England?
In 1759 the Council of Emperors of the East and West was organized in Paris ; its members styled themselves Sovereign Prince Masons,
etc. This body constituted Lodges of Sublime Freemasonry, chapters
and colleges. The first three degrees-Symbolic-were conferred in
Symbolic Lodges.
In 1761 this Council granted a patent to one Stephen Morin, deputiaing him as a Grand Inspector of the body, with authority to establish
"Perfect and Sublime Masonry" in all parts of the world.
Morin gave the degree of Grand Inspector General to one Andrew
Fraucken sometime prior to 1767 at Jamaica. Fraucken subsequently
communicated it to one Moses M. Hayes at Boston. Hayes to Barend
M. Spitzer at Charleston, S. C., and Spitzer to John Mitchell on the
2nd day of April, 1795, and on the 31st of May, 1801, John Mitchell
and one Frederick Dalcho organized the Supreme Council of the 33rd
degree for the United States of America at Charleston, South Carolina, and on February 21, 1802, this Supreme Council granted one
Count Alexander Francois Auguste de Grasse-Tilley a patent certifying
that he possessed the degrees from Secret Master (4th) to Sovereign
Grand Inspector General, inclusive, etc., over two hemispheres.
It must now be noted that Tilly had no power or authority from
the 1st to 3rd degree inclusive, but only from the degree of Secret
Master. Tilley went to France and on September 22, 1804, with
others, organized and established the Supreme Council of the 33rd
degree for France at Paris and on July 4, 1811, the Count de GrasseTilley founded a Supreme Council of the A. and A. S. R. 33rd degree
for Spain at Madrid. 4 Gould 120.
Previous to this time there had been several Lodges organized
under the Grand Lodge of England, but all had surrendered their
charters or ceased to exist by reason of non-activity long before 1811.
There is no contention on the part of the Grand Orient of Spain
or the Spanish Grand Orient that they were not founded by, or that
their history starts prior to, de Grasse-Tilley in July, 1811. This being
admitted by all parties and from the historical fact that Tilly only

possessed the right to confer from the 4th to the 33rd degree we fail
to find how or where these so-called Grand Orients secured the legiti~
mate right to confer the Symbolic degrees from Tilly even if Tilly's
power. was regular.
The Supreme Council could not give any man the power to confer
any degrees of Symbolic Masonry for the reason that Mitchell and
Dalcho had no authority to confer that privilege on the Supreme
Council: there is no claim that the Supreme Council has this power
and it does not now and never has claimed this right when the
Supreme Council could not at any time from its inception legally
confer any of the Symbolic Degrees of Masonry, then where can the
Grand Orient of Spain or the Spanish Grand Orient or the Regional
Grand Lodges acting under either of · these Grand Orients trace their
title? There is but one answer-to de Grasse-Tilly who never had
the authority, nor could the authority· be granted to any one man to
confer the Symbolic Degrees of Masonry at his pleasure by even a
regular Grand Lodge for reasons well known to all regular Masons,
i. e: there must be a charter or dispensation, issued by a regularly constituted Grand Lodge; there must be not less than seven to constitute
a Lodg.e of Entered Apprentices; not less than five to form a
Lodge of Fellow Crafts and not less than three to organize a Lodge
of Master Masons.
The applicant must of his own volition present his petition for .
the degrees to a lawfully constituted lodge and if elected; to receive
the degrees through an officer authorized to confer them; these
degrees must be lawfully conferred, otherwise all obligations and
ceremonials would be valueless. -Hence making a Mason at sight is
illegal.
It is as necessary that a subordinate or Grand Lodge be lawfully
constituted as that an applicant be lawfully made a Mason. "Special
Report on Cuba and Colon." Grand Lodge Proceedings of Illinois,
1877, page 22 of Report.
Therefore no Grand Lodge, Orient or Supreme Council who has
obtained its charters from Grand Bodies who do not trace their
origin to the Grand Lodge of England is legitimate.
If a Grand Lodge has illegally come into. existence and other
regularly constituted Grand Lodges through their own ignorance or
gross negligence have entered into fraternal relations with such
Grand Lodge, can it be said that this is sufficient to make legal that
which has no legal existence? or is the Regular Grand Lodge barred
' by the doctrine of equitable estoppel from now declaring illegal that
which it had declared legal?
If it is estopped from henceforth questioning the legality of such
Grand Lodge, then where is the remedy for this disregard of
Masonic Law? The only course left open is to place such regular

1lrand Lodge in the same category as the illegal Grand Lodge; cut

It is the opinion of your committee that a man who has taken
the degrees of Masonry in an illegal Lodge-founded without authority-has not been regularly made a Mason and is therefore not
entitled to any more consideration from a regular lodge of Masons
than a member of any other fraternity. This now brings us to the
very pith of our inquiries.
TO WHOM SHOULD WE EXTEND MASONIC CHARITY?
Masonry is the bulwark of equality for all men within her ranks;
we kn ow no distinction, we have all assumed the same obligations
nnd are therefore by reason thereof entitled to the care and protection
of all regular Masons whithersoever dispersed, we must aid and
assist our less fortunate brethren so far as it lies in our power so
to do.
In large Cities, Boards of Relief have been established for the
purposes of taking care of unfortunate members of the fraternity; in
smaller places this duty is· taken care of by the individual lodges.
Relief is granted too many men who have no better claim to this
Masonic privilege than a profane; for instance a person calls at the
office of the' Board, produces his receipt for dues or some other
evidence that he is a member of a Masonic Lodge and nine times out
of ten he is assisted and it may be that he is a member of an
illegal lodge, and while a list of Regular Jurisdictions and Lodges has
been supplied by this Grand Lodge to its Subordinate Lodges, yet
this list does not contain all of the Grand Lodges considered regular
by the Grand Lodge of California and discretion is of necessitY.

With the question of the regularity of Grand Lodges settled, if it
ever comes to that desirable end, the question of relieving distressed
members, their widows and orphans by Boards of Relief would
o.dj ust itself.
The question of relief applies to Masons individually who covennnt to relieve to the extent of their ability.
But when Lodges either jointly or severally are called upon to
extend any relief to a sojourning member of a sister Lodge or of
nnother jurisdiction then the Lodge to which the member belongs
should in all fairness reimburse the Lodge or Board of Relief, to the
extent of its ability.
This is the fundamental principle of civil government and of every
stable institution. It has however been held by some Masonic Jurists
that "As the Lodge owes nothing to a member, it can owe nothing
to another Lodge who furnishes him assistance*•of course..it would
be highly Masonic for Lodges more happily situated to aid them in
their duty."
Proceedings Grand Lodge of Nevada, 1873;
Illinois, 1874; Rep. Com. on Cor. New Hampshire, 1873.

Is the Grand Orient of Spain irregulM or is it an illegal body?
In 1797 it had been declared the law of the Grand Lodge of
England, that, "if any s~t or number of Masons shall take upon themselves to form a Lodge, without the Grand Master's Warrant, the
regular Lodges are not to countenance them, nor own them as fair
brethren duly formed, nor approve of their acts or deeds." Eighth
old Regulation.
The formation of the Grand Orient of Spain by Count de GrasseTilley in 1811 was contrary to this regulation and therefore illegal,
hence clandestine, not merely under the Masonic law as it now exists,
but under the law as it then existed, and this rule also applies to all
other so-called Masonic Grand Orients or Grand Lodges formed
under like conditions.
The recognition of such bodies cannot be brought about without
violating the lan.Qmarks of Masonry.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A similar matter was very ably discussed by the Grand Lodge of
Maine in 1876, and the same conclusion arrived at.
It has always been the rule, in fact, since the foundation of the
Supreme Council of the A. & A. S. R. in the United States, that no
authority was ever vested in such Supreme Councils over the first
three or symbolic degrees of Masonry. Josiah H . Drummond, Sovereign Grand Commander of the Northern Jurisdiction of the United
States said that the constitutions excluded any such claims, adding,
"If this disclaimer is not strong enough write it stronger and I will
sign it."
Henry L. Palmer, also Soverign Grand Commander of the same
jurisdiction, stated that Supreme Councils of the 33rd. degree never
possessed the power to constitute and administer Symbolic Lodges,
A. F. & A. M. Rep. Cor. Com. Wis., 1910, p. 32.
Louisiana in February, 1910, adopted a resolution declaring that
Lodges and Grand Lodges lawfully organized by the authority of the·
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite in countries where that is the
dominant Rite are legitimate and are entitled to Jurisdiction over
the first three symbolic degrees. The chairman of the Committee was
the Reverend Bro. Herman C. Duncan. All we have to say about
its legitimacy has been said hereinabove, but it does seem that
Masonry in Louisiana needs better protection than that which it has
received at the hands of the Reverend Brother.
According to statistics there appears to be approximately 1,594,902
regular Masons in the world and approximately 149,274 illegal and
irregular Masons throughout the world.

may be thereby brought into existence.

principles of Masonry and each agreed that they could not bind their

recognize each other. He said : "To illustrate, for instance, Illinois
will recognize several jurisdictions, while there are many others it

"It seems to me that the question that should be brought before
