11nly in America but · in foreign countries. We should have some
1·ummon ground to go upon as to which ones should .be recognized."
Brother Pierce was interrupted by another Grand Master in
•1rder to disclaim any intention on the part of the Grand Masters to
form a National Grand Lodge, when there was no intention or inclin11tion to discuss such a proposition.
Grand Master Bell of Illinois suggested that the matter be
r·e ferred to the several committees on correspondence of the several
Grand Lodges, with the request that each Grand Lodge deny or withhold recognition to any Grand Lodge of the United States which is
not recognized by our Grand Lodges.
It seemed to be the sense of the conference that it was powerless
to deal with this important question other than by the following
resolution : "That we request all foreign Grand Lodges with which
our respective Grand Lodges maintain Masonic Correspondence to
deny or withhold recognition to any so-called Lodge within the
domains of the United States which our respective Grand Lodges do
not recognize" and that conference· should have included foreign
countries as well.
We confirm our report as adopted at the last Communication of
this Grand Lodge as to each of the Grand Orients or Grand Lodges
in Spain.
We are more than convinced that no Masonic Jurisdiction has
a higher regard for the principles of Masonry than the members of
the Craft in California; that it is their greatest aim and purpose to
see that exact and even justice be done to all regular Masons, their
widows and orphans and your Committee believes that some suitable
steps should be taken by this Grand Lodge to regulate the abuses and
evils pointed out in this report.

206

207

Therefore we offer the following resolutions and recommend their
adoption :
Resolved, that the Grand Lodges of Scotland, Ireland, Maryland, Georgia, Oklahoma, New Zealand, New South Wales and
British Columbia be and they are hereby requested to discontinue
fraternal relations with the Grand Orients .of Spain or at our next
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California give their
reasons why such Lodges have entered into fraternal intercourse with
·said Grand Lodges.
Resolved, that each regular Grand Lodgee throughout the
world be requested to enter into an agreement with this Grand Lodge
whereby funds furnished to distressed Masons, their widows and
orphans will be refunded upon a request therefor.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Resolved, that each regular Grand Lodgee throughout the
world be and they are hereby requested to refrain from recognizing
Grand Lodges or Orients who disregard the Sovereignty of Sister
Grand Lodges.
Resolved, that each regular Grand Lodgee throughout the
world be and they are hereby requested to publish in their annual
reports a ·synopsis of the evidence upon which Grand Lodges of the
future · are recognized.
Resolved that a copy of this report be furnished to each and
every regula; and irregular Jurisdktion throughout the world wi_th
the request that the suggestions herein made be taken up and discussed and acted upon.
Resolved, that all Regular Grand Masters throughout the
world be and they are hereby invited to attend a conference and if it
be desired to meet and discuss the resolutions set forth in this report;
that the question of the formation of a National or In.t ernational
Grand Lodge shall not be discussed nor any action taken thereon.
That such meeting take place at San Francisco, at the PanamaPacific Exposition in 1915.
Respectfully submitted,
H. M. OWENS,
R. W. MEEK,

CLAIMS OF THE VARIOUS LODGES.

Your Finance Committee, to whom was referred the petition of
Keystone Lodge, No. 161, asking for a remission of its Grand Lodge
dues for the year, ·a fter considering the same, find as follows:
That said Lodge has a depleted treasury, is heavily indebted and
has a membership of only thirty-one. We, therefore, offer the following
resolution and recommend its adoption:
R esolved, That all the Grand Lodge dues of Keystone Lodge, No.
161, for this year, be, and the same are hereby remitted.
Your Finance Committee, to whom was referred the resolution of
Janesville Lodge, No . . 232, asking for an appropriation of $500.00 to ·
assist them in the re-erection of their hall which was recently blown
down by a cyclone, have had the matter under careful consideration, and
believe that to appropriate any of the funds of this Grand Lodge for
the purpose quoted, would establish an undesirable precedent. We, therefore, recommend against the appropriation of any Grand Lodge funds
for said purpose. However, your Committee is of the opinion that
Janesville Lodge is a proper subject for charitable consideration from
the "Special Fund" created out of the money remaining from the funds
heretofore donated for the Italian earthquake sufferers, and refer the
matter to the judgment of the Grand Master.

AMENDMENTS.

AMENDMENTS TO CONSTITUTION,
Adopted October, 1910.
Part II, Article VIII (New).
OF THE GRAND LECTURER.

"Section 1. It shall be the duty of the Grand Lecturer to teach
the ritual and esoteric work to the Inspectors of the jurisdiction; to
visit the several Inspectio~ Districts and hold schools of instruction
where most convenient, and not only to exemplify the adopted work,
but to require conformity therewith. It shall also be his duty to require the Inspectors to examine all Masters-elect in so much of the
Constitution, Edicts and Regulations of the Grand Lodge as refers to
the government of subordinate Lodges, as well as in regard to their .
proficiency in the work and lectures, and to withhold certificates from
all who refuse or neglect to make themselves proficient. And it shall
be the further duty of the Grand Lecturer to renper a report to the
Grand Lodge at each Annual Communication, giving a full and explicit
account of his services within the year, and setting forth the condition
of Lodges throughout the jurisdiction."
Section 1, Article IV, Part II:
"!st. To record all the transactions of the Grand Lodge pr,:>per to
be written, and to superintend the publication thereof immediately ~fter
the close of each Communication, under such instructions as may be
given by the Grand Lodge."
·
(5th paragraph of same section) "To report at each Annual Communication a detailed account of all moneys received by him within
the year, with a specific statement of the source whence they were derived, and to present therewith the receipts of the Grand Treasurer
therefor," etc.
(10th paragraph) "To transmit to each Lodge within the jurisdiction a list of all expulsions, suspensions, and restorations of which
he shall have been notified by the several Lodges, and shall keep in
his office a full and complete list and record of all such expulsions, suspensions, and restora tions of which he shall be notified by the several
Lodges."
(15th paragraph) "To report at each Annual Communication all
unfinished business of the Grand Lodge, and present to its notice all
other matters as may properly come within his province."
(16th paragraph) "To draw warrants upon the Treasurer for all
appropriations by the Grand Lodge, for all orders of the Grand Master

AMENDMENTS TO UNIFORM CODE OF BY-LAWS.
Art. III, · Sec. 1. '"I'he stated meetings of this Lodge shall be
holden .on the ...... . . .. in each month, at .... . ..... o'clock."
Art. IX. Sec. 3. "Should any member, suspended for non-paym.e nt
of dues, neglect for the period of two years to pay said dues or have
the same remitted by his Lodge, said member may be restored to good
standing only as provided by Section 11, Article III, Part III, of the
Constitution."
·
Art. XIII, Section 1. "These By-Laws, so far as relates to the
times of meeting, and the amounts of fees, dues, and disbursements by
the Charity Committee, may be amended at any stated meeting by the
votes of two-thirds of the members present ; provided, that written notice of such amendment shall have been given at the stated meeting
next preceding; but such amendment shall have no effect until approv.ed
by the Grand Lodge or Grand Master, and until such approval shall have
been transmitted to the Grand Secretary. The Secretary of the Lodge
shall note upon the minutes of the Lodge the notice of proposed amendment when made, and in transmitting an amendment for approval shall
forward a certificate, under seal, showing that the law has been complied with and that the amendment has received the requisite vote."

REGULATIONS.
91. No Lodge shall confer a degree at the request of and on behalf
of a Lodge belonging to the jurisdiction of any other Grand Lodge, unless the request of such Lodge be attested by the Grand Secretary of
such jurisdiction and bear the seal of such Grai1d Lodge attached.
92. In the event of a final judgment of conviction against a Mason
in the State or Federal courts of a crime involving moral turpitude, it
shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of any Lodge having jurisdiction of such Mason to prefer charges against the Mason so convicted
on account of the matters involved in said conviction; provided, that
such charges have not already been preferred, and' to· press to conclusion a trial on account thereof.

GRAND MASTER' S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's Address is a full and exhaustive statement of
his official activities during the year.
An extremely large number of special dispensations were granted
for the purpose of conferring degrees out of time. Marked activity
was manifested in the direction of laying foundation stones for public
buildings, not less than ten Special Communications of the Grand
Lodges, having been called for this purpose ; but the one thing above all
others which seems to .distinguish the Grand Jurisdiction of Alabama
is its extremely fruitfulness in the matter of new Lodges, no less than
twenty-three dispensations having been granted to form new Lodges,'
and while the net gain in membership since the last Annual Communication was scarcely more than 1000; and, in that respect, Alabama holding no more than · a medium position with"other Grand Lodges, yet in
the matter of new Lodges, we do not at the present moment recall any
jurisdiction that has granted disp.ensations for so many new Lodges in
a single year.
The total membership of the Lodges of Alabama is only slightly in
excess of 20,000, and the t'otal number of Lodges is 515, the average

3

"It is competent for a Lodge to fix by its by-laws the hour for
Special Communications. In the absence of such by-laws the hour for
the meeting of any Special Communication may be fixed by the Wor-hipful Master."
·
We fail to understand what there is in this ruling that is objectionable, and therefore why it should have failed to receive the approval of the Jurisprudence Committee. We fail to understand why the
Worshipful Master of a Lodge may no~ be privileged to call a special
1neeting, for the purpose, say, of conferring a degree, to meet at an
earlier hour, than the usual meeting hour in order, for example, to dispose of degree work in time for a banquet, or some other function to
occur later.
By virtue of an order of the Grand Lodge at the last Communication, the Grand Secretary, through correspondence with other Grand
Secretaries throughout the United States, upon the subject of requiring
from a visitor documentary evidence as to his Masonic standing, was
nble to report that twenty Grand Lodges in the United States require
documentary evidence; twenty-eight do not, which leaves· ten, from
which no replies were received.
One of the so-called landmarks enumerated by cer~in Masonic
authorities, Mackey among the number, is the "right of visitation," and
the Grand Lodges that are requiring "documentary evidence" are to
that ext~nt turning down one of the Ancient landmarks.

ALBERTA, 1909.
Fourth Annual Communication. Lethbridge.

All the recommendations of the Committee were adopted.
Concerning the controversy between New Jersey and Mississippi
over the question of the negro Lodge in the former jurisdiction, the
Committee on Foreign Correspondence submitted the following report,
which, with an amendment to the effect that the Grand Master of Alabama might, after receiving the information sought for, act as in his
judgment seemed prop~r, was adopted:
"WHEREAS, a correspondence between the Grand Master of th~
Grand Lodge of Mississippi and the ·Grand Master of the Grand
Lodge of New Jersey unfolds the fact that, in August, 1908, there
existed in the city of Newark, N. J., a Lodge composed of white
men and negroes-mostly of the latter, under the obedience of the
Grand Lodge of New Jersey, and
WHEREAS, It is of vital importance that we do our best to maintain our beloved institution in its purity and integrity, therefore
Resolved, That the Grand Master be authorized and requested.
to enter into correspondence with the Grand Master of New Jersey
for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not the Grand Lodge of
New Jersey continues to hold the allegiance of said negro Lodge.
Resolved, further, That, on information that the said Grand Lodge
continues to recognize said negro Lodge, and M: . w:. Grand .
Master be empowered and requested to declare fraternal correspondence with the Grand Lodge of New Jersey severed until such
time as said Grand Lodge shall cease to have under its obedience
a Lodge composed wholly, or in part, of negroes."

The Fourth Annual Communication of the M:. w:. Grand Lodge
of Alberta, Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons, was opened in the
Masonic Hall, at the City of Lethbridge, Province of Alberta, on
Wednesday, May 26, A. D. 1909, A. L. 5909, at the hour of 10 o'clock
A. M., Rev. Canon Hogbin, Grand Master, presiding.
Three Special Communications of the Grand Lodge were held
within the preceding year, one for laying the corner-stone of the Lethbridge Public School; one for ,paying the last tribute of respect to
the memory of Thomas Alexander McLean, Past Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of Prince Edward Island; and the other for the purpose
»f dedicating the Masonic Temple at Calgary.
On account of the change of residence of the Grand Master, quite
unexpectedly necessitated from Calgary to Banft, he was unable to
visit officially as many of the Lodges of the jurisdiction as he had intended to visit, but he nevertheless rep.orts that he had the privilege of
consecrating and constituting no less than eleven of the fourteen
1,odges to which charters were granted at the last Annual Communication.
He is gratified to be able to report that only one member of the
Grand Lodge had been called to his reward in the year.
He reports only two rulings upon Masonic law; one was to the
effect that in case of a Masonic trial, the Worshipful Master of the
J,odge cannot act as counsel upon either side. Another decisio~ defined the relative positions of the Past Masters and the Wardens of
the Lodge in the absence of the Worshipful Master. Both were exceedingly elementary in character.
The report of the Grand Treasurer shows that the Grand Lodge
enjoyed an income during the preceding year of something in excess
of $4000, with disbursements of the same amount and accumulated
funds of about $3000. In view of the fact that the Grand Jurisdiction
Is scarcely more than four years old, and has repaid to the mother
Grand Lodge of Manitoba an advance of $1000, made when the new
Grand Lodge was established, the financial showing is certainly very
aatisfactory.

ARIZONA, 1910.
Twenty-eighth Annual Communication. Tucson. February 8, 1910.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of Arizona commenced its Twenty-eighth Annual Communication at ·
the Masonic Temple in the City of Tucson, on Tuesday, the eighth day
of February, A. D. 1910, at 10 o'clock A. M., M. '. W.'. Fletcher ·
Morris Doan, Grand Master, presiding.

After a few brief words of introduction, the Grand Master, in his
address, approached the subject of Necrology, and mournfully reiretted the death in the preceding year of what is almost unprecedented
In Grand Lodge histories, even in jurisdictions many times the size of
Arizona, of three Past Grand Masters dying in a single year, Ansel
Mellen Bragg, first Grand Master of the Grand Lodge, who passed
nway at his home in Los Angeles, June 24, 1909 ; George Shand, Grand
Master of the Jurisdiction of Arizona, during the year 1905, who died
11t Tucson, Arizona, February 1, 1909, and Francis Marion Zuck, Grand
Master of the Jurisdiction in 1902, who died at his home in Holbrook,
·
Arizona, June 16, 1909.
These honored Masons had all been active and influential in the
work and counsels of the Craft in Arizona, and the calling home of
three in one year, who had occupied the Grand East of the Grand
f,odge, made a deep impression upon the Fraternity of Arizona.
As evidence of the fact that Grand Master Doan is a genuine and
aincere man, and not one who poses as a great expounder of masonic
law, we quote from his report under the caption of decisions what
might, in our opinion, be profitably copied by Grand Masters in certain
other jurisdictions whose principal conception of the office of Grand
Master is to grind out a lot of stuff that they are pleased to label as
decisions. This is what Grand Master Doan says:

The Grand Jurisdiction of Arizona is patterned largely after California, which is of course complimentary to the Grand Jurisdiction.
"Anderson's Manual,'' our own familiar "Anderson's Manual," is the
official Masonic text book of Arizona, and through the guidance of
that excellent work, Arizona will not stray far from the correct masonic
highway.
The Grand Lodge has an accumulated fund of nearly $26,000; more
than $20,000 of which belongs to the Widows and Orphans' Fund. This
fund shows a substantial increase from year to year, and when the
jurisdiction shall have attai~ed sufficient strength numerically, it will
be in position financially to establish and equip a suitable Masonic
Home, should this be the final wish of the Grand Lodge.
Fraternal recognition was extended to the new Grand Lodge of
the State of Oklahoma, and in accordance with the recommendation of
the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, similar recognition was
extended to the Swiss Grand Lodge Alpena. This latter action was
contrarv to the action of most of our American Grand Lodges, not
more than three or four of which have granted recognition to the socalled Swiss Grand Lodge Alpena. This body has not been able to
satisfy such Masonic Jurists as the late Dr. Robbins of Illinois, and
many others, that it is of legitimate origin, or that it in certain respects conforms to the universally accepted Ancient Landmarks of our
Institution. No particular good can accrue to the Jurisdiction of
Arizona from the recognition as a sovereign, independent Grand Lodge,
the Grand Lodge of Alpena, and neither can any particular good inure
to the benefit of Alpena because of the recognition of its legitimacy
by so small a jurisdiction as Arizona, containing a total membership of
scarcely 1,800 Masons. In our opinion, the subject of recognition of
this alleged Grand Lodge might judiciously have been deferred.
There is no report on Foreign Correspondence.
Frank Thomas (Phoenix), Grand Master.
George J . Roskruge (Tucson), Grand Secretary.

CHIEF MASONIC EVENTS DURING THE YEAR.

The event of greatest interest that occurred during the year in the
Masonic Jurisdiction of Arkansas was the comp~tion and dedication
of the Orphans' Home at Batesville, Arkansas. The dedication of the
Orphans' Home was performed at an Emergency Communication cf
the Grand Lodge held at Batesville, Arkansas, September 30, 1909. At
this event there were present the Most Worshipful Grand Master, and
practically all of the officers of the Grand Lodge, and a large attendance of representatives and brethren from the various Lodges throughout the jurisdiction. In addition to the usual dedicatory ceremonies, the
exercises consisted of various addresses by the President of the Home
and other officials, and the reading of a poem written for the occasion
by Brother Fay Hempstead, Poet Laureate of Freemasonry.
'
The Home at the date of the Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge, had no~ been opened for the reception of orphans: although it
was the expectation that the home would be ready to receive the beneficiaries at an early date, as soon as the important question of ways and
means of maintenance is solved.
·
GRAND MASTER' S ADDRESS.

From a perusal of the Grand Master's address, one learns that
the official year with him had been one of activity and usefulness.
Dispensations were granted by him to form eleven new Lodges.
Emergency Communications of the Grand Lodge were held for the
purpose of placing a number of corner-stones of public buildings. He
was called upon to exercise his prerogative of discipline by suspending
for unmasonic conduct, a Worshipful Master of one of his Lodges.
He also found it necessary to arrest the charter of another Lodge,
and was called upon for a number of decisions touching Mas~nic Law,
of which the following two are quoted:
"A District Deputy Grand Master can~o~ le&:ally op~n a Lodge
even when he visits for the purpose of g1vmg mstruchons, in the

10

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

absence of the Worshipful Master and both of the Wardens. A Lodge
cannot be legally opened for any purpose in the absence of the Worshipful Master and the Wardens, except by the Grand Master. The
authority conferred by the Constitution upon a District Deputy Grand
Master is to visit and instruct Lodges, and not mere assemblages of
Masons, unless convened in accordance with Masonic law and usage.
A gathering of Masons does not constitute a Lodge unless it is legally
opened."
"When a Lodge of this State waives its jurisdiction in favor of
a Lodge, either in this or another State, over a Fellow Craft, and the
Lodge in whose favor the jurisdiction is waived declines to accept
jurisdiction on account of the alleged physical disability of the Brother,
he does not become the property of the last-named Lodge, but remains
the property of the Lodge which had original jurisdictio~, and that
Lodge can proceed to finish him up. A Lodge waiving jurisdiction
does not lose it until the waiver is accepted by the Lodge in whose
favor it was granted."

govern its treatment of profanes within its own jurisdiction, according
to its own law, and if California has jurisdiction over the candidate,
according to its law, there is no discourtesy intended, in governing
itself according to its own law, even if in so doing it runs counter td
the penal jurisdiction of other Grand Lodges.
There are, as is well known, probably ten or a dozen Grand Lodges
in the United States that claim perpetual penal jurisdiction, but the
tendency in recent years, among the American Jurisdictions, has been
to recognize the right of every Grand Jurisdiction to treat profanes
within its own territory, according to its own law.
The following quotation from the Grand Master's Address affords
a glimpse of his lofty conception of Masonry and its place in the
history of the world :

Concerning forel"gn relations, the Grand Master refers to the
several meetings during the past two or three years, called by certain
Grand Masters of Eastern Jurisdictions of Grand Masters from the
various States of the Union, and expresses his idea: of the natural conclusion that these conferences might give rise to the idea of their ·
foreshadowing an effort to form a General, or Supreme Lodge of
Masons in the United States, and adds the statement to which most
Masons will agree, that "against such a movement, we should firmly
set our faces, for this Grand Lodge should, in my judgment, never
surrender a particle of its sovereign powers."
Under the heading, also, of foreign relations, the Grand Master
refers to an incident which arose in connection with the conferring
of the degrees of Masonry upon a former resident of Arkansas by one
of our California Lodges. The facts were substantially as follows:
A profane, residing in California, and having been a resident of
California for nearly five years, applied to one of our Lodges for initiation, and it developed in connection with his petition for the degrees
that prior to his departure for California, he had been rejected by an
Arkansas Lodge. The petitioner, however, so far as his character and
worth were concerned, successfully passeq the scrutiny of our Investigating Committee, and was upon the report of the Committee elected
to receive the degrees in our California Lodge and the degrees were in
due course conferred upon him.
The Grand Master of Arkansas objected to our failure to recogniZe their law of penal jurisdiction, which holds for a period of five
years, but acted, rather, upon our own law, whillh does not recognize
the penal jurisdiction over profanes, resident of California, beyond the
period stipulated by our law, which is one year. No discourtesy was
intended toward the Jurisdiction of Arkansas, nor its Grand Master,
hut it is the generally recognized rule of all Masonic Jurisdictions to

11

"The calm reflection that Masonry has for ages stood for the
moral and fotellectual advancement of mankind, that it has, as no
other fraternal society and few other institutions of any kind have
done, proved its ability to stand the test of time, that it has always
successfully resisted innovations upon its sacred purposes, that it has
never yielded to nor been swayed by either political, sectional or purely
commercial purposes, but has steadily maintained its standard of
purity, justice and uprightness, undismayed by fierce op.posit.ion, unshaken by tempest of warfare and unaffected by mutations of time,
and that it has contributed so much to the world's material and moral
welfare should be a source of increasing gratification to its votaries.
Its achievements are the common heritage of all of us, from the roungest Entered Apprentice to the Grand Master, and in its splendid history there is glory enough and to spare for us all."

In the year five Especial Communications of the Grand Lodge were

to the Relief Fund of the Grand Lodge of Italy at the time of the destructive earthquake in December, 1908, in certain districts of that
country.
The Grand Master again complains that the contributions, from
the subordinate Lodges of the jurisdiction to the Semi-Centennial
Benevolent Fund, have not been liberal, and urges the Lodges to
greater activity in their manifestations of sympathy in connection with
this magnificent Grand Lodge undertaking. The total amount to the
credit of the fund at the close of the year was $51,759.90.
From the Grand Master's report, it appears there is more than
one jurisdiction in North America where irregular methods have been
resorted to to secure the election of a petitioner for degrees, where in
the ordinary course of events, he would probably be _rejected. One of
the methods not unfrequently resorted to is the surreptitious abstraction from the ballot box of all of the black balls, thereby preventing a
brother who might desire to cast an adverse ballot from doing so.
Another method some times in vogue, is for the Master of the
Lodge to call the meeting to order a little ahead of the time fixed by
the by-laws, and upon occasions of this kind, it is not impossible for
a Master to be misled by an inaccurate timepiece, and then to have
the balloting for the petitioner, about whom there is a suspicion that
he might be rejected, hurried forward and the result of the ballot
announced before the arrival of the objecting 'member.
It is seldom in one year that both of these methods are resorted
to in the same jurisdiction, but such appears to have been the case i.n
the jurisdiction of Canada, in the Province of Ontario, in the past
year, and the irregularities receive special consideration in the Grand
Master's Address.
Here is a warm one for the Order of the Eastern Star. We quote
from Grand Master's Address:
"In March of this year I learned that a· Lodge in the western
part of the Province had permitted a society of ladies called the Order
of the Eastern Star to meet in the Lodge room. I instructed the
District Deputy Grand Master to admonish the Worshipful Master of
the Lodge that this could not be permitted."
Think of the feminine adjunct of Masonry being referred to by a
Grand Master in such an icy manner as a "society of ladies called the
Order of the Eastern Star!"
The Grand Master condemns electioneering for office, and particularly criticises the practice of sending circulars for the purpose of promoting the interest of a candidate for Masonic honors.
The reports of the Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer and
the District Deputy Grand Master show that the jurisdiction is in a
healthy and prosperous condition:

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

At the opening of his address, the Grand Master makes a brief
statement as to the income and expenditures of the Grand Lodge,
from which it appears that the total income for the preceding year was
$37,446.60, being a decrease, as compared with the previous year, of
$1,300.20, and the expenditures during the year aggregated $41,349.93,
which exceeded the income by $3,903.33.
The total grants for benevolence during the preceding year were
$26,372, which is, as will be observed, a large percentage of the income
and speaks highly of the genuine spirit of charity of the jurisdiction.
The Grand Master states that he was called upon in the year to
render a large number of interpretations of Masonic law, but that
only five questions were presented that called for official opinion from
him of a character to be entitled to be -designated as decisions. Two
of the decisions were as follows :
"A candidate was regularly proposed; his petition was received
by the Lodge, and referred to a committee for investigation. Then it
was discovered that the applicant had not resided for one year within
the jurisdiction of the Lodge. What course should the Worshipful
Master take? Ans.-He should direct the petition to be withdrawn."
"On a petition for initiation the ballot was taken; the ballot-box
was inspected and placed upon the altar; and after a reasonable
time, the Worshipful Master declared the result. Afterward the Tyler
· objected to the validity of the ballot on the ground that he had not
been given an opportunity to vote. Ruled.-That the declaration by
the Master is final, and the ballot cannot be re-opened. The Tyler
had a right to vote, but he did not claim that right, and his neglect
cannot affect the result."

"It was during the reign of Catherine II. that the first Lodg~ was
formed in Russia. The prime mover was a German, Bro. Von Re1chell,

March 1771. It started with 14 members-ten Germans, three Alsatians
and one Russian. In June of the same year a second Lodge was
opened in St. Petersburg under the patronage of England, and they
promptly declared the first Lodge illegal. A message was sent fr?m
London to Berlin that 'the London Grand Lodge had the exclusive
right of constituting othe; Lo?ges in t~e who!~ ~or\d.'. The Germans
temporized, fearful of an mvas10n of their own iurisd1ct1on by England.
The German Lodge was rather weak then, and had troubles of their
own, so they did not desire any more complications. if they could be
avoided. The Appollo Lodge suspended work, but m 1773 Bro. Von
Reichell founded another Lodge (with a Russian Prince at its head),
and afterwards three others. The Appollo Lodge was also re-opened.
"In 1774 the English orga!lized five Lodges--:-three in St. ~eters­

is in process of accumulation ancl amounts now to something in excess
of $25,000, and from this fund disbursements are made to distressed
Masons, their widows and orphans, and in a jurisdiction not in a position financially to adequately support a Masonic Home, the method

was disbursed last year from this fund for the relief of aged and indigent Masons, and the widows and orphans of Masons.

The Grand Master's report disclosed a year of devotion to duty
11nd useful effort. He regrets his inability to have visited every Lodge
In the jurisdiction, but from the table of visits given by him, it appears
that he traveled over 7,000 miles and gladdened with his presence
Lodges in nearly every portion of his broad and mighty jurisdiction.
Dispensations were granted by him to form two new Lodges and
1everal petitions for new Lodges were refused by him.
A large number of Special Communications of the Grand Lodge
were held for various purposes ; po less than fourteen of such Communications were convened for the purpose of laying corner-stones of
public buildings.
Under the heading of decisions, the 9rand Master states that he
wrote during the year a large number of letters construing the laws
of the Grand Jurisdiction, and citing the decisions of former Grand
Masters; but that he was not called upon to make any what he cared
to designate as decisions, all questions ·presented to him having been
decided, as stated above, by reference to the Constitution and Laws and
rulings of former Grand Masters.
This is in ~arked contrast to many other jurisdictions, numerically
no larger than Colorado, where so-called decisions frequently number
fifty or more.

celebration of the Fiftieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
which occurs next year; and, in accordance with that resolution, the
Fiftieth Anniversary of the establishment of the Grand Lodge of Colorado will no doubt be duly celebrated in 1910.

GRAND MASTtR'S ADDRICSS.

The Grand Jurisdiction of Delaware contains a membership of
about 5,600, probably three-quarters as many Masons as are contained
In the City of San Francisco.
The Grand Jurisdiction embraces twenty-two Lodges, and the
Grand Master is required by the Constitution of the Grand Jurisdiction
to visit personally, during the year, each one of the subordinate Lodges.
From his address we learn that he complied with this constitutional
requirement, and in addition paid fraternal visits to a number of the
1.,odges upon several occasions.
Under the heading of Necrology he is able to report that the Grim
Reaper has spared the Grand Jurisdiction of Delaware, so far as
(~rand officers are concerned, but refers feelingly to the death of other
members of the jurisdiction, including that of Past Grand Tyler, George
1'. Yates, and Past Masters, and various Master Masons.
The Jurisprudence Committee to whom was referred the Grand
Master's address commends that official for his exhaustive and o,rnate
address, felicitates him on his having visited the entire Jurisdiction, and
upon the manner in which he has upheld the dignity of the Grand
r.odge in his various visitations.
The Grand Master refers also to visitations made by him to adjoining Grand Jurisdictions, particularly mentioning those of New
Jersey and Pennsylvania. He visited also the Grand Jurisdiction of
Ohio by invitation of the Grand Master of that State upon the occa1lon of the making a Mason "at sight" of William Howard Taft, President-elect at that time of the United States. His opinion is recorded

22

REPOR1' ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

in support of the prerogative claimed by the Grand Master to make a
Mason at sight, and unquestionably the weight of opinion of writers
upon Masonic subjects throughout the United States is likewise in support of the regularity of this so-called landmark, but the weight of
opinion as to the wisdom of the exercise of this prerogative of the
Grand Master is just as strongly against its exercise~
In common with other Grand Masters, he speaks of his visit to
the Conference of Grand Masters at Philadelphia, and to the recommendations made by that conference, which recommendations were
presented by him to his Grand Lodge. Some of them were approved,
others were "turned down."
Some discussion was indulged in by the Grand Lodge upon the
question of perpetual penal jurisdiction over rejected candidates, which
the Grand Master refers to as the claim of "perpetual objection" and
his Grand Lodge declined to adopt the suggestion, so far as Delaware
was concerned of the Philadelphia Conference that the Grand Lodges
throughout the United States adopt as a uniform standard, in lieu of
the variety of rules now existing, that penal jurisdiction over rejected
candidates be fixed at five years.
While the jurisdiction of Delaware is comparatively small, as much
intelligence is manifested in that jurisdiction in the discussion of
Masonic questions as is shown in even the largest and numerically
most important of our American jurisdictions; and that Masonic law is
well understood by the Masons of Delaware is manifest from the
statement made by the Grand Master in his address that it had not
been necessary for him during the year to render anything in th.e
nature of a decision upon Masonic law, and that only a few questions had been referred to him which he had been able to clarify
without resorting to the necessity of a so-called decision.

At the Special Communication in November, resolutions were

there seems to be little, if any, doubt as to the consummation of this
plan, whereby practically all of the stock will be voluntarily and without consideration transferred to the Grand Lodge, thereby vesting in
the Grand Lodge the full control and ownership of the property. In
addition to this important fact, the Grand Lodge voted at this Sp.ecial
Communication a special per capita annual assessment of $1, to remain
until the indebtedness against the Temple shall be wiped out, and the
Grand Master, as an expression of his deep appreciation of the action
of the Grand Lodge, in so unanimously coming forward to save the
fraternity from the ·discredit that might possibly have been visited
upon it in consequence of the failure of the Masonic Temple project,
uses the following language :
"I am coming to th~ close .of my official y~ar. I ~ssure. you
nothing has happened durmg my incumbency of this office m which I

blemish-the Grand Lodge behind it."
"Some of us will be in this lodge-room when the debt shall have

"It is in order that the Grand Lodge go on record as thanking its

The Grand Master refers to the approaching one hundredth anniversary of the Grand Lodge and to steps which have been taken to
1•elebrate the centennial.
Official visitations were made by the Grand Master to all of the
constituent Lodges; but when it is considered that there are only
thirty-two Lodges in the entire district .and that the district is only
len miles square, it may be seen that to visit all of the subordinate
T,odges in a jurisdiction would be an easy task in comparison with
1uch a jurisdiction as California.
The Grand Master speaks of the Masonic Mutual Life Association
Rnd commends it to the consideration of the brethren. We fail to
discover anywhere, in a careful search of the Grand Lodge report, that
this association has any official connection with the Grand Lodge, and
assessment mutual lire associations, whether called "Masonic," or otherwise, have uniformly resulted in final failure, and in the infliction of
loss and suffering at the wind-up, they have more than offset all the
good done by them during their years of solvency. The use of the
name "Masonic" in connection with Mutual Life Association should
be prohibited unless, in fact, the life association is conductep directly by
a Grand Lodge, and the use of the name "Masonic" in connection
with these institutions in any other way is misleading and deceptive.
The request of the Grand Lodge, made last year, to the Commission appointed by Congress that the statue of Admiral John Paul
Jones should be erected in the triangular space in front of the new
Masonic Temple, was turned down by the Commission, and no doubt
on account of this actio.n, the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia
negatived a resolution that a request be made of the Commission that
the Grand Lodge be permitted to place a stone in the foundation.

along fairly well defined lines of established Masonic Law. One was
to the effect that it is against the law and usages of Masonry for
Masonic Lodges to incorporate.

CORRESPONDENCE REPORT.

The Correspondence Report, as usual, is by Past Grand Master
George W. Baird.
He gives, in our judgment, greater praise to the Grand Lodge
Swiss Alpena than it deserves. We fail to see any particular good
which this body accomplishes in the way of practical Masonry, its
entire efforts being addressed to a propaganda of advertising and circularization with a positive minimum of actual good accomplished in
the application of the principal tenets of Freemasonry.
The testimony of very creditable witnesses is to the effect that
this so-called Grand Lodge, if not atheistic, is at least what , might
be called agnostic, and has no right to be considered as a sovereign
Grand Lodge entitled to the fraternal recognition of our American
Grand Lodges, among whose first and fundamental requirements is an
unequivocal belief in the Supreme Being.

George C. Ober (Washington, D. C.), Grand Master.

"In October 11, the City and Island of Key West was swept by
a hurricane which damaged nearly every house on the island, suspended business and for the time being took away the livelihood of
many of our brethren by depriving them of their wages. At first it
was difficult to obtain a report of the extent of th.e damage, owing, of
course, to the confusion in the city, and the impaired telegraphic service.
Even before we had had any report of the extent of the loss, I received at Louisville, Ky., a telegram from M.". w:. Brother Oscar
Lawler, Grand Master of California, extending the sympathy of himself and his brethren, and authorizing me to draw on his Grand Secretary in the sum of $500 for the relief of the Craft in Key West.
Having ascertained tha~ money was sorely needed, I drew on C'llifornia
in favor of the Committee at Key West for the $500 and added to it
$375 more which was at my disposal for that purpose in the fund returned by the Grand Master of California after the sufferers in the San
Francisco earthquake had been relieved. 'l'hus all the relief which I
was able to send to Key West on this occasion w.as made possible by
the prompt generosity and the prudent management of our brethren in
California. I may add that the only notice taken of our misfortune in
other States was by California. I recommend that a suitable recognition be made at this Grand Communication in addition to the acknowledgments which I have made to the Grand Master.
"I also authorized an appeal by Dade Lodge No. 14, located at
Key West, and am informed that the particular Lodges made liberal
contributions."

MASONIC HOMll.

The enthusiasm concerning the Masonic Home has temporarily
flagged ·in Florida and complaint to this effect is made by the trustees
of the Masonic Home and Orphanage. The fund which is in process
of accumulation preliminary to the actual launching of the Masonic
Home project increased during the past year only about $1,000, and
the total amount now on hand is $16,008.25.

The action of our Grand Master was evidently appreciated and
the expressions of approval of our brethren in Florida is exceedingly
gratifying.
Numerous so-called decisions were rendered by the Grand Master,
and almost without exception they were of a strictly local character,
and, as stated by the Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, many of
them would have been wholly unnecessary, had the subordinate Lodge
officers carefully consulted the Masonic Digest, as answers could have
been obtained therefrom without causing annoyance to the Grand
~aster.

The comments of the Jurisprudence Committee upon one of the
Grand Master's decisions, while simply stating a plain truth, may
yet be of interest, as follows :
"The reversal of a sentence of indefinite suspensioa does not cr•title the Brother to apply for affiliation with another Lod~c, and in
such case the Grand Secretary's certificate of reversal of ~entenct! is 1:ot
equivalent to a dimit.
"If the sentence in this case was merely reversed, a new trial
should have been ordered, and the party affected would not have been
entitled to a certificate from the Secretarv to the effcC't d1at he was
acquitted of the charge, he would have· only been entitled to such
certificate, if the final judgment had been 'set aside' by the Grand Lodge.
If he had been entitled to such certificate he could properly have petitioned for membership in a particular Lodge."
Another decision of the Gra.n d Master was to the effect that relief
extended by another jurisdiction (in this case it was Arizona), to a
member of a Florida subordinate Lodge, formed no basis for a claim
for reimbursement unless the relief had been extended by the express
authorization of the subordinate Lodge to which the distressed Mason
belonged, and that the foreign Lodge extending the relief could claim
compensation only in the consciousness of duty well done. In other
words, on the theory that "virtue is its own reward," an easy way of
paying debts and one that California in particular has had more experience in than any other Jurisdiction probably in the world.

MASONIC HOME.

The Masonic Home continues to be managed in the most capable
manner and with a commendable degree of prudence and economy, the
management of the Home having saved, during the preceding year,
$1,200 from the appropriation made by the Grand Lodge for its support, and the per capita cost for maintenance during the year was
$174.14, a material decrease from the per capita of the preceding year,
the cost for that year having been $211.90.
At this Communication the report of. the Board of Trustees states
that there are thirty-seven residents at the Home, and that practically
the entire capacity of the Home for the accommodation of beneficiaries
is utilized.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

From a study of Grand Lodge reports from nearly every quarter
of the globe, and a careful reading of Grand Masters' addresses, we are
oonstrained to the conclusion that Grand Master Jeffries of Georgia is
the silver-tongued orator par excellence of them all. The opening and
closing paragraphs of his extensive report constitute a series of
panegyrics upon the subject of Masonry, a veritable string of pearls, as
it were, and, on account of the exalted diction, we quote in extenso as
follows:
From the opening paragraph of his address :
"When we contemplate Masonry as the ancient and honorable ancestor of all the fraternities of men; consider the power and influence
which it has wielded in the creation and consummation of the glorious
civilization we enjoy, our hearts rejoice within us that we ha1e b"en
permitted to enjoy its privileges, to partake of its advantages and
share in its glory.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"Its antecedents are ancient and honorable ; its precepts wise and
salutary; its tenets pure and catholic. Its mission is that of bearing
light to mankind; to teach the loftiest moral virtues and incorporate
them in the lives of men, and make them the measure of their actions.
Its dogma is faith in God and love for fellow men. It is the author of
no creed, the adherent of no sect, the preacher of no religion save the
religion of humanity. It denies to no man the freedom of consci<!nce,
the liberty to think for himself, the privilege to form his own conclusions. Upon its royal seat, Reason sits enthroned. Upon its sac,red
altars rests the holv word of God. Masonry believes that God is a
Paternal Being, the ·Father of Mankind. Masonry teaches that all men
are the children of God and that the souls of men are the emanations
from His Spirit. Masonry ascribes to God the perfection of every
virtue. It demands of the child of God that idealism which is attained by the selecting and assembling in one individual all the beauties
and perfections which are to be derived from the Divine Kinship.
"Masonry is the friend and coadjutor of all that is good; a promoter, not an antagonize.r; a peace maker, not a disturber.
"The hand of Masonry is clasped with the hand of every man who
would uplift humanity, who would honor God and bring blessings to
mankind.
"Om ancient Craft sprang from an association of working nienmen who were taught to work diligently, live creditably and to act
honorably. The birthright of Masonry is achievement. As the purpose
of the builders of old was to benefit mankind in providing shelter and .
protection from the vicissitudes of seasons, so the purpose of our
Science is to shield and protect men from the evil forces that beset
them from within and without.
"As toil and industry, coupled with intelligence, characterized their
labors, so diligence, assiduity and intelligence must characterize our
efforts in the noble and glorious work in which we are engaged.
"Masonry is a 'Spirit that lives throughout, vital in every part.'
It must work or die."

From the closing paragraphs of his address :
"Masonry has ever been the hand-maiden of civilization. Wherever the genius of man has opened new discoveries, wherever the intelligence of man has evolved new theories and developed broader and
more practical accomplishment, whether it be in the wake of the
sword emblazoned path, or along the highways of aggression and progression, made possible by the intelligent exercise of moral force, there
Masonry has ever been, as a missioner of mercy or a mollifier of the
passions of men. Never a trailer in the tracks of those who have gone
before, but side by side with the foremost of those who have contributed to human liberty, who have exalted human virtue, who have
proclaimed the supremacy of human reason as the cope-stone of human
accomplishment.
"Her hand is joined in friendly grasp with every hand that worketh

MASONIC HOMJ;;S.

The preceding year was one of development and growth in both
of the Masonic Homes of Illinois, there being two separate institutions in this State, one for the orphans, and the other for aged and
decayed Masons. The property belonging to the Orphans' Home, formerly in the City of Chicago, was sold in 1908 for $35,000, and in the
past year the site for a new home at La Grange, Ill., a few miles from
Chicago, was chosen, anc! the Grand Lodge at this Communication, acting upon a request from the Committee on Masonic Homes, appropriated a sufficient sum which, added to the proceeds of the sale of
the Chicago property, aggregated $100,000, with which to build and
equip a new Orphans' Home at La Grange. Both homes are in a prosperous condition, the number of residents at the Old People's Home at
Sullivan having increased from forty-eight at the beginning of the
year to seventy-six at the close of the year; and at the Orphans' Home,
the number sheltered there increased from forty at the beginning of
1
the year to fifty-six at the close of the year.
The total sum appropriated for the two Homes for the coming
year, the principal item being for construction purposes, was something in excess of $135,000, which is evidence of the broad spirit of
generosity which the Fraternity in Illinois entertains for their Masonic
Homes.
GRAND MASTJ;;R'S ADDRJ;;SS.

The Grand Master's address is a comprehensive statement of his
official actions during the year, setting forth a list of the Lodges instituted, Lodges constituted, corner-stones laid, dedications, etc., etc.,
affording evidence of an extreme.ly busy year.
The Grand Master refers to the inroads made by the Grim Reaper
during the preceding year in the Grand Lodge, calling attention to five
of the Past Grand Officers of that Body, who had been called to their
last reward.
Especial reference was made by the Grand Master to the death of
Past Grand Master Joseph Robbins, Chairman for so many years of
the Committee on Foreign Correspondence and who was ungrudgingly
conceded by every member of the Grand Jurisdiction to be the most

38

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

commanding figure in Illinois Masonry, and who was throughout the
Masonic world re-::ognized as one of the greatest Masonic scholars and
writers that this country has ever produced. As to his position in the
Masonic world, the Grand Master refers to him as follows :
"The position of Joseph Robbins in the Masonic world was unique.
In this Grand Lodge he stood for nearly half a century, like a lighthouse on the hill, to warn us of dangers on the way and to guide us
into peaceful harbors. His work as our Correspondence Committee has
commanded recognition from the world of Masonry, and his writings
have become classics in the literature of our craft. He stood always
for the dignity and pre-eminence of Ancient Craft Masonry. He was ~
wise in counsel, fearless in the advocacy of what he thought to be
right. He was forceful and convincing in his public utterances. Among.
the Masonic writers of his age, he stood as Saul of Israel among his
fellows, head and shoulders above them all."
The Grand Master also makes special reference to the death : of
R.". w:. Loyal L. Munn, who served the Grand Lodge of Illinois as its
Grand Secretary from 1881 to 1893.
Concerning decisions, the Grand Master reports that while many
questions had been submitted to him for determination during the year,
none of them involved new interpretations of Masonic law and are,
therefore, not reported.
In a Jurisdiction containing nearly 100,000 members, being numerically the second jurisdiction in the United States, this circumstance that
no new decisions were rendered, is in marked contrast to certain other
jurisdictions in our country with memberships of possibly ten or fifteen
thousand Masons, rendering so-called "decisions" numbering sometimes
from seventy-five to a hundred, which naturally lead to the conclusion
that many of the so-called decisions of certain Grand Masters are pure ·
fabrications designed by the authors to embalm themselves in the
Digest.
The Grand Master refers at length to the so-called Philadelphia
Conference of Grand Masters, called for 't he purpose of considering
questions of common interest to the various Grand Lodges in our
country, hut the purpose of which had been misinterpreted in certain
directions as a possible move toward the formation of a General or
Supreme Grand Lodge. Grand Master Bell of Illinois took a conspicuous part in the• proceedings of the conference in Philadelphia, and
reported to his Grand Lodge the several recommendations adopted at
the conference, nearly all of them being simply a statement of what
is already the law of practically all of the jurisdictions concerning the
points referred to. The one subject of real importance that was
passed upon, was the complete and emphatic disclaimer that the conference was intended, in the remotest degree, to foster the idea of. a ·
General Grand Lodge, but was designed simply and solely for the
purpose of an interchange of views, and the recommendation to the

One of the remarkable features about the Annual gathering of
the Lodges of Indiana is that practically every Lodge in the jurisdiction is represented. At the Annual Communication in 1909, only
three Lodges were missing, and at the Annual Communication of·
1910, 529, out of the total of 532 Lodges, had representatives in
attendance. This percentage of attendance is not even approximated
in any other Grand Jurisdiction.
MASONIC HOM!t.

At the Annual Communication of 1910, a committee in sympathy
with the Masonic Home idea, was appointed to formulate "and
recommend to the next Grand Lodge, plans for the providing of
funds, etc." looking to the establishment of a Masonic Home. Such
a Committee was duly appointed and at this Annual 'Communication
rendered a report, the principal recommendations of which were as
follows :
"First-That th6 Grand Lodge dues per capita be increased from
25 to 50 cents.
"Second-That the increased income of 25 cents be placed to the
credit of the Masonic Widows and Orphans' Home fund."
Which report was submitted to the Committee on Ways and Means,
and upon recommendation of that Committee, the following resolution was adopted by the Grand Lodge.
"We have examined the report of the Committee · as submitted to
the Grand Lodge and recommend its approval and formal adoption
by this Grand Lodge, and in accordance with recommendations contained therein, the annual dues be increased from 25 to SO cents per
capita, and one-half of the dues, when so collected, to be set aside
as provided in the report of the Committee on Masonic Widows and
Orphans' Home."
The early establishment, therefore, of a Masonic Home in Indiana may be confidently predicted.

Dispensations to form four new Lodges were granted, and a
charter having been granted at the last Communication to Twelve Mile
Lodge No. 673, that Lodge was duly constituted by Special Deputy,
commissioned by the Grand · Master. Several Masonic halls were

Only four decisions were rendered by the Grand Master, and
of these four only one that occasioned any discussion by the Jurisprudence Committee. This question arose over a controversy between
two Lodges, as to whose duty it was to relieve the distress of a
widow of a Master Mason, the widow having removed from the
jurisdiction of the particular Lodge to which her husband belonged;
and in response to a request made to the Lodge where she was
living, relief was granted to provide for her immediate necessities, and
subsequently, without the consent of the Lodge to which her deceased
husband belonged, further relief of a permanent nature was extended
by the Lodge to which the widow applied and this Lodge subsequently sought to enforce collection of this debt from the deceased
husband's Lodge.
The Grand Master ruled that granting relief for immediate necessities by the Lodge to which the widow applied was right and proper,
but no obligation for relief of a permanent character could be enforced against the deceased husband'i< Lodge, without the consent of
that Lodge to the expenditure.
The ruling was undoubtedly correct, but it is the duty of every
Lodge to relieve the distress of its own widows, and no Lodge
should be permitted to shirk its responsibility simply upon the pretext that permanent relief had been extended without its express
approval and consent. Co-operation between Lodges in cases of this
kin<l is essential, but every Lodge should be required, to the extent of
its ability, to provide for its own.
Elaborate preambles and resolutions were presented by one of
the Past Grand Masters, looking to the idea of committing the Grand
Lodge of Indiana to the proposition of a General Grand Lodge of
Masons for the United States, and by inference, the incidental appointment of himself as the Perpetual Plenipotentiary of the Grand
Lodge of Indiana to any conference looking to the formation of a
General Grand Lodge that might be called by any Masonic authority
In the United States; and it may be stated that this Past Grand
Master of Indiana appears to be the only Grand Maser, or Past Grand
Master in America, who favors the idea of a General Grand Lodge.
These resolutions were referred to the Committee on J urisprudence, that at the closing session of this Communication rendered a
report which was promptly adopted, thoroughly and effectually set-

"In presenting our Twelfth Annual Review, it may be of interest

The Grand Master renders five or six decisions of a local character,
construing the law of Iowa.
The decisions, if they are entitled to be called such, were approved
by the Jurisprudence Committee. One of the decisi"ns and the comments thereon by the Committee are as follows :
"Can a dimitted Mason affiliate with a Lodge outside of the one
within whose jurisdiction he resides?
"The answer is: 'No, not without a waiver of jurisdiction.'
"The ruling in a general sense is right. To avoid a misapprehension it may be well for us to say that division (E) of Section 162 of
the Code makes an exception in cases where a non-affiliate has petitioned the Lodge of his local jurisdiction for affiliation and been rejected, in which case he may, after six months from the date of such
rejection; if in good standing, and no charges are pending against him,
petition any Lodge of an adjoining Jurisdiction for affiliation."
This ruling is. of course, at variance with our California Law,
which permits a non-affiliate Mason to deposit his dimit in any Lodge
within the entire Jurisdiction.
The Grand Master reports official visits made by him to about fifty
Lodges in the jurisdiction, certainly a commendable record. He refers

three degrees, and unle~s a man has taken the so-called "higher degrees," he is not of much account as a Mason, and he points out the
fact that Symbolic Masonry is in reality the true and genuine Masonry,
and t·hat there is in the true sense of the word, nothing higher than
the three degrees of Ancient Craft Masonry.

Referring to the Widows and Orphans' Home, the Grand Master
uars the following eulogistic language :
"This monument, of which all Kentucky Masons are jus.tly proud
and which is without a superior, if an equal, among all Masonic Bodies'
nd which has been an incentive and inspiration to our sister Grand
urisdictions, who are constantly trying to come up to the standard
hat we have set, is indeed nearer to our hearts."

"Our Widows and Orphans' Home is truly a monument of which

her of decisions by Grand Masters, and concludes that the Jurisprudence
of the Order in general is probably becoming more stable and fixed and
also that Masters of Lodges and others called upon to administer the
law are becoming better informed, etc.
He regrets the apparent disposition in Masonic practice to decrease
the powers naturally inherent in the subordinate Lodges, denying them
rights, such, for instance, as the direct correspondence by a Lodge of
one Jurisdiction with a Lodge in some other Jurisdiction and many
other similar restrictions, whereby subordinate .Lodges, it1 his judgment, are being gradually stripped of their ancient rights, so as to
create the apprehension that power is becoming centralized to too great
a degree in the Grand Lodge, and he seriously recommends the incorporation in all Grand Lodge Constitutions of a Bill of Rights.
Brother Clarke has been a thoughtful student of Masonry, and his
conclusions upon any subject are worthy of serious consideration.

of their beloved Past Grand Master, Brother Edwin Marks, and their
greatly esteemed Brother, John Puleston, Senior Grand Warden, whose
sudden and unexpected demise came as a shock to his thousands of
friends throughout the Jurisdiction.
The Grand Master rendered seventy-seven decisions, most of them
simple interpretations of the law and constitution. The following decisions are noted :
"A question was asked as follows: •
"A member of a Lodge dimitted more than two years ago, but
still having his <limit in his possession, desires to" affiliate again with
his own Lodge. The question is submitted as to whether it is necessary that he shall file a regular petition, and have the same referred
to a committee, and, in fact, take the regular course for all other petitions, or whether he could simply submit his <limit and have the
action of t.he Lodge annulled, granting the same by a simple resolution.
I held that he must again petition his Lodge, the same as one who
was not a member, and accompany his petition by his <limit, and the
same should take regular course, as prescribed for all other petitions."
"The question was submitted as to whether it was necessary to
await the result of a criminal trial of a member of a Lodge before the
Lodge could proceed against him for un-Masonic conduct. I ruled that
it was not necessary to wait the result of a criminal trial, nor was the
action of a petty jury in a criminal trial conclusive against the Lodge,
but its proceedings should be entirely independent of any criminal action
before the courts.
"An inquiry was made if a Lodge could surrender its Charter by a
majority vote. I ruled that it would not as long as seven members of
the Lodge remained who were willing to hold the Lodge together under
the Charter.
"In reply to an inquiry, I wrote that a member of our Order who
was a Treasurer of a W . 0. W. Lodge, and who had defaulted, could
have charges preferred against him in our Order and be tried for the
same, and that I did not consider it a violation of one's obligations to
testify against a brother ~uilty of such an offense. It is not the purpose
of Masonry to harbor criminals, and the obligations of our Order furnish no cloak to hide the evidences of guilt. If there is one truth
above all others that Masonry teaches, it is that we shall be law-abiding
citizens, and not protect those who violate the laws of their country.
When they commit crime, they place themselves outside of the pale of
our Masonic duty.
"I wrote that waivers of jurisdiction from El Dorado, Ark., should
come direct through the office of the Grand Master of this State and
the State of Arkansas, and not by direct communication between the
constituent Lodges."
A ·committee was appointed at this Communication to take steps
looking to the celebration a year hence of the one hundredth anniversary of the establishment of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.

Louisiana has been inclined to take an extremely liberal view with
reference to the recognition of foreign Grand Lodges, and has recognized as regular certain Grand Lodges that have failed to gain recognition by other American Jurisdictions, and as a further step toward
enlarging the circle of recognition, the following resolutions from the
Committee on Foreign Correspondence were adopted by the Grand
"WHEREAS, It is desirable that all lawfully constituted Masonic
Bodies throughout the world should be in unity and harmony, and
recognize the fraternal bond for the good of Masonry, the benefit of
the individual brethren, and the happiness of the human race; and
"WHEREAS, There are m<l'ny purely technical rules and obstructions
to the realization of such a union which would justify our boast in the
universality of Masonry; and
"WHEREAS, The Grand Lodge of Louisiana has always been liberal
and prog1'essive, and under the influence of the broadest Masonic
charity, be it
"Resolved, That it is the sense of this M. '. W .'. Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons, that friendly and fraternal efforts be made
· to bring into one perfect union of harmony, concord, and fraternal
recognition all Grand Lodges of the world, organized and constituted
in accordance with the fundamental laws and usages of ancient Freemasonry, wherever the fundamental principles of morality, brotherly
love, relief, and truth, and the brotherhood of man, are taught and
inculcated, without reference to particular forms, rituals, or ceremonies
of introduction, and a due observance of the ancient charges and landmarks of the Fraternity are made obligatory, and are constantly practiced.
"Resolved, That it is made the special duty of the Committee on
Foreign Correspondence to devote its attention and to ascertain and
inform this M.'. w:. Grand Lodge at its next Annual Grand Communication, of conditions of Grand Lodges of the F. and A. M. York
Rite, and of Grand Orients or Supreme Council of the A. and A.
Scottish Rite of Freemason1'y in foreign countries, especi:i.lly France,
Germany, Italy, Belgium, Mexico, and the Central and South American
States, with the view of establishing, wherever possible and permissible,
fraternal Masonic relations with such bodies; be it
·
"Resolved, That this M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of F. and A. M. ot
the State of Louisiana, do hereby recognize the legitimacy of Master
Masons made in Lodges of the A. and A. Scottish Rite in countries
where that is the dominant Rite, and welcome them to the right of
visitation and affiliation under the usual Masonic restrictions, the same
as if made in Lodges of our obedience; provided, that the Body that
has granted a charter to the Lodge, or Lodges of such brethren has
been recognized as a legitimate Masonic Body by this Grand Lodge."
Practically all of ·our Asnerican Grancl Lodges have insisted, as
conditions precedent to the recognition of a Grand Lodge, that it shall
clearly establish its legitimacy; i. e. that it shall have· sprung originally
from a Grand Lodge recognized as regular ; secondly, that it shall confine itself strictly to the three degrees of Ancient Craft Masonry;

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

59

thirdly, that it shall recognize the Ancient Landmarks, and among
these is an unequivocal belief in the Supreme Being, and, fourthly, that
it shall be a Sovereign and Independent Body, not recognizing allegiance to any other Supreme Body or Council; and according to these
standards, very few, if any, of the so-called Grand Orients, or Supreme
Councils, upon the Continent of Europe, or so-called Orients or Councils in Central and Southern American States, are entitled to recognition as Masonic Grand Lodges, and if recognition as Grand Lodges
is to be founded, as stated in the above resolutions, upon "the fundamental principles of morality, brotherly love, relief and truth and the
Brotherhood of Man" then the so-called Grand Lodges of colored
Masons, springing from the Prince Hall Grand Lodge, are entitled to
recognition, as well as an innumerable brood of other alleged Masonic
bodies. All of which is contrary to the well defined judgment of our
most eminent Masonic jurists.
John S. Thibaut (Donaldsonville), Grand Master.
Richard Lambert (New Orleans), Grand Secretary.

The assembling at Baltimore of Grand Masters from all parts of
the United States, was in pursuance of an invitation extended by
Grand Master Shryock to consider the general welfare of Freemasonry,
and in a sense was patterned after the meeting of a similar character
during the two preceding years, the one held at Philadelphia upon invitation of the Grand Master of Pennsylvania, and the other at Boston,
Mass., upon the occasion of the celebration of the 175th anniversary of
the founding of St. Johns' Lodge.
The one definite purpose, however, which Grand Master Shryock
appeared to have in mind in connection with this gathering of G~and
Masters was to effectually set at rest the idea which had g;ined some
prevalence in certain quarters, that these annual gatherings of Grand
Masters foreshadowed an effort to form a General Grand Lodge of
Masons for the United States, and Grand Master Shryock's decided
views that anything of this character is unthinkable and absolutely impossible, found practically unanimous support, Grand Master Shryock's
views upon this subject being set forth in the following language, quoted
from his address to the assembled Grand Masters:

62

"In inviting our distinguished Brethren to this gathering and to a
conference, which will be held to-morrow, I distinctly stated that it
was with no idea, wish or desire to foster the idea of a National Grand
Lodge; that I had invited them to meet the Grand Masters of the
United States and I was gratified to receive in reply from a large number of these distinguished Brethren, a line of commendation on the
ffentiments ; showing very clearly to my mind, the formation of such a
body in the United States was not only unnecessary, uncalled for and
impracticable, but absolutely impossible."
The meeting was one of the most distinguished of its character
ever held in this country, and the occasion, as voiced by all present,
was one of rare profit and enjoyment.

As is customary in this Jurisdiction, Quarterly Communications of
the Grand Lodge were held during the preceding Masonic year, on
March 10th, June 9th, September 9th, and the Annual Communication,
which is also one of the Quarterly Communications, on the date above
mentioned, December 8th.
There were also held within the year eight Special Communications for purposes of placing corner-stones, celebrating Fiftieth Anniversaries of different Lodges, dedicating Masonic Halls, etc.
At the Quarterly Communication held in March, a memorial of
R.'. W.'. William Thomas Grammar, deceased, Senior Grand Warden
of the Grand Lodge in 1874, was adopted; also report of the Chairman
of the Committee on Masonic Home, showing progress toward the
nccumulation of funds necessary to open the home to beneficiaries, and
also a report of counsel for the Grand Lodge in an important tax
suit, were made.
:The decision in the. tax suit is important in that the Supreme
Court decided that funds given to, or held by, the Grand Lodge for
charitable purposes (and the funds in question were received by virtue
of a will of one of the deceased brothers), are not properly the subject of taxation, and the effect of the decision is to strengthen the con•
tention that the Masonic Order is a charitable or benevolent institution within the eye of the law. That this decision is considered of
great importance to the Craft generally is evidenced by the fact that
numerous inquiries from represeptatives of other Grand Lodges in
other States, that are .confronted with similar questions, have been
addressed to the Committee of the Grand Lodge in Massachusetts, and
it is stated further by the Committee in their report that the Courts
of Law are properly recognizing that whatever other obligations our
Fraternity may have, "one leading one is that of charity, supporting
the poor and indigent members, their widows and orphans."
At this Communication also there was set forth the interesting
history connected with the bringing to light of the Masonic diploma

A great calamity befell the Masonic Home of this State in that on
February 15, 1909, the main buildings of the Home were completely
destroyed by fire. The catastrophe occurred in the day time and
fortunately no lives were lost and no serious personal injuries resulted to any of those connected with the institution. The residents
of the Home were provided with shelter in various places and ha..:e
been provided for in temporary quarters ever since.
At this session of the Grand Lodge a serious question arose as
to whether the policy of maintaining a Masonic Home should be continued in this Jurisdiction, and as the result of several discussions
during the Commtulication, it was apparently fully determined that
the Masonic Home as an adjunct to the charitable administration of
Masonry would not be abandoned, but that the control heretofore
loosely vested in the several Masonic Grand Lodges of the State should
be centralized in the hands of the Grand Lopge, and that in~tead of
abandoning the present site of the Home at East Grand Rapids, in
~avor of some other one of the several locations offered, new buildings of an approved type should be built upon the present site, and as a
final result of all of the discussions relative to the Masonic Home the
following resolution was adopted :
'

A somewhat notable. case occurred in this Jurisdiction in the

search for the missing man. More than $1,600 was contributed by

search, which, however, resulted in failure and disappointment.
The Grand Master, in speaking of the work of the Committee on

physical defect:

to you radical, is the changing of that part of the law relative to
physical disqualification. The position of the committee upon this
question is that, as the Lodge must be the judge of the mental and
moral qualifications of a petitioner for Masonry, being guided in their •
decisions only by the Ancient Landmarks, the same guide (Ancient
Landmarks), may safely be take.n as the standard for physical eligibility.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRl!SS.

The Grand Master presented a straightforward, business-like statement of his official actions during the year. Certain special dispensations were granted and others refused ; three Grand Lodge Special
Communications took place for the laying of corner-stones of public
buildings ; several Masonic Halls were dedicated; and other miscellaneous work in connection with the Grand Master's office creditably
performed.
An especial feature of the Grand .Master's activities d.u ring the
year is found in the large number of visitations made by him to subordinate Lodges. It was his purpose, so he informs us, when elected
to the honorable position of Grand Master of the Jurisdiction of Minnesota, to visit as many Lodges as possible, being particular to favor
in this respect those Lodges situated in out-of-the-way places and
therefore usually overlooked by Grand Masters. His visitations nu~­
bered, we believe, more than eighty, and the distance traveled by
him to accomplish these results was more than 10,000 miles.
There is nothing, in our opinion, that a Grand Master can do in
connection with the administration of his high office, that is so beneficial to the Craft generally as paying official visits to subordinate
Lodges, remembering especially the districts not usually favored by
the presence of a Grand Master, and we have no doubt that the
seventy-five or eighty visits paid by Grand Master Swan to the subordinate Lodges of his Jurisdiction wrought an immense amount of
good, the effects of which will not disappear for several years to come.
The Grand Master was fortunate in being able to report to the
Grand Lodge that the Grim Reaper had not invaded, within the preceding year, the ranks of the Grand Lodge.
Minnesota has just passed through the process of a revision and
recodification of its laws, pruning away dead material, reconciling contradictory decisions, and generally straightening out inconsistencies,
thereby giving to the Jurisdiction a virile code of sound and consistent
law. The trouble, we apprehend, with Minnesota, as well as with
many other Jurisdictions, has been that for many years past, each
Grand Master has yearly rendered an innumerable number of decisions, amounting annually some times to as many as a hundred, the
natural and inevitable result being a Masonic code expanding into
unreasonable proportions and containing scores of unsound and frequently contradictory decisions.
The decisions of Grand Master Swan were few in number, not
exceeding five or six, the two or three that met the approval of the

~

Grand Lodge expenses are held at a minimum, and surp us arising

A practice prevailing in Mississippi that might wisely be copied by
other Jurisdictions is a system of assistance e:xtende? b! .the Gra~d
Lodge to individual Lodges to aid them toward maintaining certa1.n
indigent aged members, who, under or~i~ary circ~~stan~es, would be
received into Masonic Homes under s1m1lar cond1t10ns in o~her Jurisdictions, but here the Trustees of the Grand Lodge Charity Fund
mav assist such indigent member to the extent of $50 per annum, upon
co~dition that the individual Lodge to which the indigent member belongs will contribute toward his support a like sum. In this m;mn~r,
many worthy decayed and decrepit brothers are enabled to remain
among their own people at their own homes, where they have _them,
thereby enjoying the comforts of individual freedom an~ association
with old friends instead of being required to become residents of an
institution, like a Masonic Home, which, even if cond~cted upon a
plan of great kindness and consideration toward the residents, nevertheless has an atmosphere of a charitable institution and cannot afford
the sense of comfort inseparable from association with one's home
and friends.

t~on can .find plell:sure and profit in that association; and, therefore as
