1~c man, there can be no such thing as negro Masonry and it is for

"There has been such a constant repetition of the phrase, which
has sprung up in Masonry, that it knows no race, color, or religious
condition that people have lost sight of the fact that this was but a
glittering generality upon the part of Masonic orators, indulged in
for the most part for the purpose of calling forth the applause of the
unthinking or uninformed Masons. It is not true now and never was,
and probably never will be, that the doors of Freemasonry are open to
men of all races, conditions, and creeds, and while the utmost tolerance is shown, there are existing people of numerous races who would
not be admitted into Masonry; there are others whose social and moral
conditions are such that they could not be, and there are others whose
religion is repugnant to the very fundamental principles upon which all
Masonry is based; it is not necessary that we should particularize where
these people are to be found; it suffices to say that there are numerous
races steeped in ignorance and 1.lnfitted for association with others, in
an Institution where the social element is cherished and developed to
its utmost extent, as in Freemasonry.
"It is only right and proper that we should say, that the attitude.
of the Southern States towards the negro race is misunderstood, and
a great wrong is done to both races, owing to that misunderstanding.
This question of negro Masonry is not involved .in the politieal conditions by which we are surrounded, although, doubtless, the sympathies
of our Northern brethren have been aroused against us, in consequence
of this misunderstanding. It should be stated, emphatically, that the
. people of Mississippi look upon the negro as a burden which God, in
His wisdom, has placed upon their shoulders; that they have not, and
never will do anything to harm him; that because they cannot associate with him on terms of social equality, either in the Lodge or outside of it, it is not to be assumed that there is any enmity or animosity existing towards him. In their eyes, he is simply a poor, unfortunate being, whom God has l>laced on a lower scale than others of
His people, over whom He exercises a fostering care. He is our neighbor, around whom we will throw the protection of wise and just laws
and enforce them in his favor, and provide suitable education for him
and his children, care for him in sickness and so far as may be protect him against his own follies and improvidences, and by every means
in our power, endeavor to make him better fitted to fill the sphere
which the Grand Architect of the Universe has provided for him, but
this does not mean that those lines of demarcation which the Almighty
has set up between the white and black races, can or will be disregarded. They are as everlasting as the hills themselves, and it is not
prejudice, but the recognition of a fact, insurmountable, arising from
an ethnological difference, which prevents, and will ever continue to
prevent, anything like social equality between the races.
"As Freemasonry is, pre-eminently, a social condition, it is manifest that only those who stand upon a plane of equal social qualihca-

MASONIC HOM!l.

The Masonic Home pr.o ject has been advanced to the point of the
completion of the edifice and its furnishings, so that the reception
of residents is the only thing remaining to the full fruition of the ·
project. The report of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Home
discloses the fact that the plant, so to speak, and equipment is worth
$85,000 or more, against which there is a comparatively small outstanding indebtedness.
Provision has been made for an income sufficient to maintain the
Home and provide for say twenty-five beneficiaries. This income arises
from a per capita assessment of $1 against the membership, the largest
per capita assessment for that purpose of any Jurisdiction in the United
States outside of California, and interest upon a small endowment
fund. The total prospective income for the next succeeding year is
fixed at about $8,000. Considering the size of this Jurisdiction, the
total membership being only slightly in excess of 5,000, Montana has
achieved a distinctly notable result in providing so complete and thoroughly equipped home for its unfortunate members.

GRAND MAS'l'tR'S ADDR:l!SS.

It is not uncommon for Grand Masters, at the outset of their annual address to Grand Lodges, to picture the ideal man as created
through the application of the magnificent and exalted principles of
our Fraternity; and, in reading Grand Lodge reports, a reviewer will
occasionally run onto a poetical quotation, or some other specimen of
exalted diction descriptive, as stated above, of the ideal Masonic character, and here is one that has done yeoman service in the past and is
likely to continue to do so in the future, and is here quoted to give
the common every-day Mason a glimpse of some of the specimen blocks
chiseled from qu~ries to which Grand Masters are wont to resort for
material from which to construct their addresses to the Craft. This
quotation is splendid, and can be found embedded in the annual address of one of our own Grand Masters :

"God give us men ! A time like this demands
Strong minds, great hearts, true faith and ready hands;
Men whom the lust of office does not kill;
Men whom the spoils of office cannot buy ;
Men who possess opinions and a will.
Men who have honor, men who will not lie;
Men who can stand before a demago~ue,
And damn his treacherous flatteries without winking;
Tall men, sun-crowned. who live above the fog
In public duty and in 9rivate thinking;
For while the rabble, with their thumb-worn creeds,
Their large professions and their little deeds,
Mingle in selfish strife, lo I Freedom weeps,
Wrong rules the land, and waiting Justice sleeps I"

FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCE.

The Report on Foreign Correspondence is by Past Grand Master
James H. Wroth. He reviews in a comprehensive manner between
fifty-five and sixty American and foreign Jurisdictions.
California, 1908, is considered, with liberal quotations from the
address of the Grand Master, etc.
Brother Wroth thinks that what constitutes Masonic offenses
should be more clearly defined by different Jurisdictions in order 'that
a Mason· moving from one Jurisdiction to another, may be advised,
because what was not a Masonic offense in the Jurisdiction of his
former residence may be such in the Jurisdiction into which he removes.
We apprehend that if a Maso9, regardless of his place of residence, observes the obligations he has assumed in the several degrees,
and further observes the laws of the land wherever he resides, will
not commit any Masonic offense, and it should not be very difficult
for him to do both of these things, and Brother Wroth's misgivings
about the possibilities of a Mason unwittingly committing a Masonic
offense are, if we may be permitted the opinion, unjustified.
He also expresses the fear that the desire for "legislation," so
generally manifested in different Jurisdictions, may have the effect of
undermining the landmarks. Brother W roth's fears in this respect
are, we think, unfounded. There certainly has been no proposed legislation of which we have any knowledge, that appears to threaten any
of the ground works of Freemasonry.
Frank Johnson (San Marcial), Grand Master.
Alpheus A. Keen (Albuquerque), Grand Secretary.

. MASONIC HOME.

The Masonic Home of New York continues to be the one great
matter of concern of the Grand Lodge. It is the most elaborate institution of its kind in the world, and in comparison with other Masonic
H omes is in a class entirely by itself.

100

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

All of the arguments in the Grand Lodge during the past two
or three years over the management of the properties belonging to the
Grand Lodge in the City of New York, have been addressed to the
one idea of so developing and managing those properties as to produce an income that may be applied to the administration and betterment of the Masonic Home at Utica.
At the date of this Communication of the Grand Lodge, there
were 403 beneficiaries sheltered at the Home, of which 92 were children; 110 were women; and 201 were men.
The annual cost of maintenance during the preceding year was.
$79,167.87, an average per capita of $200.92. The Grand Master, in his
adrlress touching the Home, voi<;es his high opinion of the institution
as follows:
"We are sheltering at this time four hundred and three people, of
whom ninety-two are children. In age they range from two to ninetyfive years; the problem of maintaining discipline, and at the same time
securing the happiness of so large and varied a family is, at times,
embarrassing, but we are confident no other institution in the country
can show better results in the general good order and contentment of its
population than we do.
"Beneficent and serviceable as are our charities to the old. it
is, nevertheless, in the care-and education of the young that the most
satisfactory and valuable results are had. No brother within the sound
of my voice has more just reason to be proud of his own children than
he has to be proud of those little ones whom Providence has placed in
our care. Without exception they are manly boys and womanly girls.
"Sixty-nine of them are in the public schools of the City of Utica;
their school reports show them the equals of any, and the unofficial
statement of the teachers having them in charge is, that the children
of the Home are in many respects the best of all under their supervision."

may best· be improved so as to insure the largest possible revenue to

NEW ZEALAND, 1909.
Twentieth Annual Communication. New Plymouth, May 5-6, 1909.
The Twentieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons of New Zealand was held at New
Plymouth on Wednesday and Thursday, May 5 and 6, 1909, His Excellency the Right Honorable Lord Plunket, Grand Master, presiding.
On the first of January, 1909, there were 159 active Lodges in the
Jurisdiction; with a total membership of 10,020, showing an increase of
seven new Lodges over the preceding year, and a gain in membership
of 782.
Financially the Grand Jurisdiction of New Zealand is comparatively strong. The balances to the credit of the various funds amount
in round figures to the equivalent of $100,000.
The first business of the Annual Communication was the presentation of the balance sheet and statement of accounts, after which
followed the nomination of officers for the next succeeding year, the
Most Worshipful William Lee (Baron) Plunket being unanimously
and "with demonstrations of applause" re-elected Grand Master.
The Widows and Aged Masons' Fund now amounts to the equivalent of more than $50,000, and pensions, or annuities, are apportioned
yearly from the fund to various deserving and distressed Masons, the

"Brethren, my period of public office in New Zealand, and my
position in the Chair of King Solomon, come to a close in about a
year's time. I shall find it hard to leave this country, where I have
spent some of the happiest years of my life. To you, my brother
Masons, I owe many debts of gratitude. Notwithstanding the wise
counsel and whole-hearted loyalty whidh the members of Grand Lodge
have ever extended to me, I feel very conscious of much work ill done
and much not done at all. I can only say that during my final year
as Grand Master I will do all I can to merit the confidence you have
again shown in me and strive to advance the welfare of Freemasonry
in general and our own Constitution in particular."
There is a report on Fraternal Correspondence, which, in many

MASONIC ORPHANS' HOME.

If there is one Masonic charity in the United States that is preeminent above all others, it is, in our opinion, the Masonic Orphans'
Home of North Carolina.
The following quotation from the report of the Board of Directors
of the Oxford Orphans' Asylum, as it is called, refers to the inception
and growth of this institution, and will be of interest to Masons
generally:

"This Grand ~odge, more than a .third o_f a century ago, ventured
on .an almost ~n~ned system of Masonic 7hanty-;-the maintenance, education and trammg for the useful pursmts of life of the destitute orphans of ~he State. . There is always something peculiarly affecting to
every feeling heart m the appeal of the fatherless and motherless children1 helpless and neglected until cared for by the generous and
charitable people who are ccnfrOnted with their sad condition.' Although animated by a genuine spirit of charity and .benevolence the
active advocates of the establishment of an orphan asylum by the Grand
Lod~e of North Carolina met with many discouragements and were
confronted by many difficulties. Yet imbued with the spirit of patience and perseverance and strong faith in the success of the undertaking, they never relaxed their efforts until their foridest hopes had
been realized.
"To-day the Oxford Orphan Asylum stands as monument to the
wisdom of those good men and Masons who were instrumental in

a

•

On account of the advanced age of the venerable Superintendent,
Brother J . W. Hicks, his resignation from that office was tendered, to
take effect September 1st, and was reluctantly accepted.
·
Brother Hicks, in his final report to the Board of Directors of the
Asylum, also adverts to the small initial step of the beloved institution,
with which he had been so long connected, in the following language:
"Brethren :-Before entering upon another annual report may we,
for a moment, view together a scene of thirty-seven years ago?
"Past Grand Master Francis D. Winston, then a student at Horner
School, an appreciative eye-witness of the scene, brings it vividly
before us:
"'It was on Saturday afternoon. A dull cloud hung in the sky.
A man with a one-horse wagon drove to the door . Mr. Mills, with
gruff voice, asked his mission. He told it. The gigantic form of our
friend shook with emotion. He lifted the pale youth from the wagon
with the paw of a lion. He raised him in the air, and with melting
pity and tears, let him drop upon his heart and kissed him. It was
indeed the caress of the lion, but it was t ruly the caress of love.'
"Through the years, though .not without its difficulties, its struggles, the institution thus started by the Masonic Fraternity of North
Carolina has survived, has performed a great service, has grown in
strength and efficiency. We may humbly and gratefully say: 'How
wondrously, how gloriously our God hath wrought! How vastly p,rivileged have been His helpers in this work of measureless worth I' '
The North Carolina Masonic Orphans' Home endeavors to .combine with moral and mental guidance, manual training, and connected
with the Institution we find mention of a sash, door and blind factory, the printing office, a shoe shop, farm, etc. The total income of
the Home last year was $45,733.54, and after deducting expenses in
connection with the printing office, sash, door and blind factory, etc.,
a balance remained of $7,033.21.
It is worthy of mention that there is a singing class, possessing
a high order of ability, composed of children of the Home, and it is
customary for this singing class to give concerts in different portions
of North Carolina, and last year a net profit appears in · the schedule o~
receipts from concerts given by the singing class of $8,391.87, a not
unimportant factor in the total income of the Institution.
At the date of this report there were 324 children in the Institution, almost equally divided as to girls and boys, there being 164 girls
and 160 boys. There were 63 admissions during the year, and 64
passed out of the school to approved homes, positions in life, etc.
The per capita cost of maintenance was approximately $78.

might not be a few, even in that wonderfully blest Commonwealth of

There is only one Jurisdiction in the United States, and that is

The Grand Secretary of North Dakota, who appears to be the

approval with which his report on Masonic Homes, etc., was received by
Masons throughout the country, and refers to the fact that instead of
having 300 copies of this report printed for general distribution, he was
obliged, in order to satisfy the clamorous demands throughout the
country for his production, to have 500 printed, even though it necessitated his asking the Grand Lodge to be forgiven for the additional
expense thrust upon it in connection with providing the additional
copies.
When we consider the fact that old Jurisdictions like Massachusetts,
and Alabama, and others are at the present hour getting into line with
the vast majority of American Jurisdictions and establishing thoroughly equipped Masonic Homes, and when we consider further the
present exceedingly comprehensive improvements and expansions of
these institutions under way by such Jurisdictions as Pennsylvania and
New York, we are constrained to the conclusion that the action of
North Dakota upon this subject is unique; and the Grand Secretary,
holding his twenty-eight paged pamphlet aloft, may be compared to
the elderly female who, standing upon the sea shore, essayed to sweep
back the advancing tide with her broom.
If North Dakota fails to shine as a star of the first magnitude in
other respects, she assuredly does shine without any rival whatever
among Grand Lodges of the earth, in having established as a Grand
Lodge adjunct, with suitable prices annexed thereto, an annual Oratorical Contest, participated in by budding Demostheneses from' the
various educational institutions of the State, and the Grand Lodge
funds are appropriated each year for the purpose of providing suitable prizes to the winners, and as an evidence of the broad catholicity
of spirit with which this contest is conducted, it is not limited to the
sons of Master Masons, but is a wide-open, free-for-all race.
The Grand Secretary, who gives us an account of the 1909 Contest, states that the subject upon which the winner discoursed was
"The German American," and as a Masonic theme it surely was a
peach.

GRAND MASONIC RELIEF FUND.

Some two years ago the Grand Lodge of North Dakota ·in order
to justify the reversal of its previously expressed purpose t~ found a
Masonic Home, appointed the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary a
Committee of One to scour the Masonic earth with a view of discovering, if possible, some method other than the Masonic Home
proposition of administering this form of Masonic charity, and as a
result of that investigation, a little booklet of some twenty-eight pages
was issued containing the report of this committee. He discovered
that certain foreign Jurisdictions, notably England, had established an
annuity fund, from which annual stipends were distributed to certain
needy and distressed members, etc., and the Grand Lodge of North
Dakota, basing its change of policy upon this report, abandoned the
Masonic Home idea and established in lieu thereof, the high-sounding
adjunct called the "Grand MQJSonic Relief Fund," and the work of the
year of this magnificent charity was summarized in the report of the
Board of Trustees as follows :

"It is with a great deal of pr1de we report that not a 'single call
has been made upon us for aid."
In other words, no cry of distress penetrated their hermetically
sealed, cyclone cellar of retirement, and, as a financial proposition, it is
vastly superior, as may be inferred from the glow of pride mentioned,
to the Masonic Home idea.
In explanation of their providential immunity, they spoke of their
great, and growing, and prosperous Commonwealth, in which, of course,

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Grand Master's address is a lengthy and exhaustive statement of his official acts during the .year, together with a general survey of the work of the Jurisdiction during his tenure of office as Grand
Master, it having extended over a period of five yeal's. He refers
to the fact that when he was elected in 1904, the Jurisdiction had a
membership of 4,171, which had increased during his incumbency in
the Grand East to 1,650, and that during the same time the income
of the Grand Lodge had advanced from $5,016 to $8,090. He regarded this as eminently satisfactory and as showing commendable
progress.
He also refers with great pleasure to the fact that during his
incumbency, the Jurisdiction had acquired and paid for, and opened a
fully equipped Freemasons' Home which, he believes, will not only
prove a blessing to those for whom it is intendeg, but will open up
new avenues of Masonic activity, and be a distinct credit to the Craft in
the Jurisdiction of Nova Scotia, and he adds that, considering the
size of the Jurisdiction, wonders have been accompli~ed, in his judgment, in connection with the Home, and that what has been done
speaks volumes for the liberality and true Masonic spirit of the
members.

the Grand Lodge of Nova Scotia, and therefore peculiar to that Jurisdiction, they may not be considered as of general interest, but as

Grand Master of the Jurisdiction and for a great many years Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence. Of Brother Cunningham, the Grand Master makes the following appreciative remarks:

MASONIC HOME.

The Grand Lodge of Ohio continues to manifest its great function
of charity through its Masonic Home, surely one of the best and most
capably managed homes in the country. Everything is done in this
home to eliminate whatever would cause the recipients of the Grand
Lodge bounty to feel that they are mendicants, and constant effort is
made to cause them to regard the Masonic Home as truly their home,
without any suggestion of the ordinary public charitable institution.
The Home enjoys an ample income, a per capita tax of 30 cents
upon the membership, being perhaps the main reliance, although contributions towards i:he maintenance of the home are made by other
Grand Masonic Bodies in Ohio, and these direct contributions are supplemented by the income from the Permanent Endowment Fund, which
amounts now to more than $100,000, and is receiving accretions each
year from various sources.
At this Communication the total residents of the Home numbered
174, divided as follows: Men, 73; W(')men, 46; boys, 31; girls, 24.
The President of the Home, Hon. James W. Iredell, Jr., of Cincinnati, has been re-elected many times to that honorable position.
His administration of the affairs of the Home has been of a high
order; he brings to the discharge of his trust splendid executive ability,
a comprehensive knowledge and appreciation of the Grand Institution
of Freemasonry, and a heart full of compassion and tenderness for the
unfort~nate members of our institution, who are obliged to seek the
shelter and protection of the Masonic Home. These qualities all render
him an ideal 'President of the Ohio Home.
GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

At the outset of his address, the Grand Master comments upon
the fact that the Grand Lodge of Ohio has just entered upon the
second century of its existence and thaf it is enjoying unexampled
prosperity.
,Nearly 76,000 Masons in good standing are carried upon the
rosters of its su'bordinate Lodges, and while the numerical gain from
year to year is highly gratifying, it is more pleasing to know that the
' quality of the young men seeking admission into the institution is of
the highest order.
The Grand Master is obliged to record the death in the preceding year of the one, who in many respects, was the foremost
Mason of Ohio, and one of the best known Masons in the world, Most
Worshipful Brother William Moore Cunningham, the oldest Past

Dispensations were issued by the Grand Master to form six new
Lodges. Special Communications were held for the purpose of laying
foundation stones for nine public buildings. The four Lodges to
which charters were granted at the preceding Communication were
duly constituted, and there were fifteen dedications of Masonic Temples and Lodge-rooms, altogether a year of marked activity.
Perhaps the most notable event occurring during the year was the
Occasional Grand Lodge, convened by the Grand Master at Cincinnati,
February 18, 1909, for the purpose of making William H . Taft a Mason
at sight. A large number of Grand Masters from various Jurisdictions
throughout the United States were present, and probably no event
of the year has been commented upon so extensively as has this occurrence. The Grand Master unquestionably acted within his authority, as the Constitution of Ohio expressly recognizes this prerogative as belonging to the Grand Master.
The candidate assumed in the regular manner all of the obligations and was vested ·with the secrets in open Lodge and in regular
manner, so that the "making a Mason at sight" in that case amounted
simply to waiving certain formalities that, because of his well-known
character, were not strictly essential.
The practice, however, of making Masons at sight is one that
must, upon general principles, be disapproved, and is an ancient landma1·k of doubtful authority.

issued Code."

MASONIC HOMF..

Oklahoma for a number of years past has been actively engaged
in accumulating a Masonic Home Fund, which at this date amounts
to about $40,000. Indian Territory had proceeded one step farther in
the matter, and within the last two years had acquired a Masonic
Home, which had finally been located temporarily at Ataka, Oklahoma,
this location having been established after it became apparent that
there would be a merger of the two Grand Jurisdictions.
There are now sheltered in this Home about sixty children, but
the demands for space are increasing to such an extent that it will
no doubt be necessary soon for the consolidated Jurisdiction to obtain
other and more commodious quarters, and with the combined resources
of the two Jurisdictions, a splendidly equipped Home, with ample
funds for its maintenance, will no doubt soon be established.

the past year a site for the home, costing nearly $150,000 and consisting of nearly l,000 acres, was selected, located about twenty miles

The Thomas Ranken Patten Bequest, amounting to more than a
million of dollars, for a Masonic Institution for Boys, will become
available soon after the probable completion of this home, and it is
the expectation that this institution will be established in connection
with the Masonic Home, and also that the present Masonic Home, ·
located in North Broad Street, in the City of Philadelphia, will be consolidated with the projected institution, so that in time all of these
charities will be assembled at this one central location. There appears
to have been some difficulty, during the past year, in obtaining a legal
transfer of the title to the property of the present Masonic Home in
Philadelphia to the new Board, but it is anticipated that these difficulties will, during the present year, be overcome, and that in another year the entire Masonic .Home paraphernalia will be under the
direction of the Grand Lodge.

GRAND MASTER'S ADDRESS.

One of the principal matters referred to by the Grand Master in
his address is a report of the Conference of Grand Masters held in
Philadelphia by virtue of his invitation, on the first, second and third
days of June of the current year, and from the report of Brother
James M. Lamberton, Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence,
who was present at these conferences, which report of Brother. Lamberton was rendered at the Quarterly Communication on December
!st, we learn that the work of the Conference of Grand Masters was
epitomized in the adoption of the following recommendations addressed to the several Grand Lodges represented by the Grand Masters at the Conference, and these resolutions were also adopted by
the further conference of Grand Masters, held in Baltimore, Maryland, in pursuance of the invitation of· Grand Master Shryock of
Maryland, and in addition to the Grand Masters convened at Philadelphia in June, the following Grand Jurisdictions were represented at
Baltimore in December, to-wit:
California, Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, North Dakota, Oklahoma,
Oregon, and South Dakota.
The Conference at Philadelphia being composed of representatives from the Jurisdictions East of the Mississippi River; so the two
conferences combined represented nearly all of our American Jurisdictions.

124

REPORT ON CORRESPONDEKCE.
The following are the resolutions referred to:

"WHEREAS, The members of said Conference, explicitly disclaiming any authority to legislate for or to bind any of the Jurisdictions
represented, agreed to present to, and recommend for adoption by,
their respective Grand Lodges, such recommendations as met with the
unanimous approval of those present; and
"WHEREAS, The said Conference unanimously agreed to the following recommendations:
"l. The name of the petitioner should be subscribed in full in
the petition ;
"2. The date and place. of the birth of the petitioner should be
given in the petition ;
"3. The occupation of the petitioner should be designated in the
petition specifically and in detail, both with relation to himself and his
employer, if any;
"4. Where the petitioner resides in a city having streets that are
named and houses that are numbered, he should state in his petition
the name of the street and the number of his house ;
"5. The members of the Investigating Committee, where such a
committee is appointed, shoul.d subscribe to a report in writing, when
required, as to a thorough investigation of the character of the petitioner, this recommendation applying only to those Jurisdictions where
reports in writing are required;
"6. A petition to be made a Mason should state that the petitioner has never before petitioned a Lodge of Masons to be made a
Mason; or, in cases where the petitioner has before pethioned to be
made a Mason, he should state the name, number, location, and Jurisdiction of the Lodge previously petitioned, and the date, as near as
may be, of such petition ;
"7. A petitioner should have resided within the Jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge for one year, that is, have had a legal residence there
for one year;
"8. When application is made by a petitioner whose legal residence is in another Jurisdiction, which by its laws claims the petitioner
as its material, a waiver of Jurisdiction should be requested from the
last named Jurisdiction ;
"9. The form of 'Renunciation' used in Pennsylvania should be
required from petitioners who have been identified with clandestine
bodies;
"10. No petition to be made a Mason should be received from
one previously rejected in another Jurisdiction, within five years after
such rejection, until the rejecting Lodge has, by unanimous ballot,
waived its claim of Jurisdiction;
"11. All intra-Jurisdictional communications should be sent
through the offices of the Grand Masters."
With the exception of No. 10, we believe all of these resolutions are in harmony with our California Masonic law. California
does not recognize penal jurisdiction over rejected candidates from
other' Jurisdictions beyond a year; or, in other words, after they
have gained a legal residence in California.

Reference is made by the Grand Master to the invaluable compilation, undertaken during the year of the History of Freemasonry in

DJ(CISIONS.

Twenty or more decisions were rendered by the Grand Master
during the year, and inasmuch as decisions by the Grand Master of
Pennsylvania are final unless revoked or annulled by some succeeding
Grand Master, there is no discussion of his decision in Grand Lodge,
and no reference of the same to any Jurisprudence or other committee, such as is the practice in most Jurisdictions.
The following of his decisions are quoted :
"A non-resident of this Jurisdiction, who is a member of a Lodge
herein, is not eligible to hold an office in his Lodge.
"A Masonic Lodge must not be opened on Sunday.
"I have refused permission, in a number of instances, to permit
addresses and lectures, that have been delivered in other Jurisdictions, to be read in our subordinate Lodges."
Why? What objection would there be to the reading in one of
the subordinate Lodges of Pennsylvania of a Masonic oration, for
instance, delivered in one of the other American Jurisdictions?
"I directed a Lodge not to advance a Brother for the reason that
an investigation of his case developed the fact that he was not under
the tongue of good Masonic report. Such authority is clearly incident to the office of the Grand Master, and I consider it his bounden
duty to exercise that power when there is evidence of any lack of a

126

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

proper investigation by a subordinate Lodge, coupled with clearly
proven facts, that should prevent a man of doubtful probity becoming
a member of our Fraternity."
It would strike an ordinary observer that the Grand Master, in
assuming the right to forbid the advancement of the brother who has
been regularly initiated, is usurping arbitrary power, and denying a
brother his constitutional right, after having been initiated to something more than an ex parte hearing, and while the facts in some particular case, might seem to justify drastic action, yet we fail to understand how, even in extreme cases, the Grand Master can disregard
the universal Masonic Law which confers upon one who has been
initiated, and is therefore entitled to be called brother, certain rights
not possessed by a profane.
A resolution from the Committee on Correspondence was adopted,
extending fraternal recognition to the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of Saskatchewan.
COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The usual exhaustive and instructive report from the accomplished
James M. Lamberton, Committee on Correspondence, finds its accustomed place in the volume of the proceedings.
Under the caption of California, he speaks of our Grand Lodge
returning to the custom prevailing prior to 1906 of not having reports
of Committee of Investigation upon petitioners for the degrees read
in the Lodge. The custom up to 1906 was that these reports were
read in the Lodges, but in 1906, by virtue of a resolution adopted
by the Grand Lodge, these reports in future were not to be read, and
the only change adopted in 1908 was a slight modification of the rule
adopted in 1906, but in no wise affecting the general purpose of maintaining secrecy as to names of committeemen and the nature of their
individual reports, which was the principal change effected by the
modification of the law in 1906.
George W. Guthrie (Philadelphia), Grand Master.
William A. Sinn (Philadelphia), Grand Secretary.

"In this Province of Quebec, Masonry, through no fault of ours,
is practiced under difficulties which are little realized beyond our
borders. To the majority of our fellow-citizens, the teachings and
objects of the Order are, by the prescription of an authority which
thev respect a sealed book; a prescription to which .no exception is
or ·~an be ta'ken by those of us for whom that authority and its enactments are without sanction; a prescription which we consider to be a
matter entirely between those by whom and to whom it is addressed.
When however as a reason for such a prohibitive enactment, there
are p~blicly and privately assigned to our Fraternity aims an~ objects which are absolutely foreig~ to and expressly and ~ategonc~lly
excluded from its sphere, there 1s thereby created a pamful feelmg
of distrust," etc.
One of the landmarks of Freemasonry is belief in and reverence
for the Supreme Being. Another is belief in the Immortality of the
Soul.
Aside from insistence upon these two great fundamentals, Masonry
is tolerant of all religious beliefs, and, as is well known, political and
sectarian discussion. of any kind within our tyled Lodge-room, is absolutely prohibited, and it is undoubtedly because of this broad spirit of
toleration, coupled with a guaranteed freedom of individual investigation and thought, that Masonry has encountered the serious opposition of a certain powerful hierarchy.
The reports of the various District Deputy Grand Masters show
a careful and thorough Lodge supervision, and the reports of the
Secretary and Treasurer disclose sound and flourishing financial conditions.

FOREIGN CORRESPONDENCJ';.

The Report on Foreign Correspon<lence is by Past Grand Master
E . T. D. Chambers, his twenty-fourth. He reviews in an intelligent
manner the usual American and Foreign Jurisdictions.
California, 1900, is considered with an extensive quotation from
the oration of Grand Orator Benjamin F. Bledsoe.
In the conclusion of his report, Brother Chambers gives expression to a vein of sadness, in that the circle of writers of Correspondence Reports, that he first entered some twenty-four years ago, has
been arrowed by the touch of the Grim Reaper, and that so many
of the old members of that circle have passed silently into the shadows
of the Great Unknown.
Brother Chambers expresses regret at the tendency which he has
noticed in certain instances "to ignore the absolute requirements that
mark the dividing line between actual legitimate Freemasonry and
the plated sham that bears the name but not the hall mark-the
character-of the sterling article."
We are in hearty agreement with Brother Chambers in the belief
that every Masonic Grand Lodge, before its claim to regularity can be
recognized, should establish; first, legitimacy of its origin; secondly,
that it confines its practice to the Three Degrees of Ancient Craft
Masonry only; thirdly, that it holds itself bound to a strict observance
of the Ancient Landmarks; fotirthly, that it is an Independent Sovereign Grand Lodge, acknowledging no connection with any Supreme
Council or Superior Body of any kind whatever.
j. Alex Cameron (Montreal) , Grand Master.
Will H. Whyte (Montreal), Grand Secretary.
QUEENSLAND, 1909.
Fifth Annual Communication. Brisbane.
The Communicatiorts of the Grand Lodge of Queensland are held
quarterly and at the Quarterly Communication of June 14, 1909,
A. M. Hertzberg was elected Gtand Master, Lord Chalmsford, the
former ,Grand Master, having resigned from that position.
The Grand Jurisdiction of Queensland was apparently regularly
formed .by a constitutional number of Lodges, and now numbers
fifty-six subordinates.
9a

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

It has been engaged in a contrpversy with the mother Grand Lodges
of Scotland and England over the question of recognition as a Sovereign Independent Grand Lodge, that recognition having, up to the
present date, been refused. Queensland, however, has been recognized
as a regular Sovereign Independent Grand Lotlge by forty-three foreign Grand Lodges, thirty of them being American.
It has always been the policy of the Grand Lodges of Scotland
and England to refuse recognition of Grand Lodges erected in outside
territory in which they have had subordinates, until actually finally
forced to this action by the practically unanimous recognition of the
remaining Masonic world. The Grand Lodge of Queensland may now
be fairly considered as having established its right to a position among
the Sovereign Grand Lodges of the world, but recognition as such by
Scotland and England will no doubt be deferred for some years to
come.
During the preceding year eleven additional Grand Lodges extended fraternal recognition to Queensland, and the membership of the
Grand Jurisdiction increased from 1594 to 1794, and this, despite the
fact of all deductions on account of withdrawals, suspensions, deaths,
etc.
The total income of the Grand Lodge during the preceding year
was apparently about $6,000.
· The Widows and Orphans and Aged Masons' Fund has been
started with a credit balance at this Communication of between $6,000
and $7,000.
A. M. Hertzberg, Grand Master.
Hon. J. F. G. Foxton, Grand Registrar.

ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER.

The Grand Master's address at the Annual Communication was
a summary of his official actions during the year.
He refers to the fraternal dead, gives a list of dispensations
granted by him, mentions correspondence with subordinates upon questions of Masonic law, but renders comparatively few so-called decisions, none of them of general importance, makes certain recommendations, etc.
He declined to grant a dispensation to form a Lodge at Providence to be composed of Italian residents of that city, the work to be
done in the Italian language. His reasons for declining to grant this
dispensation were on account of the limited number of Italians resident
at Providence, and also because the experiment of a Lodge working in
a foreign tongue in Rhode Island had never been indulged in.
He paid numerous visits to the subordinates of his Jurisdiction,
several notable events having been commemorated, one being the On:!
Hundredth Annivereary of Manchester Lodge, No. 12, of Anthony,
R. I., and he concludes his report as follows:
"In concluding this report of my stewardship, I am deeply sensible of the frailty of a11 that is human, realizing that all my acts
may not meet with the unqualified approval of this august body. Any
errors of action or judgment I sincerely trust will receive such administration as will redound to the glory of our beloved Institution."
The reports of the variom District Deputy Grand Masters, of
the Grand Lecturer, Grand Secretary, and other officers, disclost: a
gratifying degree of prosperity, substantial advances having been made
during the preceding year in membership as we11 as Grand Lodge assets,
and as evidence that peace and harmony prevail throughout the Jurisdiction, the report of the Commissioners of Trials is herewith quoted :
"The Commissioners of Trials report that since the last Semi-annual Communication of the Grand Lodge there have been no ..cases of
infraction of the Masonic laws submitted to them for their considera-

MASONIC WIDOWS AND ORPHANS' HOME.

Concerning this institution, which is to the Jurisdiction of Texas
the very "apple of its eye,'' the Grand Master makes the following
comments:
"T'he question has been asked, 'What has the Grand Lodge of
Texas done to entitle it to the loyal support and commendation of
the Masons of this State?'
"To my mind, the question is easily and satisfactorily answered by
a simple reference to the establishment by this Grand Lodge of the
Masonic Home and Industrial Institute."

*

•

*

*

*

*

•

•

•

"I shall not, at this time, even briefly sketch the history of the
establishment of our Home, for this is a question that we are all
familiar with. Suffice it to say that I do not believe that any similar
institution has ever been better conducted, or received more watchful
care, than has been bestowed upon our Home by those who have
been placed in charge of it, and to whom the responsibility of its management has been committed. When we stop to consider that the
members of your Board of Directors, from the organization of the
Home up to the present time, have not received a single cent in compensation for the services they have rendered, and that they have not
only given their time and their talents to this noble work, but have
personally paid the expenses that they have been put to in their visits
to and from the Home, our grateful thanks go out to them anew.
"It is a matter of congratulation that the funds which this Grand
Lodge has set aside yearly for the benefit of the Home have been
judiciously invested, so that to-day it is a source of gratification to
know that not a cent has been lost through bad iµanagement or bad
investment, and the value of the buildings, grounds, furnishings, cash
on hand and investments, has reached the substantial sum of three hundred and twenty-six thousand nine hundred and seventy-nine dollars
and nineteen cents ($326,979.19), and it may safely be said that the
Home is on a safe, solid and sure foundation."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

From the report of the Board of Directors of the Widows and

The Home has been in existence only twenty-three years, and, as
stated above, has total assets now of $326,279.09, and is doing work
of the highest order, and it is something of which not onzy Texas
Masonry but of which Masonry of the entire American l!nion may be
proud.

The Grand Master renders a number of decisions and the comments
of the learned Jurisprudence Committee concerning a few of the decisions that were not approved, or were partially modified, were as
follows:
"Decision No. 1, which holds that the 'cor~er;sto,ne o.f a building
must be laid in the northeast corner of the building, while no doubt

technically and academically correct, is too broad for practical enforcement. Every Masonic building should be made to conform to the
rule enunciated by the Grand Master, if at all practicable, but we do
not think that a Masoinc Lodge should be compelled to refuse to lay
the corner-stone of public buildings because those in charge of the
same may not desire to place the corner-stone in the Masonic position.''
"It is the opinion Of this Committee that the requirement that the
so-called degree of Past Master is not only a useless and unreasonable one, but one that, in parts of the State that are sparsely settled,
is very onerous and opprt'ssive. Great difficulty is often experienced in
finding the required number. qualified to confer the degree, and when
at last it is conferred, the Master-elect is in no way better fitted to perform the duties of the office to which he has been elected. It is an
anomaly to prescribe that a Master Mason when elected to the office
of Worshipful Master shall not be installed unless he receives as part
of the installation service a certain degree that the members of his
Lodge do not possess, and which they perhaps may never obtain. No ,
valid reason can be assigne.d for such requirement, and it has only
been a prolific source of vexation to the different Grand Masters, and
trouble to this Grand Lodge, and we believe the different edicts permitting or requiring the conferring of the Past Master's degree should
be repealed, except the requirement in Article V, Chapter I, Section
12, which refers to the Masters of new Lodges alone. We therefore
offer for adoption the following resolution:
"Resolved, That it is not required and is deemed unnecessary that
the Worshipful Master-elect of any except a new Lodge, as provided
in Article V, Chapter I. Section 12, of the Constitution, should receive the degree of Past Master, and that he shall be fully qualified and
empowered to preside over his Lodge without receiving said Past
Master's degree, and that all edicts and laws in conflict herewith are
hereby repealed."
'
"A Fellow Craft Mason has the right to sit in his Lodge when
opened in that or the Entered Apprentice degree, although he may
have been rejected for the Master's degree, and he cannot be excluded from sittin~ in his Lodge when opened in the degrees he has
received, upon objection of some other member. He cannot be deprived of that right except by suspension or expulsion. We, therefore, disapprove of the decision to a different effect rendered by the
Grand Master."

For conciseness of statement, the Grand Secretary of Texas, the
Very Worshipful John Watson, holds the record.
His entire annual report, covering the activities of what, in many
respects, is the most important office in the immense Jurisdiction of
Texas, is condensed into a space occupying one page and five lines of
the printed proceedings, and as a sample of the extreme efficiency with
which the affairs of his office, having in charge the 805 Lodges of
the Jurisdiction, is conducted, it may be stated that the annual returns
of every subotdinate Lodge were made and all dues for the year were
paid within the limit of time prescribed by the Grand Lodge By-laws.
The report on Foreign Coi;respondence is by able and accomplished
Veteran Past Grand Master Thomas M. Matthews, Sr. It is, we think,
his twenty-fifth consecutive report, and as usual is an invaluable contribution to current Masonic lit era tu re.
In the prologue to his report, he addresses a few lines to his brethren in Texas, setting forth in extenso his views .upon two subjects
which have been matters of animated discussion in Masonic circles
during the past year; one of them was concerning the so-called prerogative of making Masons at sight, and the discussion was brought
about, as is well known, through the exercise of that prerogative by
the Grand Master of Ohio when William H. Taft, an eminent citizen
of the Republic, was created a Mason in this manner. The other subject discussed by Brother Matthews was the so-called negro question,
brought about through the controversy between the Grand Jurisdictions
of Mississippi and New Jersey on account of the negro Lodge under the
Jurisdiction of the latter State.
Our views are in accord with those of Brother Matthews upon the
subject of making Masons at sight, claimed by some to inhere as an
Ancient Landmark in the office of Grand Master. The essence of a
landmark is that it shall have existed undisputed as such for "time
whereof the memory of man runneth not to the contrary," and the
facts that it is of easy demonstration that there was a time when this
claimed prerogative did not exist and that its existence has always
been denied by certain Masons clearly disqualify this so-called prerogative for a place in the category of Ancient Landmarks.
Upon the other subject discussed by Brother Matthews, we are in
accord to this extent; we would not deny to a colored man the benefits
of the system of morality veiled in. allegory and taught by symbqls such
as Freemasonry is defined to be; but we would have him receive so
much of these benefits as it is possible for him to assimilate from this
lofty system of ethics In.Lodges of his own, chartered, perhaps, by the
so-called Prince Hall Grand Lodge. This would place him beyond the

1.50

pale of recognition of regular Masonic Bodies, and therefore limited
to Masonic Intercourse with Lodges of a derivation similar to his own,
and would still afford him whatever benefit in the way of moral up-lift
that would come to him from the study and practice of Masortic
precepts.

A few decisions of a local character were rendered by the Grand
Master, and there was a little disagreement with the Grand Lodge of
Scotland which arose from the fact that w~le a resident of Vermont
was temporarily visiting Scotland, that Jurisdiction received and accepted his petition for degrees and conferred upon him the three
degrees of Masonry, notwithstanding the fact that Vermont was his
place of residence. The correspondence between the Grand Master
of Vermont and the Grand Secretary of Scotland developed the fact
that Scotland claimed the right under its Constitution to seize upon
anythiJig, so to speak, that it found within its Jurisdiction, even though
the residence there was of the most temporary character, and declined
to render to Vermont anything in the way of satisfaction or apology of
any kind, and the Grand Master of Vermont very properly retorted
with the unvarnished statement that if the Grand Lodge of Scotland
claimed the right and the purpose to entertain petitions of men who
lived in Vermont, then, by the same rule, the Grand Lodge of Vermont •
claimed the right to refuse to recognize Masons so made, affirming
that Masons of this character might be considered Masons in Scotland,
but they would not be recognized as such in Vermont, and he thereupon issued an edict to all of the Lodges and Masons under his Jurisdiction, to hold no Masonic intercourse with the individual that had
received the degrees in Scotland, in violation of the Jurisdictional rights
of Vermont, and not to recognize that individual as a Mason unless he
receives the Masonic degrees in the regular manner, that is recognized
by the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master refers to the conference of Grand Masters held
at Philadelphia and Baltimore, and expresses his sympathy and agreement with the recommendations there adopted.
The report of the Grand Secretary shows a substantial gain in membership, with a total of nearly 13,000 Master Masons upon the rosters
of various subordinate Lodges. Brother Past Grand Master Marsh 0.

GRAND MASTl(R'S ADDRl(SS.

{\.~ in~icating the power of a kind or sympathetic word spoken at

a crucial moment when a human soul is laboring under deep oppression,
and duress, the Grand Master refers to certain events which have
occurred in his experience and as illustrating the thought that occasionally ·by giving flowers to the living, we may save ourselves the need
of tears for the dead. We quote from his address as follows :
'.'~hree. times since I was a Master Mason, and twice during my
admm1stra!ton a.s Gran? Master, I have been called upon to deliver
the Masoi:i1c burial service for one who had died by his own hand. As
I looked mto the tearful and agonized faces of the brethren assembled
on these occasions, the thought came to me with awful force that if
just one brother had been at hand at the crucial moment to offer calm
and affectionate counsel and help, the awful catastrophe might have
been prevented. We live too rtmch to ourselves. An independent man
does not seek help, in fact he often shrinks from it ; but there are
many ways in which we may give encouragement and impart mental
strength to a brother without seeming to offer it, but in order to do so
it is necessary that we keep constantly in touch 1 with the lives of those
around us. Give your flowers to the living and you will have no bitter
tears for the dead."
.

The Grand Jurisdiction of Vermont is still struggling with the
Masonic Temple debt proposition. A recommendation was made last
year by the Grand Master to increase the per capita tax for a few years
in order to liquidate the temple indebtedness carried by the Grand
Lodge. His recommendation was turned down by the Grand Lodge
and he renewed the recommendation this year in a modified form.
The Jurisdiction of Vermont appears to be very sensitive upon
the question of submitting to even a very moderate increase in the per
capita tax, and in spite of all of the influence of the Grand Master, his
recommendation was again vetoed by the Grand Lodge, and the out•
standing indebtedness against the temple appears to be in a fair way
to stand indefinitely as a Grand Lodge liability.

MASONIC HOM!l.

The Masonic Home continues to grow in the affections of the
Fraternity in Virginia, and occupies a higher position in the heart of
the Brotherhood · than ever before.
. Throughout the report of the Grand Master we catch glimpses of
his love for and devotion to the Home and find disclosed sacrifices
made by him of time and convenience wherever such sacrifices resulted in some material benefit, such as the securing of monetary contributions, to the cherished institution.
He states that of the large number of meetings of the Trustees of
the Home, he attended all save two.
The children at the institution are referred to by him as happy '
and contented and that only pleasure and satisfaction come to him
when thinking of this magnificent Grand Lodge charity. He appeals
to ~very Mason individually throughout the Jurisdiction to do at least
his mite, even if no more than a contribution of a single dollar for
the welfare of the institution, affirming, what is undoubtedly true' that
the benefit to the giver is far greater than to the orphan childre~.
From the reports of the several officers of the Home, it ·appears
that there are at present sheltered there sixty children, ranging in ages
from less than one year to ten.
The expenses of maintenance during the preceding year was something in excess of $10,000, and the accumulated funds to the credit of
the institution exceed $29,000. Now that the Home is under the full ·

J,odge full responsibility for its management, we may confidently predict for it in the future a career of increasing and expanding usefulness.

the three degrees at one special meeting, and without a special dispensation upon the candidate, resl!lting, as it did, in imposing upon the
Lodge and upon Masonry, a member against whom there had been
objection whereby the sacred landmarks of the Institution had been
violated: Grand M<1ster Eggleston's inclination was to immediately
arrest the charter of the Lodge and inflict merited punishment upon
the offenders, but his sympathetic heart softened when the Master
of the Lodge contritely confessed his grievous fault, professing innocence, however, as to any improper motive, and pleaded ignorance of
the law as to his excuse and at the same time set forth the very great
injury and hardship that would, if tpe charter were arrested, be visited
upon the old and true' members of the Lodge, genuine Masons in every
sense of the wprd. Finally, in view of all of the circllmstances and
the Worshipful Master's pleading, the Grand Master relaxed the grim
determinatiQn he had felt to inflict discipline upon the Lodge, and was
finally satisfied in administering i11 a public manner a severe and
searching reprimand.
Old records of a well nigh invaluable character were recovered
in the year through the discovery of their existence by the Grand
Master while he was in Philadelppia, supplemented by the generosity
of the Grand Librarian, Julius Fachse, wlio advanced the very considerable sum of money demanded for their surrender, the records being the Secretary's book of I):ilwinning Crosse l 1odge, No. 2, Port
Royal of Virginia, going back from 1859 ~o 1754, which books were
stolen at some time during the Civil War from that Lodge. These
books constitute an almost invaluable addition to the museum attached
to the Grand Lodge of Virginia, which historically is perhaps the most
interesting of any· Alllerican Grand Lodge.

MASONIC HOME.

Some seventeen or eighteen years ago, the initial step was taken
In the creation of a fund designated as Masonic Home Fund, to be
utilized ultimately for the purpose of establishing a Masonic Home in
the Jurisdiction of Washington. The growth of the Fund has been
comparatively slow, and there has been manifested upon several occasions a disposition to abandon the idea of a Masonic Home and use
the fund or the int:ome therefrom for the general charitable purposes
of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master, in his address reminds the brethren that if
they are serious in regard to their declarations of purpose to establish
and maintain a Masonic Home, they have been certainly very deliberate in their movements, and recommends either that the assessments
should be increased, or some other plan should be devised to accumulate funds.
The recommendation of, the Grand Master provoked discussion
upon the subject, and as a result of that discussion, the following resolution was adopted:
"Resolved That the Finance Committee be and is hereby in~tructed
to secure tenders or offers of a site for a Masonic Home., together with
prices and terms. and report same to the Grand Lodge at its next
Annual Communication."
From which it would appear that a definite step is now about to
be taken toward the actual consummation of the Home proposition.

The question of the use of "ciphers" in the Jurisdiction continues

the Grand Master has this to say:
"I regret that I am compelled to speak to you about the matter of
the use of Ciphers in this Jurisdiction.
"It has frequently been reported to me that Masons are using
them, even in open Lodge.
"Our law on this subject, contained in Section 108, 108a, 108b
nnd 108c of the Code, seems inadequate, and I would recommend that
the law be amended, making it a Masonic offense, punishable by suspension or expulsion, for any Mason to use a Cipher in the Lodgeroom, or in the instruction of a candidate; and that a Master or other
officer of a Lodge violating such a law shall be suspended from office."

officers of the Lodge, certifying to their proficiency before their installation."
One may be permitted to admire his honesty in practically admitting that he favors a cipher, yet we must express some wonder

be esoteric inflexible in his position that the esoteric work should be
transmitted only from mouth to ear, according to the ancient tradition, should countenance anything in the nature of a proposition of
reducing this work to written or printed characters.

Pro Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Right Rev.
C. 0. L. Riley, Lord Bishop of Perth, being temporarily absent in the

From the date of the organization of this Grand Lodge, in 1900,
to the present year, there has been unremitting conflict between the
Grand Lodge of Scotland and the Grand Lodge of Western Australia,
Scotland having persistently refused to recognize the Grand Lodge of
Western Australia as an independent Grand Lodge, and during the
ten years of this strife, persisted in erecting Lodges of her own in
the territory of Western Australia, which resulted in a vast amount
of bitterness and friction, but steps which were initiated in 1907 looking to an adjustment of the difference between the two Jurisdictions
and the withdrawal of Scotland's claim of the right to plant Lodges
in Western Australia,_ resulted in an adjustment of the differences between the two Jurisdictions, and the final full recognition by Scotland
of the Grand Lodge of Western Australia as an independent sovereign
Grand Lodge, and at the Quarterly Communication, held July 23rd, the
principal business transacted was a ratification of the Treaty of Recognition, so to speak, and the reception by the Grand Lodge in an official manner of representatives from the Grand Lodge of Scotland.
Upon this point, we quote · from the Grand Master's address as
foll ows:
"To-night, for the first time in the history of our Grand Lodge,
we will have with us in the}r o~cial capacity .the representatives of the
Grand Lodge of Scotland m this State. This marks the happy close
of a long and acrimonious dispute which has done great injury to the
Craft, but we hope an injury which is not beyond repair. Let .each
and all of us extend a most cordial and fraternal welcome to the
Scottish representatives and show by our warmth of feeling that no
effort will be wanting on our part to heal the sores and misunderstandings of the past."

"A pilgrim once, so runs an ancient tale,
Old, worn and spent, crept down a shadowed vale.
On either hand rose mountains bleak and high;
Chill was the heavy air, and dark the sky;
The path was rugged and his feet were bare;
His faded cheek was seamed with pain and care ;
His heavy eyes upon the ground were cast,
And every step seemed feebler than the last.
The valley ended where a naked rock
Rose sheer from earth to heaven, as if to mock
The pilgrim who had crept that toilsome way;
But while his dimmed and weary eyes essay
To find an outlet in the mountain side, .
A ponderous, ~culptored, brazen door he spied;
And tottering towards it, with fast-falling breath,
Above the portal read : 'The Gate of Death.'
"He could not stay his feet that led thereto;
It yielded to his touch; and passing through,
He came into a world all bright and fair ;
Blue were the skies, and balmy was the air.
And lo ! the blood of youth flowed through his veins,
And he was clad in robes that had no stains
Of his long pilgrimage. Amazed, he turned,
And lo ! a golden door behind him burned
In that fair sunlight, and his wandering eyes,
Now lustrous and clear as those blue skies,
Freed from the mists of age and care and strife,
Over the portal read: 'The Gate of Life.'"

During the preceding year Quarterly Communications, as usual,
were held by the Grand Lodge of Western Australia; one July 23,

the last Quarterly Communication for the year, which is also styled
the Annual Communication; was held April 22, 1909.
Reports of various Grand Officers are made at all of the Quarterly Communications and the several Communications appear to be
of practically the same importance, the one with the other.
The Communication of July and October were presided over by
Most Worshipful Brother, The Honorable N. J. Moore, C. M. G.,

The entire session was devoted . practically to addresses by representatives of the two Grand Jurisdictions, Scotland and Western Australia, filled with mutual felicitations, expressions of good will, etc.
The Quarterly Communication of October was held as usual in the
Goldfields at Boulder.
Reports were received at this time from the various Financial
Boards, and the Board of . General Purposes reported also that it was
with the greatest possible pleasure that they stated that the Articles of
Recognition agreed to by the Grand Lodge had been received, duly
executed by the Grand Master Mason of Scotland, with an accompanying fraternal letter, soliciting an exchange of representatives, etc.
This was the last and final official touch whereby the full and complete independence of the Grand Lodge of Western Australia was recognized by Scotland.
The Quarterly Communication of January, 1909, was presided over
by the Grand Master, the Most Worshipful C. 0. L. Riley, Lord Bishop

MASONIC CHARITY.

•

The only official Charity connected with the Grand Lodge is the
standing committee of the Grand Lodge known as "Committee on
Grand Lodge Educational Fund."
There appears to have been disbursed from this fund for the
year, to one worthy applicant, the orphart of a deceased Master Mason,
the sum of $150, and so far as disclosed by the Grand Lodge reports,
this was all that was done last year by the Grand' Lodge in the way
of charity. Two hundred and fifty dollars, however, appear to have
been expended for a banquet at this Communication of the Grand
Lodge, the appropriation for this purpose this year having been $50
in excess of the appropriation of the same purpose a year ago.
It is worthy of comment that of the 141 subordinate Lodges in
the Jurisdiction, 140 were represented at this Communication, a percentage of attendance, we are sure, unequaled by any other Jurisdiction in the United States; and there is a lingering suspicfon that it is
the annual Grand Lodge Feast that brings out what is nearly a hundred
per cent attendance.
As noted by us last year, when reviewing the proceedings of this
Grand Lodge, we are struck by the relatively large compensation paid
the Grand Treasurer. The total income last year of the Grand !,odge
of West Virginia was something in excess of $9,000, and the total
disbursements something in excess of $6,000. The compensation
awarded th~ Grand Tre:tsu-ter was $471, being apparently 5 per cent,
or tnereanonts, of the income ; or, upon the basis 9f outgo, about 7
per cent of the expenditures.

Ohio, just across the river from West Virginia, has a membership of 76,000, as against 13,000 in West Virginia, and has a Grand.
Lodge income of about $60,000, against the $9,000 or more in West
Virginia. The Grand Treasurer of Ohio last year received $150 for'
services. California, with a Grand Lodge income, including the portion belonging to the Masonic Home, of over $80,000, the Grand
Treasurer receives, we believe, $200.
It is nobody's concern, outside of West Virginia, what that Jurisdiction pays to its Grand Treasurer, and the· matter is mentioned
simply because it is unique. The Grand Treasurer's salary is more
than three times the amount expended by the Grand Lodge for charity.
Another feature of West Virginia Masonry is its marked activity
in the display of that function which remains as a relic of the operative days of our institution ; i. e. its activity in laying corner stones, '
no less than fifteen Special Grand Communications being held within
the year for that purpose, which is evidence, either that West Virginia ·
is enjoying an unexampled era of prosperity, or that the Grand Lodge
is called upon' to officiate in a large number of comparatively unimportant cases.

the occasion of the making of William H. Taft a mason at sight. He,
in common 'with most every other Grand M.aster who accepted that
invitation, approved the Grand Master's action and fully endorsed
the claim that making a Mason at sight is one of the prerogatives inherent in the office of Grand Master and is .one of the landmarks.
Grand Master Showalter is against class legislation, and for that
reason is not in favor of Grand Lodge laws prohibiting any class of
people, like, say, saloon keepers, from becoming members of the fraternity, his conception of our institution being that, without any special
class legislation, any person engaged in any nefarious business, whatever it may be, is excluded under the ancient regulation th.at a candidate for admission to our mysteries must be "under the tongue of
good report,'' and Grand Master Showalter in his position upon this
question is pretty nearly right.
Another matter upon which he is outspoken is the relation of the
so-called Order of the Eastern Star to Masonry. He is unable to
figure out that female Masonry is of much account anyway, and that,
in so far as it produces jealousies and provokes controversies as to
social distinctions, etc., among Masons, or their families, it is a bad
thing. The Grand Master's comments upon the Order of the Eastern
Star and class legislation are certainly refreshing.

GRAND LODGE CHARITY FUNI>.

The worthy distressed Masons, the distressed widows and orphans
of Masons, not providred foc directly by the subordinate Lodges, are
taken care of, so far as the fund will permit, by means of the Charity
Fund of the Grand Lodge. This is replenished each year by an
assessment of lOc upon each member, and the 24,946 members in the
Jurisdiction contributed, therefore, toward the Charity Fund about

$2,500.

The utmost frugality appears to rule in the administration of
the Charity Fund, and in this great Jurisdiction there appears during
the preceding year to have been only twenty beneficiaries sufficiently
worthy to entitle them to the consideration of the Committee on
Charity, and from the $2,400 placed to the credit of the Charity Fund,
by means of the assessment of 10 cents per member, $1,775 was used;
certainly an exceedingly economical administration of one of the great
functions of our fraternity.
. Figura-ively speaking, Wisconsin is in no immediate danger of
.dying from hypertrophy of the heart induced by the surging cuHents
of benevolence.

A Past Grand Master's Jewel was presented at this Communication to Past Grand Master Spencer M. Marsh, the presentation ad- .
dress having been delivered by Brother Alexander E. Matheson,
which contains a few gems of rhetoric that are worth repeating. w~'
quote a portion of his remarks, as follows :
"It is not an evidence of weakness or vanity that men and women
admire and wish to possess jewels and golden emblems and ornaments.
Such a desire is not necessarily a love of display. The savage is
content with gaudy decorations of very little value. He is satisfied
if they shine and glitter. The civilized man must have ornaments of
value and artistic worth, if he is to be satisfied.
"Gems gather the light and reflect it in myriad forms of beauty.
Henry Ward Beecher was an admirer of gems and a connoisseur
as to their value. He used to carry them unset in his pocket, and
take them out and admire them from time to time. Gold is the most
beautiful and most useful of metals. It is the unit by which the·
leading nations of the world measure values. It withstands the strongest acids. In the Book of Revelation, we read that the streets of the
New Jerusalem are of pure gold. The walls and gates of the city
are described as constructed of the richest gems. These expressions
may be merely figurative, but they were used by the writer to convey
in the strongest terms possible his ideas as to the beauty, richness and
glory of the Eternal City.
"Na tu re has labored for millions of years to produce the diamond,
and to store the gold in the rocks and mountains. God has surrounded us with riches untold and with beauty inexpressible. Gold
and jewels are· bnt types and evidences of His power, wisdom and love.
"The finest thing that can be said of a man is that his character
is pure gold or that he .is like the diamond, either in the rough or
polished. If in the rough, he has not had the advantages of training
and culture; if polished, he has had the benefits of training. In either
case, the diamond expresses in the highest terms his character."

Notice was taken of the fact of the consolidation of the t~o
Grand Lodges of Indian Territory and the Territory of Oklahoma
into the new Grand Lodge of the State of Oklahoma, whereby the
latter Grand Lodge succeeded to all of the rights belonging to the
former Grand Lodge, including the right of fraternal recognition.
On the last day of the Communication, the Grand Lodge was
favored with a short address by Brother Vincent Lamber Tissera,
member of an Iowa Lodge, although a native of Ceylon. He was
accorded courteous attention and stated that his desire in life was
to arouse the American people to a better understanding of his mother
country, India, and of his native land, Ceylon, and to make clear the
fact that the inhabitants of those countries are not all heathens and
uncivilized, but that they have the record of a thousand years of culture and refinement and are of the same Aaryan Race, with the same
blood running in their veins as in ours. Masonry, he stated, appealed
to him strongly, as th e institution stands for universal brotherhood
and the highest type of manhood.

FRA1'ERNAL CORRESPONDENCE.

The report on Fraternal Correspondence is by that accomplished
Masonic scholar Most Worshipful Aldro Jenks.
He treats ~he usual reports of proceedings of American and
foreign Grand Lodges with discriminating judgment, and with a genuine
spirit of courtesy.
.
We do not happen to be in accord with him upon the subiect of
Masonic Homes but upon the point that this method of discharging
the charity obli~ations of a Grand Lodge is an expensive one, we are
in perfect agreement with him.
He is inclined to refer to anything in connection with reports of
committees on Masonic Homes that indicates an absence of perfect
satisfaction as evidence 'that the Masonic Home idea is a failure.
Under the caption of California, reference is made to the remarks of the Grand Master and the report of the Committee to the
effect that the Home was ~ot entirely satisfactory, and seizes upon
the opportunity to call our attention to the f~ct that in .Wisconsin
10 cents per capita was found to be amply suffic1e.nt to prov1~e for ~he.
charity needs of the Grand Lodge, with the imphed conclusion, wh1cn
we are permitted to draw, that if we would do likewise there would
be an immense saving in expense.
The expression of dissatisfaction over anything is simply an expression of that discontent inherent in the idea of progress. Perfect
satisfaction in this world with anything is well nigh impossible. We
suppose even the Masons of Wisconsin may not .be. fully satisfied w~th
the charity administration of the Grand Lodge hm1ted to a p~r ca~1ta
of 10 cents, and when we of California .express a lack of sat1sfact1on
with our Masonic Home work, it is because we are moving upward
and have not yet arrived at that period of stagnation where we suppose it might be possible to say that we are satisfied. Masonry itself
is not a system of perfected truth. It is not as a diamond cut and
fixed but rather as a plant that grows, and so long as there is life
ther: is growth, and so long as there is still an elei;ient of di~sati~­
faction with what we have done or what we are domg, there is stt11
hope f~r advancement and growth.

"I wish at this time to bring to the attention of every member

as generally as it should be. I would strongly urge all present to
bring this to the attention of the members at home, and encourage
the reading of this document by every brother."

The assets of the Home now amount to $60,437.23, and it enjoyed

Some four years ago a Committee appears to have been appointed
by the Grand Lodge for the purpose of obtaining tabulated statements
and intimate information in reference to subordinate Lodges.
This Committee appears to have taken ample time in which to
prepare their report, but when it was finally rendered at this Annual
Communication, it contained information of a character that is little
short of sensational, and one may be permitted to express astonishment that in an enlightened American Jurisdiction such as Wisconsin
such practices as are set forth by the Committee could possibly be
indulged in, and we almost gasp with amazement when we reflect
upon the fact that such irregularities could take place in a Jurisdiction adorned by Masons of the character of the eminent Chairman of
the Committee on Foreign Correspondence and others.
Here are some of the irregularities reported by this Special Committee of the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin, and in considering this report, one must remember that he is not reading about Patagonia or
Kamchatka, but about the great and enlightened and sovereign State
of Wisconsin. Here are some of the practices, and they are all set
forth in the quoted words of the Committee:
"INNOVATIONS IN RITUAL.

"The laws of the Grand Lodge forbid the making of any innova!
tions in the Ritual. The Ritual was adopted by the Grand Lodge and

"VIOLATION OF JURISDICTION.

"The Grand Lodge has enacted a law making it unconstitutional
for Lodges to make agreements among themselves regarding territorial
jurisdiction. A few Lodges are violating this law. One Lodge in
particular has by resolution permitted material residing in its own
Jurisdiction to petition another. Lodge in the Jurisdiction of which
the petitioner does not reside. By this agreement the fees are shared.
"LODGES NOT PROPERLY OPENED, NONE OF THE THREE PRINCIPAL OFFICERS
BEING PRESENT.

"There are sever~! Lodges that were not properly opened, due
to the fact that none of the three principal officers were present.
"LODGES WHO CHANGE WORK TO GET GOOD STAGE EFFECT.

"In a number of Lodges stage settings, paraphernalia, robes, lanterns and other accompaniments are used in the Masonic ceremonies.
In some of these Lodges an effort is made to give the esoteric work
dramatic effect, and from this effort results a transposition of the
Ritual that the best stage effect may be obtained.
"OFFICERS WHO OMIT IMPORTANT LECTURES AND THUS MAR THE WORK.

"In some Lodges the custom prevails of omitting parts of the
esoteric work, and the monitorial work almost entirely. It appears
that in one Lodge three candidates were being initiated the same evening; and as it grew late, instead of finishing the work and giving each
candidate the work complete, it was deferred until some subsequent
communication. Several Worshipful Masters deem it one of their
prerogatives when the hour is late to omit portions of the work.
"USE AND MISUSE OF MUSIC,

"It has come to the knowledge of your committee that in one
Lodge no less than fourteen different songs were rendered during the
conferring of the Master's Degree.
"TALKING OF LODGE MATTERS TO PROFANES.

"In some instances Lodge affairs are as well known to the profane
as they are to the members of the Lodge.
"AFFILIATING MEMBERS WITHOUT PETITION OR BALLOT.

"In several Lodges petitions for membership are not used. Masons
wishing to affiliate are simply balloted on, without report of an investigating committee, and in some cases the <limit is simply presented
and action taken on the <limit.

"The report shows that in one instance a member of a Lodge
so far forgot his Masonic obligations as to threaten another member'
