"LODGE OPENED WITHOUT PRAYER.

"The landmarks of Freemasonry suggest that no Masonic Lodge
should ever be opened without invocation. It has been the custom for
ages to do so and should never be deviated from. We have a number of Lodges where Masters omit this custom, feeling that it is
unnecessary.
"MASTER INTOXICATED WHIU: PRESIDING.

"There are a few Lodges in the State where the Master has been
under the influence of liquor while presiding as Master of his Lodge
in conferring· the degrees.
"MODERNIZING FREEMASONRY.

"There came to our notice in connection with this report an instance where a Master Mason who previpus to becoming a Mason had
been prominent in other societies. Being ambitious, in due course of
time he was elected Worshipful Master of his Lodge. Upon his
assuming the important duties of Master he proceeded to ignore the
beaten path of his predecessors and sought to conduct the business
affairs of the Lodge as well as the conferring of the degrees in keeping with the ideas he had absorbed in these modern societies.
"CIPHER KEYS.

"It is unfortunate that we have Masters of Lodges who, when
they were made Masons, were probably po$ted by some brother who
owned a cipher key in 'fee simple' or had opportunity for reference
to such a key. Under these peculiar conditions such officers feel that
they have the correct work and consequently when the Grand Lecturer
visits such Lodges officers of this class are indifferent to in&truction.''

When one reflects upon the amount of the annual dues charged
Wisconsin Masons to enable them to benefit humanity in general and
distressed Masons in particular, we are constrained to repress any
expression of surprise that the per capita tax contributed to the
Grand Lodge Charity Fund is only 10 cents; and while we would not
under any circumstances question the belief expressed by the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence in his review of California,
that every Wisconsin Lodge is at all times adequate to the performnnce of the charitable obligations imposed upon it to afford relief to
nil worthy indigent members of the Lodge, no matter whether domiciled within Wisconsin, or in some foreign Jurisdiction, yet we are
forced to the conclusion that the requirements of the indigent members would need to be judged upon an extremely frugal and slender
basis.

MASONIC HOME.

Even in the Jurisdiction of Wyoming, which has a total membership of only 2,400, about one-third of the number of Masons that
reside within the City and County of San Francisco, it has become· a
settled purp9se to establish a Masonic Home, and a per capita tax
upon the membership of SO cents was voted about three years ago,
and a fund has already been accumulated, amounting to approx'imately $3,000.
Among the recommendations made by the Grand Master in his
annual address at this Communication is the following:
"That we take active steps at once to procure a si~e for a Mas?:r:iic
Home, by trying to get donations therefor from different localities
within our Jurisdiction., that the. same be secured so as to. be submitted to the next meetmg of this Grand Body. ~ ma~e this. r~co.m­
mendation as I find there are several members m this Junsd1ctton
who would like to enter such a Home."·
In pursuance of this recommendation the following resolution was
unanimously adopted :
"Resolved That a committee of three members be appointed as a
Committee on' Masonic Home, and they be instructed to follow out
the recommendation of the Grand Master and report at the next Annual
Communication of this Grand Lodge."
We have no doubt that a Home will shortly be established in
Wyoming, and it will unquestionably reflect credit upon the stalwart
type of Masonry of that Jurisdiction.

The Grand Master manifested commendable zeal and activity in
visiting the subordinates of his Jurisdiction, and, in view of the long
distance separating the Lodges of this Juris.diction, the Grand Master,
in visiting the majority of the subordinate Lodges, does so at the cost
of much time and inconvenience to himself and is, therefore, entitled
to especial praise.
The Grand Master refers to the efforts made in the past by
spurious Masons to establish clandestine l.;odges, and, in order to
make this nefarious practice more difficult in the future, the Grand
Master, by proper presentation of the matter to the Legislature,
caused a law to be enacted, patterned after the New York law upon
the same subject, making it a penal offense for any person to go
about the State organizing spurious or clandestine Lodges, or selling
degrees of ·any kind, which no doubt would have the effect of stopping
performances of this kind in the future.

''Again, and. for the twenty-fourth time, we have performed the

In the Grapd Jurisdiction of Maryland there is no Jurisprudence
Committee, and for the quarter of a century of the incumbency of
Grand Master Shryock as chief official of the Craft he has never
rendered a single decision on Masonic law, the law in Maryland being
so well established and so thoroughly known that no decisions or
Interpretations have been necessary.
P:ENNSYLVANIA,

Pennsylvania has no Jurisprudence Committee and the decisions
of the Grand Master are not subject to even consideration by the
Grand Lodge, but are final and stand as the law of the Jurisdiction,
unless and until reversed or annulled by some succeeding Grand
Master.
This jurisdiction also is noted as possessing the most costly and
beautiful and most magnificent Masonic Temple in the world. Pennsylvania also lays claim to the distinction of being the first American
colony in which Freemasonry was established. This claim is stoutly
controverted by Massachusetts, which maintains that the oldest Masonic
Lodge in America, possessing continuous existence, is St. John's Lodge
of Boston, with unbroken records running back to 1733. The claim
of Pennsylvania, fortified by the recent discovery of certain manuscripts, is to the effect that a regular Masonic Lodge (St. John's
Lodge) was in active operation in 1727, seven years prior to the
establishment of St. John's Lodge of Boston, and that in the Province
of Pennsylvania a Grand Lodge was in existence as early as 1731, being
the third Grand Lodge in the world, having been preceded only by
that of England, ·established in 1717, and of Ireland, in 1729.
The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, if there was a Grand Lodge
as early as 1731, was formed, the same as the Grand Lodge of England, through the voluntary coming together of previously existing,
regular Masonic Lodges, and it is not wholly improbable that Lodges
of this character existed in both Massachusetts and Philadelphia even
prior to the year 1727, the alleged date of the establishment in Philadelphia of St. John's Lodg~.

United Grand Lodge of England, with subordinates in every 4uarter
of the Globe, is that of New York, with a membership of 163,341;
the United Grand Lodge of England having a membership, according
to the figures taken from the calender for 1909, issued by the International Office for Masonic Intercourse, Neuchatel, Switzerland, of
152,000 ; and it ·may be also of interest to know that the Grand
Lodge o( Scotland, supposed to be one of the greatest in the world,

MASONIC HOMES.

We have to a certain extent made a feature in our reviews of
Masonic Hom~s, because of all the practical questions with which our
American Grand Jurisdictions have to deal the Masonic Home is preeminent and by far the greatest.
T'he Masonic Home proposition is not recommended as an income saver, nor because of intrinsic economy, for, as a matter of
fact, it involves a large initial expense and an increasing outlay from
year to year. Nevertheless it is unquestionably the only means of
accomplishing certain absolutely necessary work in large Jurisdictions ; and the first question to consider is, Is the Masonic Home
idea right? and, if so, the matter of expense is only secondary; and
when consideration is given to the splendid achievements of such
homes as exist in North Carolina and Texas and Kentucky and Missouri and New York and Kansas, and many other ::?tatei;, in making
grand and noble and useful men and women out of homeless, helpless, deserted waifs that would otherwise, most likely, drift into the
slums of society, or be swallowed up in the eddies and whirlpools of
vice and dissipation, we are satisfied that, no matter what the expense may be of maintaining our orphanages and Masonic Homes,
they are essential to the fulfillment of our obligations, and in their
maintenance we may justly feel a glow of pride and satisfaction.
Another eleq'irnt to be considered in this connection is that one
is raised by raising others, and, in maintaining a system of Masonic
charity that involves some sacrifice and effort · on the part of the
giver, he is a sharer in the good which his beneficence accomplishes',
and the moral uplift imparted to him in giving is of as much value
as is the sense of gratitude created in the beneficiary in receiving.
To illustrate this point, we invite the attention of our reader!
to an incident which occurred in the Grand Jurisdiction of New Yori<:
in its last Annual Communicatbn, set forth in our review of that
Jurisdictibn for the current year:
Ninety-two children from the Masonic Home at Utica, without
previous notice, appeared before the Grand Lodge by arrangement

made with the officers of the Home and the chief Grand Officers, and
rendered before the Grand Lodge a literary and musical program <?f
rare excellence, creating as they did a deep impression, and on the
following morning, upon the reassembling of the Grand · Lodge, · a
member arose in the midst of the Grand Body and stated that, ·s tirred

wished, on behalf, first, of the Masters of his District, to contribut~

who was not a Mason, but who had seen the children on the pre-•
vious day, another $100; and, finally, on behalf of himself, another
$100, making $400 in all.
The record of the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge tells us that
the scenes upon 'the floor of the .Grand Lodge, after the brother had
taken his seat, beggared description; and member after member, Lodge
after Lodge, District after District, demanded the privilege of contributing to this fund, and before the incident was closed more than
$17,000 had been cast upon the altar, so to speak, as a free-will offering
to the children of the Home, and while the children were thereby
immensely· benefited in the possibilities of the good that can come
to them through the use of this large sum of money, the greatest good
resulted to the givers, whose hearts were touched by love for the
fatherless, motherless children.
To any Jurisdiction 'a n incident such as this, because of the
moral enthusiasm it awakens, is above a money value. To loosen
the purse 'strinR"S it is only necessary to touch the heart, and God
pity the Mason or the body of Masons, that is never privileged to
sacrifice to the sentiment of compassion and love.

MAKING MASONS AT SIGHT.

The action of the Grand Master of Ohio in exercising his prerogative of making a Mason at sight of William H. Taft, an eminent
citizen of the Republic, caused a great deal of discussion throughout
the American Jurisdictions of this so-called prerogative of the Grand
Master.
The Grand Master of Ohio was clearly within his legal rights,
because the Constitution of that State expressly recognizes this prero~ative as belonging to the Grand Master, and upon general principles the weight of opinion seems to be in favor of this so-called
landmark.
While our own particular views may not be of importance, we
disagree with the majority of current opinion upon this subject. The
essence of a landmark is that it shall have existed undisputed as such
by recognized authorities for "time whereof the memory of man runneth not to the contrary," and the facts that it is of easy demonstration
that there was a time when this so-called prerogative did not exist,
anJ further that its existence has always been denied by recognized
Ma~onic scholars, clearly disqualify this so-called prerogative of making a Mason at sight for a place in the category of Ancient Landmarks.
NEGRO MASONRY.

One of the subjects very generally discussed by Correspondence
Committees during the past year related to the Coqferences held at
Philadelphia, and later at Baltimore, of Grand :Masters. The recommendations of these Conferences amount'~d, to atf "intents and purposes, simply to a reaffirmation of practices already almost universally
existing in all of the American Grand Jurisdictions. The only recommendation, the adoption of which would render uniform a variety of
practices concerning the matter, was to the effect that penal jurisdiction over rejected candidates for degrees should be fixed at a period
of five years.
The most significant action taken at the Baltimore Conference
was a resolution, unanimously adopted, to the effect that the meetings were not intended, either directly or indirectly, to foster or
encourage the idea of a General Grand Lodge; and .further posi-
